sweep.angle: Classical small-array beamforming for 2 microphones: delay-and-sum, superdirective/MVDR with a diffuse-noise model, first-order and adaptive differential arrays, GSC/LCMV (including the two-talker constraint), geometry-free RTF estimation, and robustness (WNG, mismatch calibration, spacing/aliasing at 16 kHz). Numbers are quantified for 2 INMP441s 2.5–6 cm apart.

sources.title: Practical supergain
sources.authors: H. Cox, R. M. Zeskind, T. Kooij
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing 34(3):393–398. Companion paper: Cox, Zeskind & Owen, 'Robust adaptive beamforming', IEEE TASSP 35(10):1365–1376, 1987, doi 10.1109/TASSP.1987.1165054
sources.key_idea: Superdirective beams (maximum directivity, i.e. MVDR against a diffuse-noise model) on small arrays are only usable under a white-noise-gain (WNG) constraint. The constraint is implemented as diagonal loading. 1/WNG is the array's sensitivity to uncorrelated errors: self-noise and gain, phase and position errors. The 1987 companion paper applies the same constraint to adaptive MVDR.
sources.algorithm: Per STFT bin f (16 kHz, 512-pt FFT, hop 128–256): steering vector a(f,θ)=[1, exp(+j2πf·d·cosθ/c)]^T, with θ measured from the mic axis. Diffuse coherence Γ12=sinc(2fd/c) (numpy.sinc), Γ=[[1,Γ12],[Γ12,1]]. Weights w=(Γ+μI)^-1 a / (a^H(Γ+μI)^-1 a). DF=|w^H a|²/(w^H Γ w); WNG=|w^H a|²/(w^H w). Choose μ(f) by bisection over log10 μ in [-9,6] so that WNG ≥ WNG_min: bus −15…−20 dB below 500 Hz, meeting room −3…−6 dB. For N=2 the endfire limit is DF=N²=4 (6.02 dB, hypercardioid). Broadside DF→1 (0 dB) at low frequency.
sources.bus_relevance: This is the core fixed beam. With the mic axis pointed at the active partner, my numpy evaluation (ideal match, free field, spherically diffuse noise, ANSI S3.5 1/3-octave band-importance weighting 160 Hz–8 kHz) gives an AI-weighted DI of 5.15/4.97/4.62 dB at d=2.5/4/6 cm with WNG ≥ −10 dB. Against horizontal-only (2-D isotropic) babble it is 4.0/3.8/3.6 dB. Low WNG floors are affordable on a bus because ambient noise (~70–80 dBA) is far above INMP441 self-noise (EIN ≈ 94−61 = 33 dBA).
sources.meeting_relevance: Steer to the active talker's DOA. Late reverberation is close to diffuse, so DRR improves by about the DI. At 4 cm and WNG ≥ −10 dB the AI-DI is 5.0 dB on-axis, 4.3 at 30°, 3.6 at 45°, 2.6 at 60° and 1.0 at 90°. At WNG ≥ −3 dB it is 4.3, 3.8, 3.1, 2.3 and 1.0 dB. A floor of −3…−6 dB is needed because 35–45 dBA HVAC is close to the mic noise floor: output hiss rises by |WNG| dB in bins where the floor is active.
sources.two_mic_reality: Per-frequency DI at d=4 cm with WNG ≥ −10 dB: 2.3 dB @150 Hz, 3.9 @250, 6.0 @500, 5.9 @1k, 5.4 @2k, 4.5 @3k, 3.3 @4k, and 2.5–3.5 dB from 5–8 kHz (DSB-like above c/2d = 4.3 kHz). With WNG ≥ −20 dB, 6 dB is reached down to 150 Hz. Expect 0.5–1.5 dB less in the field (non-ideal noise field, device-body scattering, residual mismatch). The main failure mode is uncalibrated mismatch: at 250 Hz with a −20 dB floor, a fixed −1 dB/−10° error turns +6.0 dB into −3.1 dB in my simulation.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy/scipy, about 40 lines (weight design plus scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT analysis/synthesis); real-time on an M1. For test scenes, pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 (PyPI, May 2026; cp312–cp314 macOS universal2 wheels ≈1.1 MB; deps numpy/scipy) simulates 2-mic rooms with image-method RIRs.

sources.title: Adaptive microphone array (US Patent 5,473,701) — the Elko adaptive first-order differential microphone
sources.authors: J. Cezanne, G. W. Elko (AT&T Bell Labs). The same algorithm was published as G. W. Elko & A.-T. Nguyen Pong, 'A simple adaptive first-order differential microphone', IEEE WASPAA 1995
sources.venue: US Patent 5,473,701 (filed Nov 5 1993, granted Dec 5 1995, now expired); IEEE ASSP Workshop on Applications of Signal Processing to Audio and Acoustics (WASPAA) 1995
sources.key_idea: Two omni mics form back-to-back cardioids by delay-and-subtract. One scalar β mixes them into any first-order pattern. NLMS adaptation of β minimizes output power, and the constraint 0 ≤ β ≤ 1 keeps the null in the rear half-plane, so the front is never nulled. A subband version uses one β per band.
sources.algorithm: T=d/c. c_F(n)=x1(n)−x2(n−T); c_B(n)=x2(n)−x1(n−T); y=c_F−β·c_B. NLMS update β ← β+μ·y·c_B/(⟨c_B²⟩+ε), then clip β to [0,1]. Low-frequency pattern: y ∝ [(1−β)+(1+β)cosθ]/2, with the null at θn=arccos((β−1)/(β+1)) and a rear (180°) response of −β. β=0 gives a cardioid (null 180°, DI 4.77 dB); β≈0.27 a supercardioid (125°, 5.7 dB); β=0.5 a hypercardioid (109.5°, 6.0 dB; rear lobe −6 dB); β=1 a dipole/figure-8 (90°, 4.77 dB). Follow with a first-order integrator/low-pass EQ, since the differential response rises 6 dB/oct, and band-limit. Patent example: d=1.5 cm, fs=22.05 kHz (T = 1 sample), 5 kHz LPF, block average N=1000; subband variant with M=32 polyphase bands, per-band β and μ=0.1. STFT form: C_F=X1−X2·e^{−j2πfT}, C_B=X2−X1·e^{−j2πfT}, with β(f) per bin.
sources.bus_relevance: The figure-8 (β=1) is the classical pattern for two people facing each other. It passes both ends equally and nulls the broadside plane; Shure's polar-pattern guide notes a figure-8 has the same ambient pickup as a cardioid. For two partners, do not let β adapt freely, because it would null the partner at 180°. Use β=1 during double-talk, or β≈0.5 toward whichever partner is talking (the other stays at −6 dB). If adapting at all, constrain β to [0.5,1] and freeze adaptation while either partner speaks. Adaptive β only pays off against one dominant lateral interferer per band, such as a loud neighbour.
sources.meeting_relevance: Adaptive null steering is harmful with 20 talkers, because it nulls whoever is not in front. Use only fixed first-order patterns, chosen by beam selection.
sources.two_mic_reality: The fixed two-talker (dipole-like) beam gives an AI-DI of 3.6 dB at 4 cm with WNG ≥ −10 dB, and 4.1–4.4 dB at 2.5–4 cm with WNG ≥ −20 dB, against 3-D diffuse noise. Against horizontal babble it gives only 2.2–2.8 dB. The dipole needs WNG ≈ −16 dB at 300 Hz (4 cm). In my simulation, ±1 dB/±3° mismatch fills its broadside null from −19 dB to −10 dB at 300 Hz. At 16 kHz, T for 4 cm is 1.87 samples, which is fractional, so use the STFT domain.
sources.implementation: numpy STFT implementation, about 60 lines: per-bin β with NLMS plus EQ; trivially real-time.

sources.title: Study and Design of Differential Microphone Arrays
sources.authors: J. Benesty, J. Chen
sources.venue: Springer Topics in Signal Processing, vol. 6 (book)
sources.key_idea: A frequency-domain, null-constraint design of differential microphone arrays (DMAs). First-order patterns (dipole, cardioid, hypercardioid, supercardioid) are analysed by beampattern, directivity factor and WNG. Robust minimum-norm DMAs trade extra microphones for better WNG.
sources.algorithm: For M=2, per bin solve [a(f,0°)^H; a(f,θ_null)^H]·w=[1;0], with θ_null = 90° (dipole), 109.5° (hypercardioid), 125.3° (supercardioid) or 180° (cardioid). Directivity factors: dipole 3 (4.77 dB), cardioid 3 (4.77 dB), supercardioid 3.73 (5.72 dB), hypercardioid 4 (6.02 dB). WNG falls like (kd)² at low frequency, so regularize (diagonal loading) or crossfade to one omni at low f. Minimum-norm robustness needs M > order+1, so it is unavailable with 2 mics.
sources.bus_relevance: Gives closed-form weights for the two patterns needed: the dipole for both partners and the hypercardioid for the active partner. Frequency-invariant beams keep both voices' timbre stable.
sources.meeting_relevance: First-order beams can be steered to any DOA, but with 2 mics, steering away from endfire degenerates (broadside is ≈ omni at low f). Only near-endfire talkers gain.
sources.two_mic_reality: Only first order is possible, with a 6.02 dB maximum. The WNG penalty below 500 Hz is 10–20 dB for d=2.5–6 cm. Above ~c/(4d) (2.1 kHz at 4 cm) the first-order approximation breaks down, so hand over to per-bin superdirective weights there.
sources.implementation: Closed-form 2×2 solves per bin in numpy, about 30 lines.

sources.title: An alternative approach to linearly constrained adaptive beamforming (Generalized Sidelobe Canceller)
sources.authors: L. J. Griffiths, C. W. Jim. It implements O. L. Frost's LCMV (Proc. IEEE 60(8):926–935, 1972, doi 10.1109/PROC.1972.8817)
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Antennas and Propagation AP-30(1):27–34
sources.key_idea: The GSC implements Frost's LCMV without constraints in the adaptive part: a fixed beam, a blocking matrix that produces target-free references, and an adaptive canceller.
sources.algorithm: Two mics with the target time-aligned: fixed beam y_f=w_q^H x (DSB or superdirective); blocking signal b=x1−x2 (for an endfire target A this is the backward cardioid); output y=y_f−h*·b. Update per bin with NLMS, h ← h+μ·b*·y/(|b|²+ε), or use a 32–128-tap time-domain FIR. Adapt only when the target is absent (VAD or coherence gating) and apply a norm constraint on h. LCMV fact for N=2: constraints for talker A at 0° and talker B at 180° use both degrees of freedom. Responses (1,1) force w=[1,0], i.e. a single omni. Responses (1,−1) give the dipole, which is the maximum-DI two-talker solution (4.77 dB at low f). A two-talker GSC is therefore left with an empty blocking matrix.
sources.bus_relevance: It provides one adaptive null per frequency. That is useful only if a single nearby passenger dominates a band. In diffuse babble it adds ≲1 dB over the fixed beam (Bitzer et al. 1999).
sources.meeting_relevance: Avoid. With RT60 0.5–0.9 s, reverberant target energy leaks into b and causes target cancellation, and one degree of freedom cannot protect 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: One degree of freedom. Gain against diffuse or reverberant noise is about 0–1 dB. Against a single point interferer in low reverberation it can reach several to 15 dB. Target-cancellation risk is high, so use VAD-gated adaptation with leakage control.
sources.implementation: numpy STFT NLMS, about 50 lines; real-time OK.

sources.title: Theoretical noise reduction limits of the generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) for speech enhancement
sources.authors: J. Bitzer, K. U. Simmer, K.-D. Kammeyer
sources.venue: IEEE ICASSP 1999, Phoenix, vol. 5, pp. 2965–2968
sources.key_idea: The GSC's noise-reduction ceiling depends only on the input auto- and cross-spectra, i.e. the noise coherence. In a diffuse field, the standard model of a reverberant room, the GSC cannot reduce noise further than about 1 dB, confirmed in reverberant simulations. It works well only when T60 is below ~100 ms.
sources.algorithm: Analysis of the optimal (Wiener) GSC in terms of the noise spatial coherence. Practical rule: measure the magnitude-squared coherence (MSC) of noise-only segments; adaptive cancellation can only remove the coherent part.
sources.bus_relevance: Bus babble plus cabin reverberation is close to diffuse at 4 cm, apart from a few nearby talkers. Expect ≲1 dB from any adaptive stage beyond a fixed superdirective beam. Spend the effort on the fixed beam, calibration and post-filter instead.
sources.meeting_relevance: T60 of 0.5–0.9 s is far above 100 ms, so a GSC or adaptive null steering is not worth it in the meeting room.
sources.two_mic_reality: With 2 mics, the coherent part of diffuse noise exists mainly at low frequency (Γ=sinc(kd) > 0.9 below ~1.07 kHz at 4 cm), which is exactly what a fixed superdirective beam already exploits.
sources.implementation: Use as a design check: run scipy.signal.coherence on babble-only recordings to predict the ceiling of any adaptive stage.

sources.title: Multi-microphone noise reduction by post-filter and superdirective beamformer (APES)
sources.authors: J. Bitzer, K. U. Simmer, K.-D. Kammeyer
sources.venue: International Workshop on Acoustic Echo and Noise Control (IWAENC) 1999, Pocono Manor, pp. 100–103
sources.key_idea: A small-aperture DSB with a Zelinski post-filter cannot suppress low-frequency diffuse noise. The paper adds a superdirective path and a second post-filter W1=P_ZZ/P_YbYb (PSD of the superdirective output over PSD of the DSB output). W1 tends to 1 for a coherent target and falls below 1 where the superdirective beam removes diffuse noise. It notes that Frost/GSC converge to the superdirective beam in isotropic noise (via Cox), and that non-adaptive beams (DSB, superdirective) improve speech quality through dereverberation while adaptive schemes cause signal cancellation. It also introduces a master/slave evaluation in which adaptive weights are copied to speech-only and noise-only paths.
sources.algorithm: For N=2: Y_b=(X1+X2)/2 after alignment; Z=w_SD^H X. Zelinski filter W0=N/(N−1)·(P_YbYb−(1/N²)ΣP_XiXi)/P_YbYb; second filter W1=P_ZZ/P_YbYb. Output = Z·clip(W0·W1, 0.05, 1). PSDs by recursive smoothing (α≈0.8–0.9 per 8–16 ms hop). The paper evaluated N=4 with T60=150/450 ms, endfire and broadside.
sources.bus_relevance: A directly implementable 2-mic post-filter on top of the talker-steered superdirective beam. W1 adds extra diffuse-noise attenuation of about the DF ratio of the two beams (up to ~4–6 dB at low f); W0 works at higher frequencies.
sources.meeting_relevance: Supports the rule of no adaptive beamforming in reverberant rooms. Use only mild post-filtering (floor 0.2–0.3) so far, reverberant talkers are not distorted.
sources.two_mic_reality: With N=2, W0 assumes uncorrelated noise. That is false below ~1 kHz at 4 cm, so W0≈1 there and W1 must carry the low-frequency work. Floors that are too low produce musical noise.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 40 lines on top of the beamformer.

sources.title: Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence
sources.authors: I. A. McCowan, H. Bourlard
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Speech and Audio Processing 11(6):709–716
sources.key_idea: Generalizes the Zelinski post-filter to an arbitrary known noise coherence, such as the diffuse sinc model. This is essential for closely spaced mics, where noise is correlated at low frequencies. It improved quality and ASR on real office noise.
sources.algorithm: One mic pair. From smoothed Φ11, Φ22 and Φ12, with the diffuse model Γ=sinc(2fd/c) or a measured Γ̂ from babble-only frames: φ̂_s=[Re{Φ12}−Γ·(Φ11+Φ22)/2]/(1−Γ). Gain H=clip(φ̂_s/((Φ11+Φ22)/2), H_min, 1), applied to the beamformer output, with H_min≈0.1–0.3. Regularize or fall back to a single-channel noise estimate where 1−Γ is small.
sources.bus_relevance: A cheap classical post-filter matched to diffuse babble. The near partners at 0.3–1 m are coherent and the babble is diffuse, so discrimination is good above ~1 kHz.
sources.meeting_relevance: For far talkers (DRR −10…−16 dB) the speech itself is mostly diffuse, so this filter attenuates and can over-suppress them. Use a high floor, or target only HVAC noise.
sources.two_mic_reality: Ill-conditioned where Γ→1. Γ=0.9 at 1.07 kHz (4 cm), 1.7 kHz (2.5 cm) and 0.71 kHz (6 cm), so there is little discrimination below those frequencies. Larger spacing helps this post-filter while smaller spacing helps the beam; ~4 cm is a reasonable compromise. Gain/phase mismatch biases Re{Φ12}, so calibrate first.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 30 lines.

sources.title: Signal enhancement using beamforming and nonstationarity with applications to speech (TF-GSC)
sources.authors: S. Gannot, D. Burshtein, E. Weinstein
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Signal Processing 49(8):1614–1626
sources.key_idea: Replaces free-field delay steering with relative transfer functions (RTFs, ratios of acoustic transfer functions), estimated from the nonstationarity of speech. The resulting GSC (TF-GSC) works in reverberant rooms with arbitrary transfer functions and needs no array geometry.
sources.algorithm: Per bin, RTF g=H2/H1, estimated on frames where the target is active (nonstationarity-based least squares, or the covariance-whitening method below). Fixed beam y_f=(e1+g e2)^H-style distortionless combination, i.e. w0=[1,g]/(1+|g|²). Blocking signal u=x2−g·x1 (target-free). Noise canceller y=y_f−h*·u, with NLMS updates only on noise-only frames.
sources.bus_relevance: Geometry-free steering toward each partner: near-field effects, device-body scattering and mic mismatch are absorbed into g. Keep one RTF per partner and select by the active talker.
sources.meeting_relevance: Tracking per-talker RTFs for 20 talkers is fragile with 2 mics, and reverberant leakage into u cancels the target. Use only the fixed RTF-MVDR part.
sources.two_mic_reality: One blocking channel gives at most one null. Gain against diffuse babble is small (see Bitzer 1999). The benefit is a more robust distortionless constraint, not more DI.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 60 lines.

sources.title: Performance analysis of the covariance-whitening and the covariance-subtraction methods for estimating the relative transfer function
sources.authors: S. Markovich-Golan, S. Gannot, W. Kellermann. Builds on Markovich-Golan & Gannot, ICASSP 2015, pp. 544–548
sources.key_idea: Analyses the two standard geometry-free RTF estimators used by MVDR/MWF: covariance subtraction (CS) and covariance whitening (CW). CW was superior in every tested scenario; the analysis proves it for spatially white noise and for uniform source/interference powers.
sources.algorithm: Inputs: noise covariance Φ_w (noise-only frames) and noisy covariance Φ̂_x (frames with the target active). CS: ĝ=(Φ̂_x−Φ_w)e1 / e1^T(Φ̂_x−Φ_w)e1. CW: factor Φ_w=Φ_w^{H/2}Φ_w^{1/2} (Cholesky), whiten z=Φ_w^{−H/2}x, take ψ̂ = principal eigenvector of Φ̂_z, then ĝ=Φ_w^{H/2}ψ̂/(e1^T Φ_w^{H/2}ψ̂). This equals the principal generalized eigenvector of (Φ̂_x, Φ_w), normalized. MVDR: w=Φ_w^{−1}ĝ/(ĝ^HΦ_w^{−1}ĝ). Everything is 2×2, so closed form.
sources.bus_relevance: Learn ĝ_A and ĝ_B on frames where each partner clearly dominates (high coherence and TDOA ≈ ±d/c). For Φ_w use the babble-only covariance, or the calibrated diffuse model φ_v(f)·Γ̂(f)+σ²I. This removes dependence on the uncertain 2.3–4 cm spacing and on mic mismatch.
sources.meeting_relevance: Can supply per-talker RTFs (clustered by DOA) for an RTF-MVDR steered at the active talker. Early reflections captured in ĝ add a small matched gain. Tracking 20 talkers is the hard part.
sources.two_mic_reality: Needs reliable labels for target-dominant and noise-only frames. With non-stationary babble, Φ_w is the weak point, so a hybrid (measured RTF plus model diffuse Φ_w) is the most robust. DI is still bounded by 6 dB.
sources.implementation: numpy plus scipy.linalg.eigh (generalized eigenproblem), about 40 lines.

sources.title: Superdirective beamforming robust against microphone mismatch
sources.authors: S. Doclo, M. Moonen
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, and Language Processing 15(2):617–631 (doi 10.1109/TASL.2006.881676)
sources.key_idea: Fixed superdirective beamformers on small arrays are highly sensitive to gain, phase and position errors. The paper designs with the error statistics, comparing a WNG constraint, a mean noise/distortion trade-off, minimum mean pattern deviation, and maximizing the mean or worst-case DF. Maximizing mean or worst-case DF is preferred, and parameter ranges are given for the other methods.
sources.algorithm: Model each mic as (1+δa_i)e^{jδφ_i} with known variances. The mean-DF design replaces a·a^H and Γ by their expectations over the errors; for small independent errors this acts like extra diagonal loading of order σ_a²+σ_φ². A practical surrogate: per bin, pick μ (the WNG floor) by Monte Carlo to maximize mean DF under ±1 dB/±3° errors.
sources.bus_relevance: Sets how aggressive low-frequency superdirectivity can be with uncalibrated INMP441s (±1 dB). My Monte Carlo at 4 cm endfire: ≤0.3 dB DI loss at WNG ≥ −10 dB; at 250 Hz with WNG −15 dB, ~0.9 dB mean loss (1.8 dB at the 10th percentile); after calibration to ±0.1 dB/±0.5°, negligible loss.
sources.meeting_relevance: Same, with a stricter WNG floor because of self-noise. A robust design avoids phasey low-frequency artifacts on far talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Statistical robustness cannot fix a large systematic error. An I2S half-sample skew (31 µs) is 27% of the 117 µs endfire TDOA at 4 cm. Measure and compensate systematic errors first, then use the robust design for the residual.
sources.implementation: Offline numpy Monte-Carlo weight design (~50 lines); store the weights per bin.

sources.title: Gain self-calibration procedure for microphone arrays
sources.authors: I. Tashev (Microsoft Research)
sources.venue: IEEE ICME 2004 (doi 10.1109/ICME.2004.1394367). Deployed on ten Microsoft meeting-capture stations
sources.key_idea: Real-time gain self-calibration from ordinary speech. Whenever a single talker dominates and a DOA is available, per-channel energies are projected onto the DOA line, fitted with a straight line, and the channel gains are updated slowly. It achieved ±0.45 dB channel matching from mics with ±4 dB sensitivity spread, and ran stably for months on meeting-capture stations.
sources.algorithm: E_m = frame energy of channel m; d_m = projection of mic m's position onto the DOA. Least-squares fit Ẽ(d)=a1·d+a0. Gain estimate g_m=G_m^{n−1}·E_m/Ẽ(d_m), normalized G_m=g_m/mean(g). Update G_m^n=(1−α)G_m^{n−1}+α·G_m with α=0.001 in the real system (0.01 in controlled tests). Updates happen 0.5–15 times per second, only when one source dominates, and implausible estimates are rejected.
sources.bus_relevance: For 2 mics, run it per 1/3-octave band on far-field or diffuse segments, where true levels are equal. Exclude the near partners: a talker at 0.3 m on the axis produces a true 1.2 dB inter-mic level difference at 4 cm (0.7 dB at 0.5 m). Calibration is what makes WNG floors of −15…−20 dB usable on the bus.
sources.meeting_relevance: This is exactly the meeting-capture use case it was built for. Talkers at 1–6 m are far-field for a 4 cm array, so the equal-energy assumption holds.
sources.two_mic_reality: Gain only. Add phase/delay calibration: in diffuse babble the true cross-spectrum is real-valued (sinc), so a linear phase slope in the measured cross-spectrum reveals any fixed inter-channel delay, such as an I2S L/R skew. With ±0.25 dB/±1° residuals the DI loss is negligible in my simulation.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 30 lines, runs online.

sources.title: AN-1140: Microphone Array Beamforming
sources.authors: InvenSense Inc. (now TDK InvenSense, the maker of the INMP441), application note AN-1140-00 rev 1.0
sources.venue: InvenSense application note (TDK listing dated 31 Dec 2013; Mouser mirror)
sources.key_idea: Vendor guidance for MEMS mic arrays. Broadside arrays simply sum the mics. Endfire differential (delay-and-subtract) arrays give cardioid, hypercardioid or supercardioid patterns with better off-axis rejection. The cost is a high-pass response rising 6 dB/oct that needs an EQ filter, an on-axis null at f_null=c/(2d), and a requirement for closely matched sensitivity and frequency response.
sources.algorithm: Choose d=n·c/fs so the inter-mic delay is an integer n samples. f_null=c/(2d); for example 21 mm with a 3-sample delay at 48 kHz puts the null near 8.2 kHz. EQ with a first-order low-pass up to f_null. For a fixed delay, spacing below the matched value gives a subcardioid and above it a hypercardioid.
sources.bus_relevance: At 16 kHz, one sample corresponds to 21.4 mm. The ~4 cm spacing is 1.87 samples, so time-domain delay-and-subtract needs fractional delays. The cardioid on-axis null at c/2d = 4.3 kHz (4 cm), 6.9 kHz (2.5 cm) or 2.9 kHz (6 cm) is inside the speech band. Implement differential beams per STFT bin with distortionless weights, or crossfade to one mic above ~0.8·c/2d.
sources.meeting_relevance: Broadside summing of 2 mics gives only ~3 dB SNR against uncorrelated self-noise and ≈0–1 dB diffuse DI. It is not a directivity tool; it helps only with self-noise in a quiet room.
sources.two_mic_reality: Consistent with my numbers at 4 cm: endfire DSB AI-DI 1.9 dB, broadside DSB 1.0 dB. Differential designs require calibration.
sources.implementation: Design guidance only; the numbers reproduce easily in numpy.

sources.title: UM2214: Getting started with AcousticBF real-time beam forming middleware
sources.authors: STMicroelectronics
sources.venue: ST user manual UM2214 (first release 18 May 2017, latest revision 27 Oct 2021); part of X-CUBE-MEMSMIC1
sources.key_idea: A shipping 2-mic MEMS beamformer. A cardioid is formed by delay-and-subtract (Δ=d/c) with EQ for the 6 dB/oct roll-off. Adaptive 'ASR' and 'strong' modes use a GSC in which back-to-back cardioids feed an adaptive filter, i.e. the Elko structure. Spacing below 40 mm is advised, with a 21 mm default, which is exactly 1 sample at 16 kHz PCM.
sources.algorithm: Fixed path: cardioid = x1 − delay(x2, d/c), then EQ. Adaptive path: the backward cardioid is the noise reference into an adaptive canceller, plus optional denoising. Vendor ASR test: white-noise source at 90°, speech at 0°, isolated words, counting matched words with confidence > 80%. At 0 dB SNR: omni 6, cardioid 16, ASR mode 56, strong 46. At −5 dB: 1, 7, 38, 36. At 15 dB: 70, 81, 81, 65 (strong mode distorts at high SNR).
sources.bus_relevance: Shows what an industrial 2-mic adaptive differential stage achieves, but against a single point noise at broadside, which is the best case for an adaptive null. Diffuse babble will yield far less (Bitzer 1999). The aggressive mode loses at high SNR, so gate any adaptive stage by SNR.
sources.meeting_relevance: Fixed single-look cardioid product, not intended for 360° multi-talker capture.
sources.two_mic_reality: 21 mm spacing is chosen so the delay is one sample at 16 kHz. With 4 cm, an STFT/fractional-delay implementation is needed. The reported gains come from point-source nulling, not diffuse noise reduction.
sources.implementation: Closed-source C library for STM32; re-implement the same structure in numpy (about 60 lines).

sources.title: Espressif Microphone Design Guidelines (ESP-SR Audio Front-End)
sources.authors: Espressif Systems
sources.venue: ESP-SR documentation, a living document ('latest', ESP32-S3 page) accessed Nov 2026
sources.key_idea: Vendor requirements for mic arrays feeding Espressif's audio front end (BSS/NS/AGC): two-mic spacing 4–6.5 cm with the axis horizontal and centred; same mic model; sensitivity difference within 3 dB (±1 dB tolerance for arrays); phase difference within 10°; SNR ≥ 62 dB (≥ 64 dB recommended); response within ±3 dB from 50 Hz to 16 kHz; port hole > 1 mm with a short pipe so the structural resonance is above 9 kHz, and depth:diameter < 2:1.
sources.algorithm: Hardware/structural checklist, plus a consistency check that the sampled signal difference between mics is < 3 dB.
sources.bus_relevance: Same ecosystem as the user's ESP32. Their 4–6.5 cm targets BSS/DOA, which favour larger spacing. My AI-DI analysis puts the optimum for classical superdirective beams at 16 kHz at ~2.5–4 cm. The current ~4 cm satisfies both, so do not move to 6 cm.
sources.meeting_relevance: The INMP441's 61 dBA SNR is just below Espressif's 62 dB minimum, which confirms that self-noise limits low-WNG superdirectivity in a quiet room.
sources.two_mic_reality: Their 3 dB/10° matching tolerance is far too loose for superdirective or differential processing. My simulation: a −1 dB/−10° fixed error at 250 Hz destroys the low-frequency gain. Software calibration is mandatory.
sources.implementation: Not code; a hardware and enclosure checklist.

sources.title: Adaptive directional microphone technology and hearing aids: theoretical and clinical implications
sources.authors: D. A. Fabry (Director of Clinical Research, Phonak LLC)
sources.venue: The Hearing Review, April 2005 (industry trade journal)
sources.key_idea: Hearing-aid industry evidence on 2-mic directional systems. Adaptive systems change the polar pattern by altering the internal delay between microphones. Lab SNR benefit versus omni ranges from 3 to 10 dB (Hawkins & Yacullo 1984: 3–4 dB). In a preliminary 7-subject test, a 20-band adaptive system gave 7.7 dB versus 5.8 dB for a broadband one. Reverberation and talker/listener distance reduce the benefit, the critical distance indoors is within a few meters, and benefit requires spatial separation of talker and noise.
sources.algorithm: Multiband adaptive first-order directional processing: per-band delay or β adaptation of the Elko type, with per-band pattern choice from cardioid, supercardioid, hypercardioid or dipole.
sources.bus_relevance: The closest commercial analogue to the bus case (a listener near talkers in babble). Expect a hearing-aid-like 3–4 dB with diffuse babble. Per-band (per-bin) adaptation beats broadband.
sources.meeting_relevance: Confirms that directional benefit shrinks with reverberation and distance beyond the critical distance, so 2-mic beams will not rescue 4–6 m talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Hearing aids use ~1–1.5 cm port spacing and calibrated, matched mics. Lab figures are an upper bound for an uncalibrated 4 cm INMP441 pair.
sources.implementation: n/a (evidence source).

sweep.takeaways:
BOTTOM LINE. With 2 omni INMP441s 2.5–6 cm apart at 16 kHz, classical beamforming buys a few dB. It cannot by itself achieve 'only the two partners audible' or 'all 20 people at even loudness'.

Hard ceiling: a first-order endfire hypercardioid, directivity factor N²=4 (6.0 dB), at low and mid frequencies. Broadside gain is ≈0 dB below ~1 kHz.

My numpy evaluation (ideal mic match, free field, ANSI S3.5 1/3-octave band-importance weights 160 Hz–8 kHz) gives these AI-weighted gains against 3-D diffuse noise, for d = 2.5 / 4 / 6 cm:
- Single-target endfire superdirective MVDR, WNG ≥ −10 dB: 5.15 / 4.97 / 4.62 dB.
- Fixed two-talker (0°/180°) phase-optimized LCMV (≈ dipole), WNG ≥ −20 dB: 4.4 / 4.1 / 3.7 dB.
- Same two-talker beam, WNG ≥ −10 dB: 3.4 / 3.6 / 3.5 dB.
- Endfire delay-and-sum: 1.3 / 1.9 / 2.3 dB.
- Broadside delay-and-sum: 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.5 dB.

Against horizontal-only (2-D) babble the gains are lower: 4.0 / 3.8 / 3.6 dB single-target and 2.2–2.8 dB two-talker. Expect a further 0.5–1.5 dB loss in the field.

Off-axis steering at 4 cm (WNG ≥ −10 dB): 4.3 dB at 30°, 3.6 at 45°, 2.6 at 60°, 1.0 at 90°.

Spacing: 2.5–4 cm is optimal for classical beams at 16 kHz. Keep the current ~4 cm. 6 cm loses ~0.4 dB and puts c/2d = 2.9 kHz in mid-band. Espressif's 4–6.5 cm rule targets their BSS front end. Orientation and calibration matter far more than spacing.

Scripts reproducing all numbers (python3 -I): /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-chpatel-Library-Application-Support-Claude-scratch-workspaces-7223bc40-0755-4c47-a940-84a904b8ead4-809a743c-126a-440a-9a06-f59818e63020-scratch-2026-11-02-5e756e/c3614d02-9a38-4a14-8dcb-766e8c2e70cf/scratchpad/calc/ (di_wng.py, aidi.py, mismatch.py, room.py, alpha_beam.py, cyl.py, cyl2.py).

CONSTRAINTS EVERY DESIGN MUST RESPECT.
1. Aliasing frequency c/2d = 6.9 / 4.3 / 2.9 kHz. At exactly c/2d the steering vectors for endfire-front and endfire-back are identical. Any A/B talker decision or front/back DOA must use frequencies below ~0.8·c/2d. Time-domain delay-and-subtract cardioids have an on-axis null there (AN-1140). Work per STFT bin with distortionless weights.
2. Self-noise. INMP441 EIN ≈ 33 dBA (94 − 61). Where WNG sits at its floor, output hiss rises by |WNG| dB. That is fine on a bus (70–80 dBA) down to −20 dB. In a quiet meeting room keep WNG ≥ −3…−6 dB.
3. Mismatch.
   - Random ±1 dB / ±3° costs ≤0.3 dB DI at WNG ≥ −10 dB.
   - At WNG −15…−20 dB the same random error costs ~1–2 dB at 250 Hz.
   - It fills the dipole's broadside null from −19 to −10 dB at 300 Hz.
   - A fixed −1 dB / −10° error at 250 Hz with WNG −20 dB turns +6 dB into −3 dB.
   - Calibrate before any superdirective or differential stage (Tashev; Doclo & Moonen).
4. Degrees of freedom. 2 mics give one adaptive null per bin. An LCMV that passes both talkers uses all degrees of freedom. Responses (1,1) give a single omni. Responses (1,−1) give the dipole, which is the maximum-DI two-talker choice. A sign flip on talker B is inaudible.
5. Adaptive cancellation (GSC, Elko β, TF-GSC) adds ≲1 dB in diffuse or reverberant noise (Bitzer, ICASSP 1999). Big gains appear only against a single dominant point interferer. Example: ST AcousticBF with one white-noise source at 90° went from 6 matched words (omni) to 16 (cardioid) to 56 (adaptive mode) at 0 dB SNR.

TEST CASE 1: CROWDED BUS (ranked).
1. Orientation. This is free and the biggest lever. Align the line through both mic ports with the line joining the partners' mouths, so the device sits between them and points endfire at both.
   - Partners at broadside (side-by-side, device in front): ≈1 dB.
   - At 30° / 45° / 60° from the axis: 4.3 / 3.6 / 2.6 dB single-target.
   - The dipole response |cosθ| costs that talker 1.2 / 3 / 6 dB.
2. Calibrate (see below), then build a per-bin 'two-talker first-order steerable beam' from three precomputed weight sets:
   - w_A: superdirective MVDR toward 0°.
   - w_B: superdirective MVDR toward 180°.
   - w_AB: two-talker LCMV whose per-bin constraint phase maximizes DF subject to WNG; ≈ dipole below ~2 kHz.
   - Select or crossfade them with a smoothed talker posterior from the GCC-PHAT TDOA sign over 200–3000 Hz (100–300 ms smoothing plus hysteresis).
   - Crossfade only A↔AB↔B, with phases aligned to the AB constraint.
   - Never average w_A + w_B: at low f it collapses to omni.
   - Never interpolate w_A − w_B at high f: in my simulation both talkers cancel above ~c/4d, by −20 dB at 4 kHz for 4 cm.
   - WNG floor −15…−20 dB below 500 Hz. High-pass at 100–150 Hz for engine rumble.
   - Expected gain: 2.5–4.5 dB AI-weighted SNR against babble and road noise. That matches the 3–4 dB lab benefit of 2-mic directional hearing aids (Fabry/Phonak).
   - Gain is larger against a single lateral talker (dipole null) and zero against noise arriving from the partners' own directions.
3. Post-filter: Bitzer APES W1 = P_SD/P_DSB combined with the McCowan–Bourlard diffuse-coherence gain, floor 0.1–0.3.
   - Adds ~3–8 dB of perceived noise attenuation, mostly above ~1 kHz at 4 cm, because the coherence model is ill-conditioned below 1.07 kHz.
   - This improves comfort and quality. Classical single-channel-type post-filtering rarely raises intelligibility on its own (Hu & Loizou, JASA 122:1777, 2007), so tune for low distortion.
4. Geometry-free RTF-MVDR per partner, using covariance-whitening RTFs learned on frames where each partner dominates. For Φ_w use the calibrated diffuse model or the babble-only covariance.
   - Same ~4–5 dB ceiling.
   - Robust to the uncertain 2.3–4 cm spacing, to near-field effects (a talker at 0.3 m gives a 1.2 dB inter-mic level difference at 4 cm) and to device-body scattering.
   - Worth A/B testing against item 2.
5. Experimental only: subband Elko β constrained to [0.5,1] and frozen while either partner talks, or a 2-mic TF-GSC. Expect ≲1 dB in babble, and several dB only if one loud neighbour dominates.
- Realistic total from this angle: ~3–5 dB SNR improvement plus post-filter comfort. 'Only the partners audible' needs stronger mask-based or neural post-filtering from other angles stacked on this front end.

TEST CASE 2: 20-PERSON MEETING ROOM (ranked).
Physics first:
- For a 150–300 m³ room with RT60 0.5–0.9 s, the Sabine critical distance is ≈0.7–1.4 m.
- Omni DRR is therefore ≈ −9…−18 dB at 4–6 m.
- Total (direct + reverberant) level differs only ~2–4 dB between talkers at 1 m and 6 m. The far-talker problem is clarity (DRR), not level.
- A 3–5 dB DI multiplies the critical distance by only 1.4–1.8.

Ranked steps:
1. No fixed nulls and no adaptive interference cancellation. With T60 far above 100 ms these give ≲1 dB and cause target cancellation. Non-adaptive beams improve quality through dereverberation (Bitzer 1999).
2. Placement: device at the table centre with the mic axis along the table's long axis.
   - The farthest talkers, at the table ends, are then near endfire and get 4–5 dB of DI.
   - Near talkers across the table sit near broadside (≈1 dB), but they already have positive DRR.
   - Keep the array horizontal with ports unobstructed. Mounting the ports close to the table surface (boundary effect) is worth testing.
3. Steer a superdirective MVDR (WNG ≥ −3…−6 dB) at the active talker, by one of two methods:
   - GCC-PHAT DOA, θ = arccos(cτ/d), using frequencies below 3.5 kHz, with a 300–500 ms hold. This is the talker-seeking idea of Flanagan, Johnston, Zahn & Elko (JASA 78:1508, 1985) scaled down to 2 mics.
   - Simpler alternative: three fixed beams (endfire+ hypercardioid, endfire− hypercardioid, broadside DSB) feeding a best-beam or gain-sharing automixer.
   - Follow either with per-talker AGC.
   - Expected gain: ≈2–4 dB DRR and noise for talkers within ±45° of the axis, ≈1 dB near broadside, ≈2.5 dB averaged over directions.
   - Use only a mild post-filter (floor ≥ 0.3), aimed at HVAC noise.
4. Run Tashev's DOA-gated gain calibration continuously; it was built for exactly this meeting-capture case.
- Conclusion: classical 2-mic beamforming cannot make 6 m talkers intelligible at even loudness. Pair it with multichannel dereverberation (e.g. WPE) and AGC from other angles, or add mics or devices.

CALIBRATION AND CHECKS (do these first).
1. Gain: per-1/3-octave gain from the long-term PSD ratio on far-field or diffuse segments, excluding the near talkers.
2. Fixed delay: measure it from the phase slope of the babble cross-spectrum, which should be ≈0 phase. Specifically check for an I2S L/R half-sample skew: 31 µs is 27% of the 117 µs endfire TDOA at 4 cm.
3. Spacing: confirm d from the diffuse-coherence fit (≈4 cm) and from the extreme TDOAs of endfire talkers on both sides. An asymmetry between the two sides indicates skew.
4. Target residual: ≤ ±0.25 dB / ±1°. Tashev reached ±0.45 dB starting from a ±4 dB spread.

EVALUATION METHOD. Use Bitzer's master/slave trick: run each algorithm on the mixture and apply the identical per-frame weights and gains to the separately recorded or simulated speech-only and noise-only components. This measures true SNR gain and speech distortion separately. pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 (wheels ≈1.1 MB for Python 3.12–3.14) can simulate:
- the 2-mic geometry with talkers at 0.3–1 m on the axis, plus surrounding babble sources, in a bus-cabin-sized room;
- a 10×7×3 m meeting room at RT60 0.5–0.9 s with 20 talker positions at 1–6 m.

checked.title: Practical supergain
checked.correct_citation: H. Cox, R. M. Zeskind, T. Kooij, 'Practical supergain,' IEEE Trans. Acoust., Speech, Signal Process., 34(3):393–398, June 1986, doi:10.1109/TASSP.1986.1164847. Companion (also confirmed): H. Cox, R. M. Zeskind, M. M. Owen, 'Robust adaptive beamforming,' IEEE TASSP 35(10):1365–1376, Oct. 1987, doi:10.1109/TASSP.1987.1165054.
checked.applicability_verdict: I reproduced the numbers independently in numpy. AI-DI with WNG ≥ −10 dB is 5.15/4.96/4.61 dB for 2.5/4/6 cm. At 4 cm, per-band DI is 2.25 dB @150 Hz, 3.87 @250, 5.98 @500, 5.86 @1k, 5.37 @2k, 4.49 @3k and 3.33 @4k. Off-axis AI-DI is 4.34/3.57/2.56/1.04 dB; DSB is 1.31/1.86/2.27 dB endfire and 0.52/1.04/1.53 dB broadside. These are upper bounds: free field, ideal match, ideal diffuse field. Overclaims: (a) the spacing ranking depends on the WNG floor. At the WNG ≥ −3 dB floor the agent itself prescribes for the meeting room, 2.5/4/6 cm give 4.13/4.32/4.26 dB, so '2.5–4 cm optimal, don't use 6 cm' is not supported; all differences are ≤0.5 dB. (b) A low WNG floor amplifies every spatially uncorrelated component by up to |WNG| dB, not just self-noise: also wind or vent turbulence and handling/vibration noise. This is the classic hearing-aid failure mode that makes them fall back to omni in wind. On a bus with vents or open windows, a −20 dB floor below 500 Hz can make things worse. (c) Bus babble is mostly horizontal (2-D DI 3.9 dB single-target at 4 cm) and includes nearby point sources. A realistic field gain is ~2.5–4 dB single-target. Keep: this is the right core fixed beam.

checked.title: Adaptive microphone array (US 5,473,701) / A simple adaptive first-order differential microphone
checked.correct_citation: J. Cezanne, G. W. Elko, 'Adaptive microphone array,' US Patent 5,473,701 (AT&T), filed 5 Nov 1993, granted 5 Dec 1995, expired. Same algorithm: G. W. Elko, A.-T. Nguyen Pong, 'A simple adaptive first-order differential microphone,' Proc. IEEE Workshop on Applications of Signal Processing to Audio and Acoustics (WASPAA), New Paltz NY, 1995, pp. 169–172, doi:10.1109/ASPAA.1995.482983.
checked.applicability_verdict: Patent details verified: B&K 4183 mics 1.5 cm apart; 22.05 kHz so the delay is 1 sample; y = c_F − β·c_B; LMS update β ← β + 2μ·y·c_B (normalized variant also given); β clamped to [0,1], with the null at 90° for β=1 and 180° for β=0; block N=1000; 5 kHz LPF; M=32 polyphase subbands with per-band β and μ=0.1. The β-to-pattern table is correct. The two-partner logic is sound: never adapt freely, use the dipole during double-talk. In my simulation, ±1 dB/±3° mismatch fills the dipole's broadside null to a mean of −9.9 dB, which reproduces the agent's −10 dB. Overclaim: 'adaptive β pays off against a loud neighbour'. In a reverberant bus cabin a null removes only the neighbour's direct path. Bitzer et al. (ICASSP'99, full text) simulated a point source at 2.5 m with T60 = 300 ms and found the GSC only 1.2 dB above its diffuse-field limit. Expect ~1–3 dB, not 'several to 15 dB'. Keep as an experimental option only.

checked.title: Study and Design of Differential Microphone Arrays
checked.correct_citation: J. Benesty, J. Chen, Study and Design of Differential Microphone Arrays, Springer Topics in Signal Processing (vol. 6), Springer, Berlin Heidelberg, 2013. ISBN 978-3-642-33752-9, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-33753-6.
checked.applicability_verdict: The DF values are correct: dipole 3, cardioid 3, supercardioid 3.73, hypercardioid 4. The (kd)² WNG penalty and the absence of minimum-norm robustness with M=2 are also correct. Minor inaccuracy: the per-bin null-constraint design is exact at every frequency; it is not a 'first-order approximation that breaks down above c/4d'. What actually happens is that the DF and pattern drift with frequency, and the cardioid/hypercardioid systems become ill-conditioned approaching c/2d (4.29 kHz at 4 cm), where a(0°) and a(180°) coincide. The series volume number was not shown on the publisher page; the DOI and ISBN are verified. Keep as the design reference.

checked.title: An alternative approach to linearly constrained adaptive beamforming (GSC)
checked.correct_citation: L. J. Griffiths, C. W. Jim, 'An alternative approach to linearly constrained adaptive beamforming,' IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag., AP-30(1):27–34, Jan. 1982, doi:10.1109/TAP.1982.1142739. Frost (confirmed): O. L. Frost III, 'An algorithm for linearly constrained adaptive array processing,' Proc. IEEE 60(8):926–935, Aug. 1972, doi:10.1109/PROC.1972.8817.
checked.applicability_verdict: The two-constraint LCMV analysis is right in substance. Two constraints on two mics leave zero degrees of freedom, and responses (1,−1) give the dipole; I reproduced its WNG of −16.1 dB at 300 Hz and 4 cm. Nit: '(1,1) forces w=[1,0]' holds only with the mic-1 phase reference. With an array-centre reference it becomes an EQ'd broadside DSB; both are ≈omni at low frequency. Overclaims: (1) 'Adds ≲1 dB over the fixed beam' is true only if the fixed beam is already superdirective. With an endfire-steered DSB as the fixed beam, an ideal GSC in diffuse noise converges toward the superdirective solution (Cox; Bitzer IWAENC'99) and can add a few dB at low-to-mid frequencies. (2) '15 dB vs a point interferer' applies only in near-anechoic rooms. The recommendation to avoid the GSC in both test cases is nevertheless correct. Keep as background.

checked.title: Theoretical noise reduction limits of the generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) for speech enhancement
checked.correct_citation: J. Bitzer, K. U. Simmer, K.-D. Kammeyer, 'Theoretical noise reduction limits of the generalized sidelobe canceller (GSC) for speech enhancement,' Proc. IEEE ICASSP 1999, Phoenix AZ, vol. 5, pp. 2965–2968.
checked.applicability_verdict: The abstract is confirmed (≤1 dB; works well only for T60 < 100 ms). The full text (the authors' .ps) narrows the scope considerably. The ≤1 dB is the noise reduction of the adaptive sidelobe path ON TOP OF a time-aligned (broadside) DSB, analysed for N=3–7 at d=5–20 cm. The paper explicitly states that for N=2 the sidelobe path gives 0 dB at all frequencies. The diffuse model is taken as valid for T60 > 300 ms. The simulation (point source at 2.5 m, T60 = 300 ms) came out 1.2 dB above the diffuse limit. Do not quote '≤1 dB' as a universal GSC limit, and especially not relative to an endfire DSB. The agent's actual conclusion is supported: little is gained beyond a fixed superdirective beam in diffuse or reverberant noise, so no GSC in the meeting room. Keep.

checked.title: Multi-microphone noise reduction by post-filter and superdirective beamformer (APES)
checked.correct_citation: J. Bitzer, K. U. Simmer, K.-D. Kammeyer, 'Multi-microphone noise reduction by post-filter and superdirective beamformer,' Proc. Int. Workshop on Acoustic Echo and Noise Control (IWAENC), Pocono Manor PA, Sept. 1999, pp. 100–103. The title and authors are verified from the PDF; the venue and pages come from the file name and the citation record, as the PDF does not print them.
checked.applicability_verdict: The formulas are verified from the PDF: Zelinski W0 (eq. 5), W1 = P_ZZ/P_YbYb (eq. 6), 0.05 ≤ W0·W1 ≤ 1, the master/slave evaluation, and Frost converging to the superdirective beam in isotropic noise (via Cox). CORRECTION: the paper's statement that 'adaptive schemes' degrade speech by signal cancellation refers to the adaptive POST-FILTERS and single-channel EM (APF, EM and APES itself), not to adaptive beamformers. APES degrades speech strongly at low SNR: LAR ≈4 vs ≈1.3 for the fixed superdirective beam at −5 dB SNR. The paper therefore does not support 'no adaptive beamforming'; it supports keeping post-filter floors high. The setup also differs from this project: N=4, fs = 8 kHz, T60 = 150/450 ms, white and speech-shaped noise (no babble). Results at T60 = 450 ms endfire: APES ≈6–9.5 dB, superdirective ≈5 dB, DSB ≈3.5 dB. With N=2 the gains will be smaller. Keep.

checked.title: Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence
checked.correct_citation: I. A. McCowan, H. Bourlard, 'Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence,' IEEE Trans. Speech Audio Process., 11(6):709–716, Nov. 2003, doi:10.1109/TSA.2003.818212.
checked.applicability_verdict: The formula is correct, and the conditioning numbers are verified (Γ = 0.9 at 1.72/1.07/0.72 kHz for 2.5/4/6 cm). Overclaim for the bus: the filter suppresses only DIFFUSE energy. Nearby passengers 1–2 m away are coherent point sources, just like the partners, so they pass unattenuated. Engine and road noise below ~1 kHz is barely touched, since Γ → 1 there. '3–8 dB perceived attenuation' is plausible against diffuse far babble only; it cannot make 'only the partners audible'. With a single pair there is no averaging across pairs, so the estimates are noisy and produce musical noise unless heavily smoothed. In the meeting room it also suppresses far talkers' reverberant speech, as the agent notes. Schwarz & Kellermann's CDR estimators are the better 2-mic successor. Keep.

checked.title: Signal enhancement using beamforming and nonstationarity with applications to speech (TF-GSC)
checked.correct_citation: S. Gannot, D. Burshtein, E. Weinstein, 'Signal enhancement using beamforming and nonstationarity with applications to speech,' IEEE Trans. Signal Process., 49(8):1614–1626, Aug. 2001, doi:10.1109/78.934132.
checked.applicability_verdict: The description is accurate: w0 = [1,g]/(1+|g|²), blocking signal u = x2 − g·x1, noise canceller adapted on noise-only frames. Geometry-free RTF steering is a genuinely useful robustness tool for an uncertain 2.3–4 cm spacing, near-field partners and device scattering. The canceller part offers one null and suffers target leakage when RT60 is long (see Bitzer'99), so the agent is right to keep only the fixed RTF-MVDR part for the meeting room. No DI beyond the ~6 dB first-order bound. Keep (RTF part).

checked.title: Performance analysis of the covariance-whitening and the covariance-subtraction methods for estimating the relative transfer function
checked.correct_citation: S. Markovich-Golan, S. Gannot, W. Kellermann, 'Performance analysis of the covariance-whitening and the covariance-subtraction methods for estimating the relative transfer function,' Proc. EUSIPCO 2018 (26th), pp. 2513–2517. Prior work (confirmed from its reference list): S. Markovich-Golan, S. Gannot, 'Performance analysis of the covariance subtraction method for relative transfer function estimation and comparison to the covariance whitening method,' Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2015, pp. 544–548.
checked.applicability_verdict: Content is verified from the PDF. CW ≥ CS is proven for spatially white noise and for uniform source/interference powers. CW won every Monte-Carlo case, with rare exceptions acknowledged (|ρ|² → 1 with high INR). CORRECTION to the agent's gloss: the CW estimate is ĝ ∝ Φ_w·v_max, i.e. Φ_w times the principal generalized eigenvector of (Φ̂_x, Φ_w), normalized by its first entry. It is NOT v_max itself, so taking scipy.linalg.eigh's eigenvector directly gives a wrong RTF. Scope: the analysis is narrowband, with stationary, perfectly known noise covariance and random ATFs (baseline M=10), not room acoustics. CW's advantage is largest at low SNR, which is the bus regime, but non-stationary babble makes Φ_w the bottleneck, as the agent says. Keep.

checked.title: Superdirective beamforming robust against microphone mismatch
checked.correct_citation: S. Doclo, M. Moonen, 'Superdirective beamforming robust against microphone mismatch,' IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process., 15(2):617–631, Feb. 2007, doi:10.1109/TASL.2006.881676.
checked.applicability_verdict: The abstract confirms the description: maximizing the mean or worst-case DF is preferred when computational cost allows, and parameter ranges are given for the other methods. However, the agent's Monte Carlo put the ±1 dB/±3° error on ONE mic only (a relative error); I reproduced its 0.86/1.66 dB that way. Two INMP441s with ±1 dB tolerance EACH differ by up to ±2 dB. With per-unit errors on both mics I get a mean DI loss of 0.50 dB (10th-percentile loss 1.2 dB) at 500 Hz with WNG ≥ −10 dB, versus the claimed ≤0.3 dB. At 250 Hz with WNG −15…−20 dB I get 1.4 dB mean (≈3.0 dB at the 10th percentile), versus the claimed 0.9/1.8 dB. The 'fixed −1 dB/−10° turns +6 into −3.1 dB' result is sign-dependent: the opposite sign gives +3.7 dB. The conclusion (calibrate first, then use a robust design) stands and is in fact stronger. Keep.

checked.title: Gain self-calibration procedure for microphone arrays
checked.correct_citation: I. Tashev, 'Gain self-calibration procedure for microphone arrays,' Proc. IEEE Int. Conf. Multimedia and Expo (ICME) 2004, Taipei, pp. 983–986, doi:10.1109/ICME.2004.1394367.
checked.applicability_verdict: Confirmed from the PDF: ±0.45 dB matching achieved from a ±4 dB spread; α = 0.01 in tests and 0.001 in the deployed system; 0.5–15 updates per second; 10 meeting stations running for months; hardware was an 8-mic circular array, 14 cm diameter, 44.1 kHz. CORRECTIONS: (1) The update uses the square root of the energy ratio (eq. 7), not E_m/Ẽ; implement it as an amplitude correction, G·sqrt(Ẽ(d_m)/E_m). (2) As published, the method is DEGENERATE for M=2: a straight line through two points always fits exactly, so the gain update is identically 1. What the agent proposes (assume equal per-band energy on far-field or diffuse segments, i.e. slope a1 = 0) is a different, simpler long-term level equalisation, for which Tashev is only inspiration. The method is gain-only and assumes phase mismatch <0.25°, so a delay/phase calibration must be added separately. Keep as background only.

checked.title: AN-1140: Microphone Array Beamforming
checked.correct_citation: J. Lewis, 'Microphone Array Beamforming,' Application Note AN-1140, originally Analog Devices; reissued by InvenSense (now TDK) as AN-1140-00 rev. 1.0, Dec. 2013. The INMP441 itself descends from ADI's ADMP441.
checked.applicability_verdict: NOT re-fetched in this pass: mouser.com and analog.com timed out twice and TDK's old URL returned 404. Its existence rests on prior knowledge. The specific example (21 mm, 3-sample delay at 48 kHz, null near 8.2 kHz) is unverified, though the arithmetic is self-consistent. The physics (f_null = c/2d, 6 dB/oct EQ, need for matched mics) is standard. The derived numbers check out: c/2d = 6.86/4.29/2.86 kHz and d/c = 1.17/1.87/2.80 samples at 16 kHz. Design guidance only. Keep.

checked.title: UM2214: Getting started with AcousticBF real-time beam forming middleware
checked.correct_citation: STMicroelectronics, UM2214, 'Getting started with AcousticBF real-time beam forming middleware' (X-CUBE-MEMSMIC1 middleware), user manual.
checked.applicability_verdict: NOT re-fetched: st.com timed out three times. Existence rests on prior knowledge. The ASR word counts (6/16/56/46 at 0 dB SNR, etc.), the 21 mm default and the <40 mm advice are unverified in this pass. Even if exact, the numbers come from a single white-noise point source at 90°, which is the best case for an adaptive null. They do not transfer to diffuse babble or reverberant rooms, so they must not be quoted as expected gains. Keep only as an industry analogue of the cardioid-plus-adaptive structure.

checked.title: Espressif Microphone Design Guidelines (ESP-SR Audio Front-End)
checked.correct_citation: Espressif Systems, 'Espressif Microphone Design Guidelines,' ESP-SR documentation (Audio Front-End, ESP32-S3), 'latest' version, accessed Nov 2026.
checked.applicability_verdict: All numbers verified on the page: 2-mic spacing 4–6.5 cm with the axis horizontal; ±1 dB tolerance for arrays and ≤3 dB difference; ≤10° phase; SNR ≥ 62 dB (≥ 64 dB recommended); ±3 dB from 50 Hz to 16 kHz; port >1 mm; depth:diameter <2:1; resonance >9 kHz; consistency test <3 dB using white noise at 0.5 m and 90 dB. The INMP441's 61 dBA is indeed below their minimum. 'Their 4–6.5 cm targets BSS/DOA' is the agent's speculation; the page gives no rationale. 'Do not move to 6 cm' is overstated: 4 vs 6 cm changes AI-DI by only 0.06–0.35 dB depending on the WNG floor. 6 cm also improves DOA resolution (2.8 vs 1.87 samples), low-frequency WNG (~+3.5 dB) and coherence-post-filter conditioning (Γ = 0.9 at 0.72 vs 1.07 kHz), at the cost of aliasing at 2.86 kHz. Keep as a hardware checklist.

checked.title: Adaptive directional microphone technology and hearing aids: theoretical and clinical implications
checked.correct_citation: D. A. Fabry (Phonak LLC), 'Adaptive directional microphone technology and hearing aids: theoretical and clinical implications,' The Hearing Review, April 2005.
checked.applicability_verdict: The numbers are confirmed (3–10 dB lab benefit; Hawkins & Yacullo 3–4 dB; 7.7 vs 5.8 dB). The agent omitted that the 7.7/5.8 dB came from a preliminary 7-subject test with DISCRETE noise sources: low-pass noise at 180°, high-pass at 90°/270°. That is the best case for adaptive nulling, not diffuse babble, and the test was run by the manufacturer's research director on its own products. Hearing aids also benefit from head-shadow directivity that a free-standing PCB lacks, and everyday benefit is often smaller than lab benefit (Cord et al. 2004). Treat 3–4 dB as an UPPER bound for the bus case. Keep as an expectation-setting source.

Ward (eds.), Microphone Arrays: Signal Processing Techniques and Applications, Springer, 2001, pp. 19–38, doi:10.1007/978-3-662-04619-7_2. M. Buck, 'Aspects of first-order differential microphone arrays in the presence of sensor imperfections,' European Trans. Telecommunications 13(2):115–122, 2002, doi:10.1002/ett.4460130206. Quantifies the 2-mic mismatch problem that dominates this design.

verify.notes:
The WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up when I started, so I ran no web searches and did not use any search workaround. Verification instead relied on: direct fetches of each cited URL; DOI resolution through Crossref and OpenAlex (the DOI registry itself, not search); reading the PDFs of Bitzer IWAENC'99, Tashev ICME'04 and Markovich-Golan EUSIPCO'18; reading the authors' own PostScript of Bitzer ICASSP'99; and an independent numpy reproduction of every numerical claim. My scripts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-chpatel-Library-Application-Support-Claude-scratch-workspaces-7223bc40-0755-4c47-a940-84a904b8ead4-809a743c-126a-440a-9a06-f59818e63020-scratch-2026-11-02-5e756e/c3614d02-9a38-4a14-8dcb-766e8c2e70cf/scratchpad/verify_bf/check_di.py, check_2talk.py, check_mc1.py.

RESULT: All 15 sources exist and are relevant; none dropped. The inline citations are also correct: Hu & Loizou JASA 122(3):1777–1786, 2007; Flanagan et al. JASA 78(5):1508–1518, 1985; pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 (1 May 2026, 1.1 MB universal2 wheels for cp39–cp314). Two sources, AN-1140 and ST UM2214, could not be re-fetched (publisher timeouts or 404). Their existence rests on prior knowledge only, and their specific numbers are unverified.

The DI/WNG arithmetic is solid and reproduces to ±0.1 dB: single-target, two-talker LCMV, off-axis, DSB, 2-D babble, the dipole WNG of −16 dB, the c/2d values, Γ = 0.9 frequencies, Sabine critical distance, DRR, and near-field level difference.

Overclaims and errors to carry forward:
(1) Mismatch losses are understated by ~1.6–2×. The ±1 dB/±3° error was applied to one mic, but two INMP441s at ±1 dB each differ by up to 2 dB. The '−3.1 dB' fixed-error case is the worst-sign case; the other sign gives +3.7 dB.
(2) Bitzer's '≤1 dB GSC' is the adaptive gain on top of a broadside DSB for N=3–7, and the paper says 0 dB for N=2. It must not be stated as 'over the fixed beam' in general, and point interferers in a reverberant cabin give ~1–3 dB, not 15 dB.
(3) Bitzer IWAENC'99's 'adaptive schemes cause signal cancellation' refers to post-filters (APF, EM, APES), not adaptive beamformers.
(4) Tashev's line fit is degenerate with 2 mics, and the formula needs a sqrt.
(5) The CW RTF is Φ_w·v_max, not v_max.
(6) The coherence post-filters cannot suppress nearby passengers (coherent point sources) or low-frequency engine noise.
(7) The spacing advice (keep 4 cm, never 6) is overstated: ≤0.4 dB either way, and 6 cm is better at the −3 dB WNG floor and for DOA and post-filters.
(8) Low WNG floors also amplify wind, vent and vibration noise, not just self-noise.
(9) Fabry's 7.7 dB came from discrete noise sources and is vendor-run.

A realistic bus gain from this angle is ~1.5–3.5 dB, not 2.5–4.5 dB. The meeting-room conclusion (classical 2-mic beamforming alone cannot achieve this) is correct.

sweep.angle: Dual-microphone noise suppression from phones, headsets, earbuds and hearing aids (industry focus). Covers coherence-based post-filters (Allen 1977, Zelinski 1988, McCowan & Bourlard 2003), the Yousefian & Loizou dual-mic coherence algorithm, CDR estimation (Schwarz & Kellermann 2015), phone PLD/ILD methods (Jeub et al., and Audience, Qualcomm and Apple patents), phase-error TF masking (Aarabi & Shi), and hearing-aid and earbud conversation features (Phonak StereoZoom/Speech in Loud Noise, Signia Augmented Focus split processing, Oticon OpenSound Navigator, AirPods Pro Conversation Boost). For each one: which cue separates the near talker from the crowd, what the gain rule is, and what survives on 2 INMP441 omnis 2.5–6 cm apart at 16 kHz.

sources.title: Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation
sources.authors: Andreas Schwarz, Walter Kellermann
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM Trans. Audio, Speech, and Language Processing 23(6):1006–1018 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2015.2418571); arXiv:1502.03784
sources.key_idea: Estimate, per time-frequency bin, the ratio of coherent (direct-path) power to diffuse (reverb or diffuse noise) power from the complex short-time coherence between two omni mics. Use that CDR as an SNR inside a spectral-subtraction post-filter. An unbiased estimate needs EITHER the target DOA OR the noise coherence, not both. The DOA-independent estimator keeps ANY coherent near talker and removes diffuse sound, which is exactly the cue for 'keep the two nearby talkers, drop the diffuse crowd and reverb'. Related work: Thiergart, Del Galdo & Habets, JASA 132(4):2337–2346 (2012), SDR estimation. Hearable use: Ghanavi & Jin, band-weighted binaural CDR masks for real-time hearables (ICA 2022, arXiv:2207.08314; JASA 2026, PMID 41481344).
sources.algorithm: Model: Γx=(CDR·Γs+Γn)/(CDR+1), with Γs=e^{j2πfΔt} (|Γs|=1) and Γn=sinc(2πfd/c) or a measured Γn. STFT as in the paper: fs=16 kHz, DFT filterbank with window 1024, FFT 512, hop 128. PSDs: Φij(l,f)=λΦij(l−1,f)+(1−λ)Xi·Xj*, λ=0.68. Coherence: Γ̂x=Φ12/√(Φ11Φ22), clipped so |Γ̂x|<1. DOA-dependent unbiased estimator (prop1): CDR=max(0, Re{Γs*(Γn−Γ̂x)}/(Re{Γs*Γ̂x}−1)). Prop2, a magnitude variant with bias correction, was best in the tests; port it from the authors' code. DOA-independent unbiased estimator (prop3): CDR=max(0,[Γn·Re{Γ̂x}−|Γ̂x|²−√(Γn²Re{Γ̂x}²−Γn²|Γ̂x|²+Γn²−2Γn·Re{Γ̂x}+|Γ̂x|²)]/(|Γ̂x|²−1)). Pre-processor: Y=√((|X1|²+|X2|²)/2)·e^{j∠X1}. Gain: G=max(Gmin, 1−√(µ/(CDR+1))) with µ=1.3 and Gmin=0.1; output Z=G·Y, then ISTFT. Note that G(CDR=0)=1−√µ, so µ sets the maximum attenuation of diffuse bins: µ=0.3 gives −6.9 dB, µ=0.5 gives −10.7 dB, µ≥1 hits the floor. Results with d=8 cm, T60 0.4–3.5 s, distances 1–4 m, measured RIRs: ASR rate 62.2%→77.6% (prop3, no DOA) and 81.5% (prop2, DOA known); PESQ 1.27→1.42/1.48; fwSegSNR 4.7→7.0 dB. An Allen-style |Γ| gain reached only 71.7% and PESQ 1.32.
sources.bus_relevance: Primary tool for the bus case. Near talkers at 0.3–0.5 m are inside the cabin's critical distance (estimated ~0.7 m for ~70 m³ and T60≈0.45 s), so their bins have high CDR. Multi-talker babble, road noise and cabin reverb are diffuse, so they get suppressed. The DOA-free version keeps BOTH conversation partners without tracking who is speaking. Start with µ≈1.1–1.3 and Gmin=0.1 (−20 dB). It will NOT reject a loud passenger 1–2 m away, who is partly coherent; add the DOA-dependent version or the phase mask for that.
sources.meeting_relevance: Dangerous if used aggressively. Talkers at 1–6 m in a room with T60 0.5–0.9 s are beyond the critical distance r_c≈0.8 m (DRR ≈ −2 to −17 dB) and would be floored. Use mild settings (µ 0.3–0.5, Gmin 0.3–0.5) only as late-reverb reduction, followed by AGC. Schwarz's 1–4 m results show this family does improve ASR in rooms like this.
sources.two_mic_reality: How well-conditioned the estimate is depends on |Γs−Γn|. Diffuse coherence stays above 0.9 below about 1.1 kHz (d=4 cm), 1.7 kHz (2.5 cm), 0.7 kHz (6 cm) and 0.54 kHz (8 cm). At 1 kHz with d=4 cm, |Γs−Γn| is 0.09 for a broadside talker but 0.69 for an endfire talker, so orient the mic axis toward the talkers. Below ~1 kHz, use a frame-level CDR (averaged over 1–4 kHz) or single-channel noise suppression. Coherence is immune to the ±1 dB gain mismatch but sensitive to phase mismatch from unequal mounting. Uncorrelated INMP441 self-noise (EIN≈33 dBA) lowers coherence in quiet bins, which acts like a gate; that is fine on a bus. Estimation variance at λ=0.68 causes musical noise, so smooth G over time and frequency. The paper used d=8 cm; 6–8 cm spacing would help.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 60–80 lines including STFT via scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT; easily real-time on the M1. The authors' MATLAB reference (BSD-style license) is at http://www.lms.lnt.de/files/publications/cdr-dereverb.zip, with a GitHub fork at https://github.com/Haibit/cdr-dereverb (originally andreas12345/cdr-dereverb); port the DOA-free and unbiased estimators. No new dependencies; works on Python 3.12–3.14.

sources.title: Robust coherence-based spectral enhancement for speech recognition in adverse real-world environments
sources.authors: Hendrik Barfuss, Christian Huemmer, Andreas Schwarz, Walter Kellermann
sources.venue: Computer Speech & Language 46:388–400 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2017.02.005); arXiv:1604.03393
sources.key_idea: A real-world check of Schwarz-type CDR post-filtering after a beamformer, on CHiME-3 tablet recordings that include a real public-transport BUS environment. This is the closest published evidence for the crowded-bus test case.
sources.algorithm: Weighted delay-and-sum beamformer (BeamformIt), then a CDR-based Wiener-type post-filter G=max(Gmin, 1−√(µ/(CDR+1))), with Gmin=0.1, λ=0.68 and STFT window 1024 / FFT 512 / hop 128 at 16 kHz. CDR is computed over all pairs of the 6 mics and averaged. µ was optimized on the dev set: 1.1 (DOA-independent), 1.2 (DOA-dependent), 0.4 (Thiergart), 0.8 (Jeub). Model: CDR=(Γn−Γx)/(Γx−Γs), Γs=e^{j2πfτ}, Γn=sinc. Real-data eval-set WER: BUS 18.53%→17.71% (DOA-independent) and 17.42% (DOA-dependent); CAF 11.39%→9.36%; average 12.67%→11.63% (−8.2% relative). Dev set: up to −11.3% relative.
sources.bus_relevance: Sets expectations. On real bus recordings with the talker holding a tablet (~0.3–0.5 m), the CDR post-filter gives only about 4–6% relative ASR gain on top of a 6-mic beamformer. The DOA-dependent CDR, which knows the talker direction, slightly beats the DOA-free one. Also shows µ≈1.1–1.2 is a good starting point.
sources.meeting_relevance: Low: there is no meeting-room data. It does confirm that DOA-dependent CDR adds directional filtering, which is counterproductive for 20 talkers all around the table.
sources.two_mic_reality: This used 6 mics on a tablet (apertures ~10–20 cm) plus a beamformer. With 2 mics at 2.5–6 cm there is no beamformer gain and low-frequency conditioning is worse, so expect equal or smaller gains. ASR with a noise-trained DNN under-reports perceived noise reduction, so listening tests are still needed.
sources.implementation: Same numpy code as the Schwarz CDR entry; multi-pair averaging is not needed with 2 mics.

sources.title: Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence
sources.authors: Iain A. McCowan, Hervé Bourlard (generalizing R. Zelinski, 'A microphone array with adaptive post-filtering for noise reduction in reverberant rooms', ICASSP 1988, pp. 2578–2581)
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Speech and Audio Processing 11(6):709–716 (DOI 10.1109/TSA.2003.818212); Idiap RR 01-40
sources.key_idea: Zelinski (1988): after steering, the average CROSS-PSD between mics estimates the target PSD, because noise is assumed uncorrelated and its cross terms vanish. The average AUTO-PSD estimates target plus noise. Their ratio gives a Wiener post-filter. McCowan & Bourlard replace the uncorrelated-noise assumption with a known noise coherence (for example the diffuse sinc). That change is what makes it usable for closely spaced mics.
sources.algorithm: First steer (phase-align) the channels to the target TDOA. Zelinski with M=2: H=Re{Φ12}/(½(Φ11+Φ22)). McCowan: Φ̂ss=[Re{Φ12}−Re{Γn}·½(Φ11+Φ22)]/(1−Re{Γn}), with Γn=sinc(2πfd/c); H=clip(Φ̂ss/(½(Φ11+Φ22)), Hmin, 1), applied to the beamformer (or averaged) output. Use recursive PSD smoothing with α≈0.6–0.8. This is equivalent to a DOA-dependent CDR Wiener gain; Schwarz & Kellermann place both in one framework.
sources.bus_relevance: Suppresses diffuse babble and road noise relative to a steered talker. With two talkers you must steer per hypothesis or switch per frame. The DOA-free CDR (Schwarz prop3) is simpler for a two-person conversation.
sources.meeting_relevance: A classic conferencing post-filter for diffuse HVAC noise. Same caveat as CDR for far, reverberant talkers. It also needs a known steering direction, which you don't have for 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Zelinski's uncorrelated-noise assumption fails at 2.5–6 cm: diffuse Γn stays above 0.5 below about 4.1, 2.6 and 1.7 kHz for 2.5, 4 and 6 cm, so there is little suppression below those frequencies. McCowan's denominator (1−Γn) goes to 0 at low frequency (Γn(1 kHz)=0.91 at 4 cm), so the estimate gets noisy. Clamp Γn to ≤0.7–0.8, or bypass below ≈1.9 kHz (4 cm) or ≈1.3 kHz (6 cm). Steering must be sub-sample (max TDOA is 117 µs = 1.87 samples at 4 cm), so do it as STFT phase rotation.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 30 lines.

sources.title: Multimicrophone signal-processing technique to remove room reverberation from speech signals
sources.authors: J. B. Allen, D. A. Berkley, J. Blauert
sources.venue: J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 62(4):912–915
sources.key_idea: The first coherence-based two-mic post-filter. Split the signal into frequency bands, co-phase and add the two channels, then weight each band by a gain derived from the inter-mic cross-correlation. Coherent direct sound passes; incoherent late reverberation and diffuse noise are attenuated.
sources.algorithm: Take the STFT of both channels. Co-phase: X̃2=|X2|e^{j∠X1}, then Y=(X1+X̃2)/2. Gain G(l,f)=|Φ12|/√(Φ11Φ22), the coherence magnitude; a variant uses |Φ12|/(½(Φ11+Φ22)). Smooth the PSDs recursively and output G·Y. In Schwarz & Kellermann's comparison (d=8 cm, reverberant rooms) this gain is gentle: ASR 62.2%→71.7% and PESQ 1.27→1.32, versus 77–81% and 1.42–1.48 for CDR-based gains.
sources.bus_relevance: A simple baseline and first prototype for diffuse babble: low distortion, but low suppression.
sources.meeting_relevance: Usable as a gentle, low-distortion late-reverb reducer that does not wipe out far talkers as hard as a CDR gain with large µ.
sources.two_mic_reality: At 2.5–6 cm the diffuse field itself is highly coherent at low frequencies (Γn>0.9 below 0.7–1.7 kHz), so G≈1 there and suppression happens only at higher frequencies. The short-time coherence of incoherent noise is biased upward (≈0.3–0.5 with λ≈0.7), which caps attenuation at a few dB. Gain mismatch does not matter because the measure is normalized.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 20 lines.

sources.title: A Dual-Microphone Speech Enhancement Algorithm Based on the Coherence Function
sources.authors: Nima Yousefian, Philipos C. Loizou
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, and Language Processing 20(2):599–609 (DOI 10.1109/TASL.2011.2162406; PMC3246289)
sources.key_idea: For a closely spaced endfire pair (hearing-aid BTE, 20 mm) with the target at 0°, the real and imaginary parts of the short-time coherence show whether a bin is dominated by the frontal target or by a source at another azimuth. The gain comes straight from the coherence, so no noise-PSD estimation is needed.
sources.algorithm: fs=16 kHz, 20-ms frames, 75% overlap. PSD smoothing λ=0.6; Γ̂=Φ12/√(Φ11Φ22). G1=1−|Re{Γ̂}|^{P(ω)}, with P=α_low=16 for f≤1 kHz (|ω|≤π/8) and α_high=2 above. G2=µ=0.05 if Im{Γ̂}<Q(ω), else 1; the β_low/β_high thresholds that define Q were not captured. G=G1·G2, applied to the front-mic STFT. Results (normal-hearing listeners, IEEE sentences, KEMAR with BTE mics, RT60≈220 ms, sources at 1.2 m): single masker at 75° and −5 dB SNR, 17%→74% words (beamformer 7%); masker at 90° and −5 dB, 15%→82%; multiple maskers at 0 dB, 26%→68–82%; average PESQ +0.7. The authors' own limits: performance degrades in more reverberant (less coherent) noise, and there is no benefit when the masker is within 45° of the target.
sources.bus_relevance: Strong when interferers are discrete and off-axis; useful as a directional add-on that keeps endfire talkers. For two people facing each other, place the device on the line between them so both are endfire, and replace G2's one-sided Im test with |Im{Γ̂}| to keep 0° and 180°. That adaptation is ours and untested. Diffuse bus babble is this method's weak case.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not suitable: it assumes a single frontal target and would suppress most of the 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Designed for 20 mm, so a 2.5 cm pair fits its parameters. At 4–6 cm the phase ωτ is 2–3× larger and endfire aliasing starts at c/(2d): 4.3 kHz at 4 cm, 2.9 kHz at 6 cm. Retune α, β and Q, and restrict the processing to below c/(2d). As transcribed, G1 with P=16 also attenuates the endfire target's low band (about −12 dB at 500 Hz for 20 mm), so check the paper's derivation before porting and add a gain floor. The reported gains are for point maskers in a mild room; expect much less in diffuse babble.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 40 lines. Audio demos: https://ecs.utdallas.edu/loizou/speech/COH_Audio_Demo/index.htm

sources.title: Phase-based dual-microphone robust speech enhancement
sources.authors: Parham Aarabi, Guangji Shi
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Part B 34(4):1763–1773 (DOI 10.1109/TSMCB.2004.830345)
sources.key_idea: A time-frequency 'phase-error' filter: bins whose inter-mic phase difference disagrees with the target's TDOA are attenuated. Because it depends only on phase, it is immune to mic gain mismatch.
sources.algorithm: Phase error: θ(l,f)=wrap(∠X1−∠X2−2πfτ̂), where τ̂ is the target TDOA (from GCC-PHAT). Mask: η=1/(1+γθ²) with γ fixed; larger γ is more aggressive, which helps at low SNR and hurts at high SNR. Output: η·(X1+X2e^{j2πfτ̂})/2. With more than 2 mics, take the geometric mean of the pairwise masks (as reproduced in arXiv:1510.00268). Kim et al. (Interspeech 2009) note that extra time and frequency smoothing of the phase is needed for good ASR.
sources.bus_relevance: Provides the DIRECTION cue. With two talkers, use two hypotheses τ=±d/c (axis orientation) and θ=min_k|θ_k|. This suppresses side passengers, whose TDOA≈0. It complements CDR, which handles diffuse interferers but not coherent ones.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not useful for 20 talkers around a table: it would need 20 TDOA hypotheses, and a 2-mic TDOA is ambiguous front-to-back.
sources.two_mic_reality: At 4 cm the max TDOA is 117 µs, and the max IPD is only 21° at 500 Hz and 84° at 2 kHz. Diffuse-noise phase scatter dominates below ~1 kHz, so use 1–4 kHz only; endfire aliasing starts above 4.3 kHz at 4 cm. Two mics give a cone of confusion (θ and −θ about the axis look identical), so only the angle from the axis can be resolved. Hard masks cause musical noise, so use a soft mask with smoothing and a floor.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 25 lines.

sources.title: Noise Reduction for Dual-Microphone Mobile Phones Exploiting Power Level Differences
sources.authors: Marco Jeub, Christian Herglotz, Christoph Nelke, Christophe Beaugeant, Peter Vary
sources.venue: IEEE ICASSP 2012, pp. 1693–1696 (best paper award); related patent US 8,903,722 B2 (Intel Mobile Communications, priority 2011)
sources.key_idea: In handset position the mouth is much closer to the bottom mic than to the top or back mic. Speech therefore shows a large power level difference (PLD) between the mics, while diffuse noise has equal power at both. The normalized PLD drives both the noise-PSD estimator and the gain.
sources.algorithm: Smooth Φ11 and Φ22 recursively; normalized PLD ΔΦ=(Φ11−Φ22)/(Φ11+Φ22). Noise PSD: if ΔΦ<φmin, σN²=ασN²+(1−α)|X1|²; if φmin≤ΔΦ≤φmax (speech present), σN²=ασN²+(1−α)|X2|², because the secondary mic is noise-dominated; if ΔΦ>φmax, hold. Gain: G=ΔΦ'/(ΔΦ'+γ(1−|H12|²)σN²) with ΔΦ'=max(Φ11−Φ22,0)≈Φss(1−|H12|²). This is equivalent to a Wiener gain Φss/(Φss+γσN²), with |H12|²≈(Φ22−σN²)/(Φ11−σN²). Decision-directed smoothing reduces musical noise. The thresholds and constants are not public in the patent text. For hands-free use (phone on a table, talker far away), the same group switched to a coherence plus speech-presence-probability noise-PSD estimator, because the PLD vanishes (Nelke, Beaugeant & Vary, ICASSP 2013).
sources.bus_relevance: Only useful if the geometry produces a real level difference, for example one mic within ~5–15 cm of a talker's mouth. With a tabletop device the cue is unusable. If the mics were re-wired as two lavaliers (one per talker, on longer I2S leads), each talker would get a PLD of 10+ dB, enabling strong per-talker gating.
sources.meeting_relevance: None for a central tabletop device: the PLD is ≈0 dB for all 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: The near-field PLD for an endfire talker is 20log10((r+d)/r). With d=4 cm that is only 1.1, 0.7 and 0.3 dB at 0.3, 0.5 and 1 m (still only 2.1 dB at 0.3 m with 8 cm spacing). That is below the ±1 dB INMP441 sensitivity tolerance unless the mics are calibrated, so the noise-PSD switch would misfire. The estimator structure (update the noise PSD from the secondary channel while speech is present) is still reusable if the secondary channel is replaced by a spatial noise reference, such as a null-steered or back-cardioid beam.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 40 lines.

sources.title: System and method for utilizing inter-microphone level differences for speech enhancement (US 8,345,890 / US 8,867,759) and System and method for utilizing omni-directional microphones for speech enhancement (US 8,194,880)
sources.authors: Carlos Avendano, Lloyd Watts, Peter Santos (Audience Inc., later Knowles)
sources.venue: US 8,194,880 B2 (granted 2012) and US 8,867,759 B2 (granted 2014), priority 2006. Basis of Audience's earSmart CASA voice processors (eS305/eS310 two-mic, eS325 three-mic) used in LG, Pantech and Sharp handsets.
sources.key_idea: Audience's 'CASA' handset chips used a cochlea-like filterbank and an inter-mic level difference (ILD) to mark time-frequency cells dominated by near-field speech. The ILD can be taken between front and back cardioids formed by delay-and-subtract from two omnis. The ILD freezes a minimum-statistics noise tracker and sets the over-subtraction in a Wiener-type gain on the primary channel.
sources.algorithm: Cochlear filterbank or STFT, 4-ms frames at 16 kHz. Energies: E_i(t,ω)=λE|X_i|²+(1−λE)E_i(t−1), with λE=1−exp(−1/(T·fs)) (T=4 ms gives 0.0155). ILD=[1−2E1E2/(E1²+E2²)]·sign(E1−E2) ∈ [−1,1], or (E1−E2)/(E1+E2). In US 8,194,880: Cf=X1−g·z^{−τ}X2 and Cb=g·X2−z^{−τ}X1 (back-to-back cardioids, g matches levels), with ILD=Ef/Eb. Noise: N=λI·E1+(1−λI)·min(N(t−1),E1), where λI depends on the ILD: track when ILD is low, freeze when ILD>≈0.5. Gain: W=(Ps/(Ps+N))^α with Ps=E1−β·N; β≈2–3 dB at high ILD and 6–9 dB at low ILD; α=2 expansion when W<−12 dB. Smoothing: M=λs·W+(1−λs)M(t−1), with λs increasing with |dE1/dt|. Output S=M·X1.
sources.bus_relevance: Reusable pieces: (1) gate noise tracking with a spatial target cue, replacing the ILD with CDR or the front/back cardioid energy ratio; (2) cue-dependent over-subtraction, aggressive where the cue says noise; (3) fast-attack, slow-release gain smoothing. The handset ILD itself will not work at 0.3–1 m.
sources.meeting_relevance: Low; this is near-field handset logic. An ILD-gated noise tracker would only protect far-talker speech from being learned as noise if a reliable target cue existed, and there is none for 20 talkers at 1–6 m.
sources.two_mic_reality: The ILD between the two omnis at 0.3–1 m is at most ~1 dB (see the Jeub entry). The cardioid ratio Ef/Eb is a directional (endfire) cue that does work at small spacing above ~500 Hz in a loud bus. But the cardioid signals roll off at 6 dB/octave at low frequency (−7 dB at 300 Hz for 4 cm), so use them only as a cue and output the omni or primary channel.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 60 lines, using scipy ShortTimeFFT or a gammatone/ERB filterbank.
