sources.title: Systems, methods, apparatus, and computer-readable media for phase-based processing of multichannel signal (US 8,620,672 B2; related coherence-detection patent US 8,724,829 B2)
sources.authors: Erik Visser, Ernan Liu (Qualcomm)
sources.venue: US patent 8,620,672 B2, granted 2013-12-31, priority 2009-06-09
sources.key_idea: Per-bin phase differences give a 'directional coherency' measure: the fraction of bins pointing into a look cone. Combined with an inter-channel level-difference threshold, this forms a 'proximity bubble' for detecting a near-field talker. Frames outside the cone or bubble update a single-channel noise reference for Wiener filtering or spectral subtraction. Balanced (far-field) segments are used to auto-calibrate mic gain mismatch.
sources.algorithm: 10-ms frames, 128- or 256-point FFT. Δφ(f)=∠X1−∠X2; direction indicator r=Δφ/f (proportional to TDOA) or θ=arccos(cΔφ/(2πfd)). Mask score is 1 inside a passband (e.g., ±15° around the look direction), with soft variants; smooth over 5–50 frames or with a leaky integrator. Directional coherency is the count or average of in-band scores over 700–2000 Hz, compared to a threshold. Gain calibration: on segments flagged as balanced, compute the per-subband level imbalance L1/L2 (RMS or energy, optionally over 200 Hz–1 kHz), smooth it with α=0.8–0.99, and apply it to channel 2; the patent cites a mic sensitivity tolerance of ±3 dB. Proximity: ILD above a threshold (raised at low SNR) AND inside the forward cone. Noise reference: the primary channel during out-of-cone frames, smoothed per bin with a first-order filter, feeding Wiener filtering or spectral subtraction. Spacing guidance: d ≤ λmin/2 to avoid aliasing, about 4 cm for a 4 kHz band.
sources.bus_relevance: Directly reusable: (a) automatic gain-mismatch calibration for the ±1 dB INMP441 pair; (b) a frame-level VAD based on directional coherency, with two cones for two talkers, to drive noise-reference updates; (c) a noise reference built from out-of-cone frames. The proximity (ILD) part only becomes informative with the talker within ~0.5 m of the device AND a larger spacing.
sources.meeting_relevance: The calibration part is useful. The directional VAD is not, because talkers are everywhere.
sources.two_mic_reality: Their 700–2000 Hz band is where 4-cm phase cues are usable (IPD 30–84° for an endfire source). Even in their handset analysis, ILD differences between near and far sources are typically within ~3 dB; in our tabletop geometry they are only ~1 dB.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 50 lines.

sources.title: Audio noise estimation and audio noise reduction using multiple microphones (US 9,966,067 B2) and System and method for audio noise processing and noise reduction (US 10,176,823 B2)
sources.authors: Vasu Iyengar, Sorin V. Dusan; Sorin V. Dusan, Aram M. Lindahl, Alexander Kanaris, Vasu Iyengar (Apple Inc.)
sources.venue: US 9,966,067 B2 (granted 2018, priority 2012); US 10,176,823 B2 (granted 2019, priority 2014)
sources.key_idea: iPhone-style dual-mic suppression. An aggressive 2-channel noise estimator (the secondary or noise-beam signal minus the speech leakage implied by the primary–secondary difference) is combined with a conservative 1-channel stationary estimator. The 2-channel estimate is trusted only in frequency regions where voice-beam/noise-beam separation is large (≥10–12 dB). Elsewhere the 1-channel estimate is used: at low frequencies, where the spacing is much smaller than the wavelength, and in a mid band near the beam null.
sources.algorithm: Per bin k: ΔX=|X1|−|X2|. In speech bins (Spri>Ssec·Thr, VAD threshold ~8 dB) the 2-channel noise estimate is ≈ max(P_X2−ΔX·|H2/H1|², Smin); in noise bins it is P_X1. |H2/H1|² is a device constant, and Smin is the 1-channel stationary (minimum-statistics-type) estimate used as a floor. The combiner prefers the 2-channel estimate but reverts to or de-weights it if it exceeds the 1-channel estimate by more than ~18 dB (range 10–22 dB) during voice; an occlusion detector forces 1-channel. In US 10,176,823 a voice beam (VB) and a noise beam (NB) are formed from the two mics. The 2-channel (VB/NB) estimate is used in 0–3.5 kHz (except below ~800–900 Hz, where separation is only ~6 dB) and above 5 kHz; the 1-channel estimate is used in 3.5–5 kHz, or NB is attenuated by 2–6 dB at low frequency. A Wiener gain-versus-SNR curve is applied per bin to VB, with time smoothing plus 3-bin or fixed-bandwidth frequency smoothing.
sources.bus_relevance: The key transferable rule: decide per frequency band whether the spatial (2-channel) estimate can be trusted, based on measured separation, and fall back to a 1-channel stationary estimate elsewhere. For us: build a 'noise beam' with a null toward the currently active endfire talker (a back-cardioid) and measure its separation per band on our own recordings.
sources.meeting_relevance: The per-band 1-channel/2-channel selection and the Wiener curve apply to the HVAC noise part. The voice-beam concept does not, because there is no single talker direction.
sources.two_mic_reality: Designed for handsets, where the mouth is ~10× closer to the primary mic. For a 0.5 m talker and a tabletop 4-cm array, VB/NB separation will be a few dB to ~10 dB at mid frequencies (reverb leaks into the noise beam) and ~0 dB at low frequencies. So expect the 2-channel estimator to be usable only in a mid band (~1–4 kHz) and only for one talker direction at a time.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 60 lines.

sources.title: Augmenting Speech Recognition with a New Split-processing Paradigm (Signia AX Augmented Focus)
sources.authors: Niels Søgaard Jensen, Erik Harry Høydal, Eric Branda, Jennifer Weber; white paper by Brian Taylor and Niels Søgaard Jensen (2022)
sources.venue: The Hearing Review 28(6):24–27 (2021); Signia white paper 'Evidence supports the advantages of Signia AX split processing' (2022)
sources.key_idea: Split processing. A beamformer separates a front 'Focus' stream from a 'Surrounding' stream. Each stream has its own 48-channel processor: Focus is processed more linearly, Surrounding gets more compression and noise reduction. The streams are remixed with weights that depend on SNR and scene. The result is more contrast without a 'tunnel' effect.
sources.algorithm: Two fixed beams (front and back) produce two streams. Each stream gets its own classification plus gain, compression and noise reduction across 48 channels. Mixer weights depend on SNR, the acoustic scene, own-voice detection and motion detection; binaural beamforming can be enabled in the Focus stream in loud noise. Vendor-reported results: split processing on vs. off improved SRT80 by 3.9 dB (16 hearing-impaired adults, restaurant simulation); 2.1 dB and 7.3 dB better than two competitors; KEMAR bench output-SNR benefit of ~+6–9 dB over ADIR+DNR at 0 and +5 dB input SNR; noise-tolerance test (TNT) +3 dB.
sources.bus_relevance: An architecture to copy. Split each time-frequency bin into a 'target' stream (CDR/phase mask m) and a 'residual' stream (1−m). Process the target linearly with AGC; apply strong noise reduction or compression to the residual (−12 to −20 dB); then remix. This avoids the pumping and underwater artifacts of a single hard mask while keeping the two talkers dominant.
sources.meeting_relevance: The same architecture, with gentle residual attenuation (−3 to −6 dB) and per-talker AGC on the target stream, gives even loudness without removing room presence.
sources.two_mic_reality: Signia uses 2 mics per ear plus a binaural link. A 'front/back' split with our 2 mics at 4 cm would be a first-order back-to-back-cardioid split with poor low-frequency directivity, so do the split with time-frequency masks (CDR or phase) rather than linear beams.
sources.implementation: About 30 lines of numpy on top of any mask.

sources.title: OpenSound Navigator: Analyze / Balance / Noise Removal speech enhancement (Oticon Opn, Ponto 4)
sources.authors: N. Le Goff, J. Jensen, M. S. Pedersen, S. L. Callaway (Oticon white paper, 2016); Oticon Medical course slides (2019)
sources.venue: Oticon white paper 'An introduction to OpenSound Navigator' (2016); Oticon Medical / AudiologyOnline 'Ponto 4' course (2019)
sources.key_idea: Instead of a narrow front beam, keep access to multiple talkers. Estimate noise spatially with a fixed back-facing cardioid, place adaptive nulls on dominant noise sources BETWEEN speech sources, then remove residual diffuse noise with very fast per-band gains.
sources.algorithm: Analyze: two fixed views from the mic pair, an omni 'sound panorama' and a fixed back-facing cardioid, give a spatially informed noise estimate, updated 500 times/s in 16 channels. Balance: adaptive null steering toward dominant noise sources, updated 125 times/s; community descriptions call it MVDR-like, but Oticon has not specified it. Noise removal: 16 bands (centres 155–8750 Hz) updated every 10 ms, attenuating diffuse noise even between words.
sources.bus_relevance: Use an omni + back-facing-cardioid noise reference, plus an adaptive null on the loudest non-target source (e.g., a shouting passenger) when no target speech is active. Add a fast per-band Wiener stage for babble.
sources.meeting_relevance: The design philosophy fits the 20-talker case: do not beam toward one direction; remove only localized noise sources (projector fan) and diffuse noise, and keep all talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: A back-cardioid at 4 cm rolls off at ~6 dB/octave at low frequency and needs gain calibration. An adaptive first-order null (Elko-style β between back-to-back cardioids) can only cancel ONE direction at a time, because 2 mics give 1 null.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 40 lines, for the omni + back-cardioid reference and the adaptive β null.

sources.title: Phonak Insight: Binaural directionality — StereoZoom (with the AutoSense OS 'Speech in loud noise' program)
sources.authors: Phonak AG (white paper, July 2010); M. Latzel (Hearing Review, 2013)
sources.venue: Phonak Insight white paper (2010); Hearing Review 'Concepts for binaural processing in hearing aids' (2013)
sources.key_idea: Two-mic first-order directivity is physically limited: wide ±60° front acceptance, 6 dB/octave low-frequency loss, and higher internal noise if equalized. Phonak therefore streams each ear's first-order signal over the wireless link and combines all 4 mics into a narrow binaural beam that focuses on ONE talker in loud noise.
sources.algorithm: Each ear forms a first-order directional signal from its 2 mics. The full-band signal is exchanged binaurally, and a weighted combination gives a 3rd-order beam with nulls at ≈±45°. It runs as a program; the 'Speech in loud noise' class in AutoSense OS selects UltraZoom or StereoZoom. Hearing aids run omni at low frequencies and directional at high frequencies to limit self-noise. Result: SRT80 1.65 dB better than a monaural beamformer and 2.75 dB better than a competitor's first-order system (15 hearing-impaired subjects, cafeteria noise from 7 loudspeakers).
sources.bus_relevance: Sets realistic expectations: even 4-mic products with a ~15-cm aperture give only ~2 dB SRT over a 2-mic beam. Transferable ideas: run spatial processing only above ~0.5–1 kHz and keep low frequencies omni; offer the narrow beam only as a user-selected 'conversation' mode.
sources.meeting_relevance: A narrow single-talker beam is the opposite of what is needed. The transferable idea is classifier-driven program switching (automatic bus vs. meeting modes).
sources.two_mic_reality: Our 2.5–6 cm pair can only form first-order patterns. Theoretical diffuse-field DI is at most 4.8 dB (cardioid or dipole) to 6.0 dB (hypercardioid). At 4 cm a cardioid is −7 dB at 300 Hz (dipole −13 dB), plus +3 dB of uncorrelated self-noise. That is fine on a 70–80 dBA bus (INMP441 EIN ≈33 dBA) but gives audible hiss in a 35–45 dBA room. Gain mismatch must be well under 1 dB for low-frequency nulls to work.
sources.implementation: Implement from scratch in numpy, about 30 lines, for fixed first-order patterns with fractional delay in the STFT domain.

sources.title: Conversation Boost (AirPods Pro Transparency mode / Headphone Accommodations)
sources.authors: Apple Inc.
sources.venue: Apple Support documentation; launched with AirPods Pro firmware 4A400 / iOS 15
sources.key_idea: In Transparency mode, the earbuds' beamforming mics (plus computational audio) emphasize the person directly in front of the wearer, with an optional ambient-noise-reduction slider. Apple says it works best for one-on-one conversation with the talker right in front.
sources.algorithm: Not disclosed. Publicly known: beamforming toward the front talker, adjustable ambient noise reduction, and ML voice processing (press coverage). Apple's earbud patents (e.g., US 9,516,442) describe closely spaced omni front and rear mics per earbud plus an accelerometer VAD.
sources.bus_relevance: Confirms the industry recipe for a one-to-one conversation in noise: a focus direction plus user-adjustable residual ambience. For our device: orient the 'conversation axis' and add a residual-level slider.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not applicable: it assumes a single frontal talker.
sources.two_mic_reality: Earbud mics sit ~1–2 cm apart, right at the listener. Our device is not worn, so 'front' has to be defined by how it is placed.
sources.implementation: N/A (concept only).

sources.title: anf-generator: Generating coherence-constrained multisensor signals (Python)
sources.authors: AudioLabs Erlangen (E. A. P. Habets group). Papers: Habets, Cohen & Gannot, JASA 124(5):2911–2917 (2008); Mirabilii, Schlecht & Habets, JASA 149:1425 (2021)
sources.venue: Open source (MIT license); PyPI anf-generator 0.1.3 (April 2026)
sources.key_idea: Generates multichannel noise with an exact target spatial coherence (spherical or cylindrical diffuse, Corcos wind) for arbitrary mic positions, from any non-stationary source signals. This lets you build a controlled 'crowded bus' test set for the exact 2-mic geometry before recording in the field.
sources.algorithm: Build the target coherence matrix Γ(f) from the mic positions and the chosen model. Decompose it (Cholesky 'chd' or 'evd'), optionally with 'balanced+smooth' processing, to get a mixing matrix C(f). Mix uncorrelated inputs, such as N independent babble or road recordings, in the STFT domain. Test recipe: convolve talkers with simulated RIRs (bus cabin ~70 m³, T60 0.3–0.6 s; meeting room ~150 m³, T60 0.5–0.9 s), add diffuse babble and engine noise at −5 to +10 dB SNR, sweep d=2.5/4/6/8 cm and broadside vs. endfire orientation, and score with SI-SDR, STOI and PESQ.
sources.bus_relevance: Makes the bus test reproducible and lets you tune µ, Gmin, λ, the crossover frequency f_c and orientation objectively.
sources.meeting_relevance: Same for diffuse HVAC noise; combine with an RIR simulator for 20 talker positions at 1–6 m.
sources.two_mic_reality: Real bus noise is not perfectly diffuse: engine noise is low-frequency and partly coherent, and nearby passengers are point sources. Validate on real ESP32 recordings too, and replace the sinc model with the measured Γn.
sources.implementation: pip install anf-generator: a 13-kB pure-Python wheel; dependencies numpy≥1.22, scipy≥1.9, matplotlib; requires Python ≥3.8, so it works on 3.12–3.14.

sweep.takeaways:
BOTTOM LINE: Phones, headsets and hearing aids rely on three cues. Only two of them work for a tabletop pair of omni mics with talkers at 0.3–1 m:
- the COHERENCE cue (direct vs. diffuse sound, i.e., CDR);
- the PHASE/TDOA cue (direction).
The LEVEL-difference cue that powers phones (Jeub PLD, Audience ILD, Apple's 2-channel estimator, Qualcomm's proximity bubble) needs the mouth within a few cm of one mic. Here it is only 0.3–1.1 dB at d=4 cm, which is inside the ±1 dB INMP441 tolerance. Two omnis 4 cm apart cannot, with classical DSP, leave ONLY the two voices in a crowded bus. They can noticeably reduce diffuse babble, road noise and reverb.

HARDWARE PHYSICS (computed for this array):
- Diffuse-noise coherence stays above 0.9 below about 1.7, 1.1, 0.7 and 0.54 kHz for d=2.5, 4, 6 and 8 cm. Coherence cues are weak below those frequencies.
- How well the coherence model separates target from noise (|Γs−Γn| at 1 kHz, d=4 cm): 0.09 for a broadside talker, 0.69 for an endfire talker. So point the mic axis at the talkers, as hearing aids (front/rear mic) and phones (bottom mic toward the mouth) do.
- The maximum TDOA at 4 cm is 117 µs, or 1.87 samples, so steer by STFT phase rotation.
- First-order differential beams at 4 cm lose 7 dB (cardioid) or 13 dB (dipole) at 300 Hz, and their uncorrelated noise is 3 dB higher. That only works when ambient noise is far above the mics' self-noise (EIN 33 dBA): yes on a bus, no in a quiet meeting room.

CROWDED BUS — implement and test in this order:
1. Calibrate and fix the geometry first.
   - Match per-band gains from the long-term PSD ratio on noise-only segments (Qualcomm auto-calibration).
   - Measure Γn(f) on real bus noise and use it instead of the sinc model. Knowing Γn is enough for an unbiased CDR (Schwarz & Kellermann).
   - Place the device so both talkers sit near the mic axis, one at each end.
   - If possible, re-space the mics to 6–8 cm; Schwarz used 8 cm.
2. DOA-independent CDR post-filter (Schwarz & Kellermann prop3).
   - Settings: λ=0.68, 512-point FFT with 128 hop at 16 kHz, µ≈1.1–1.3, Gmin=0.1, magnitude-averaged input.
   - Apply it per bin above f_c (≈1.1 kHz at 4 cm, 0.7 kHz at 6 cm). Below f_c, drive the gain with the frame-average CDR over 1–4 kHz. Smooth G over time and frequency.
   - A/B against a DOA-dependent CDR with two endfire hypotheses, Γs=e^{±j2πfd/c}, taking the max over hypotheses. This also rejects side passengers, and the DOA-dependent version was best on CHiME-3 BUS.
3. Add single-channel stationary noise suppression (min-statistics or IMCRA, then Wiener or LSA) for engine and road noise.
   - Freeze noise tracking whenever CDR or phase says target (Audience's ILD-gated tracker).
   - Choose 1-channel vs. 2-channel noise estimates per band (Apple's frequency-region rule).
4. Add a phase-error mask with two TDOA hypotheses: Aarabi & Shi η=1/(1+γθ²), or Yousefian–Loizou G2 using |Im Γ|. Use it over 1–4 kHz only, soft, smoothed and with a floor.
5. Split-processing remix (Signia/Oticon): the target stream stays linear with AGC; the residual stream is kept at −12 to −20 dB. Expose a residual-level slider, like AirPods' ambient noise reduction.
6. Optional, loud buses only: dipole or cardioid features (Audience Ef/Eb cue, Oticon back-cardioid noise reference, an Elko-style adaptive null on one loud interferer).

Expected gains on the bus:
- Published results:
  - CDR post-filter on real CHiME-3 BUS recordings, after a 6-mic beamformer: WER 18.53%→17.42–17.71%, a 4–6% relative improvement (Barfuss et al. 2017).
  - Yousefian & Loizou, point maskers in a mild room: 17%→74% words at −5 dB SNR. The authors state the method fails in diffuse or reverberant noise and for maskers within 45° of the target.
  - Industry 4-mic binaural products: SRT gains of 1.65 dB (Phonak StereoZoom vs. a monaural beam) and 3.9 dB (Signia split processing).
- Our estimate for this 2-mic array (not a published number):
  - about 3–6 dB effective SNR gain against diffuse babble in 1–4 kHz, more with endfire orientation and 6–8 cm spacing;
  - a large cut in steady engine hum, which helps comfort more than intelligibility;
  - passengers within 1–2 m only partly suppressed.
- To get closer to 'only the two voices':
  - change the geometry: one lavalier-placed mic per talker on longer I2S leads gives each talker a 10+ dB PLD, enabling Jeub/Apple-style gating;
  - or add a small single-channel DNN stage (a different angle).

MEETING ROOM (20 talkers at 1–6 m) — this angle's tools are tuned for near talkers, so use them sparingly:
1. No aggressive coherence masking.
   - The critical distance is about 0.8 m (e.g., 144 m³ room, T60 0.7 s). DRR is about −1.8, −7.8, −13.8 and −17.3 dB at 1, 2, 4 and 6 m.
   - Bus settings (µ=1.3) push every bin with CDR below −2.2 dB to the floor, which would erase far talkers.
   - Use a mild DOA-free CDR instead: µ 0.3–0.5 caps attenuation of fully diffuse bins at −6.9 to −10.7 dB, with Gmin 0.3–0.5.
   - Evidence: Schwarz's tests (1–4 m, T60 0.4–1 s, d=8 cm, µ=1.3, clean-trained ASR) gave ASR 62%→78% and PESQ 1.27→1.42. Expect only a few dB less late reverb with the mild setting.
2. Sum or magnitude-average both mics (+3 dB against uncorrelated self-noise). Add stationary noise suppression for HVAC and projector noise.
3. For even loudness, apply speech-gated AGC or compression to the direct/target stream (split processing). This is the main lever for far-talker audibility.
4. Switch modes automatically with a scene classifier, using level and diffuseness (Phonak AutoSense 'Speech in loud noise' class; Oticon OSN's 'keep all talkers' approach).
5. Avoid single-direction methods (Yousefian, phase-error filtering, StereoZoom or Conversation-Boost-style beams); they would suppress most of the 20 talkers. The bigger levers here, WPE dereverberation and diarization, are outside this angle.

HARDWARE RECOMMENDATION:
- 6–8 cm spacing helps the coherence/CDR cues most: Γn drops below 0.5 above 1.7 kHz (6 cm) and 1.3 kHz (8 cm).
- Stay at ≤4 cm only if you need unambiguous phase/DOA up to 4 kHz (Qualcomm's spacing guidance). Since CDR does not need phase unwrapping, about 6 cm is the pragmatic choice.
- Mount both INMP441s identically (same port direction, gasket and PCB) so their phases match, and calibrate gain per band.

TEST PLAN:
- Use anf-generator for diffuse babble and road noise with the exact spacing, plus simulated RIRs. Sweep d and orientation, and score with SI-SDR, STOI and PESQ.
- Then record with the real ESP32 on a bus and in a meeting room. Listen for musical noise and far-talker dropouts.

checked.title: Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation
checked.correct_citation: A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann, "Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation," IEEE/ACM Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. 23(6):1006–1018, 2015. DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2015.2418571; arXiv:1502.03784. Reference code (MATLAB, BSD-2-Clause, includes estimate_cdr_nodoa.m and estimate_cdr_robust_unbiased.m): https://github.com/andreas12345/cdr-dereverb. The lms.lnt.de zip link returns 404.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Checked against the PDF. All quoted parameters match: d=8 cm, λ=0.68, µ=1.3, Gmin=0.1, filterbank 1024/512/128, and the eq. 25 prop3 formula. Table III numbers also match: ASR 62.2→77.6% (prop3) and 81.5% (prop2); PESQ 1.27→1.42/1.48; fwSegSNR 4.67→6.98; Allen 71.7% / PESQ 1.32.

Caveats the sweep omits:
(a) Every result is single-talker reverberation only. There is no babble or noise, the task is small-vocabulary GRID, and the ASR was clean-trained PocketSphinx. That setup magnifies dereverberation gains, so none of it is evidence of SNR gain against babble.
(b) The tests used distances of 1, 2 and 4 m, plus REVERB RIRs at about 0.5 and 2 m, with T60 0.4–3.5 s.
(c) The paper's 1024-window / 512-FFT filterbank cannot be built with scipy ShortTimeFFT. scipy 1.17.1 rejects it ('mfft needs to be at least the window length'). Use 512/512/128 or a custom WOLA.
(d) At 2.5–4 cm, conditioning is much worse than at 8 cm.

My quick numpy check used: Schwarz settings, ideal spherical-diffuse 8-talker babble at 0 dB SNR, an anechoic near talker (DRR +6 dB), d=2.5–6 cm, shadow-filtered components. Results:
- Noise was attenuated 4–6 dB, but the target was attenuated 3–4.5 dB.
- Net gain was about 1–2 dB broadband and 0.3–1.5 dB in 1–4 kHz (segmental SNR +0.7 to +2.1 dB).
- With λ=0.9, net gain rose to 2–3.6 dB.
- Endfire beat broadside by about 0.5–1 dB.
- A talker at DRR 0 dB (~1 m in the bus) got about 0 dB net, and negative in 1–4 kHz.

So the 'primary tool' ranking is fair, but the sweep's '3–6 dB effective SNR gain' is optimistic. 3–6 dB is the noise attenuation; the net SNR gain is closer to 1–3 dB.

Meeting room: a far talker (DRR −8 dB) was attenuated 5.6–9 dB at µ=1.3 with about 0 net gain, and 3.7 dB at µ=0.5 / Gmin=0.3 with about 0 net gain. The caution is justified. Mild settings mostly lower the level.

checked.title: Robust coherence-based spectral enhancement for speech recognition in adverse real-world environments
checked.correct_citation: H. Barfuss, C. Huemmer, A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann, "Robust coherence-based spectral enhancement for speech recognition in adverse real-world environments," Computer Speech & Language 46:388–400, 2017. DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2017.02.005; arXiv:1604.03393, which overlaps substantially with arXiv:1509.06882 (CHiME-3 workshop version).
checked.applicability_verdict:
WER numbers verified. Real eval set:
- BUS: 18.53 → 17.71 (DOA-independent) / 17.42 (DOA-dependent).
- CAF: 11.39 → 9.71 / 9.36.
- Average: 12.67 → 11.78 / 11.63, which is −7.0% / −8.2% relative.
- Dev set: best −11.31%, from the Jeub estimator.
- µ values 1.1, 1.2, 0.4 and 0.8; λ=0.68; Gmin=0.1.

Detail corrections:
- Only the 5 forward-facing mics were used.
- Per-pair CDR is converted to diffuseness D=1/(1+CDR). D is averaged across pairs, then corrected by the beamformer's diffuse-noise gain. CDR itself is not averaged.
- The ASR is a Kaldi DNN trained on noisy multi-condition data.

This is the most realistic evidence for the bus case: real bus recordings, with the talker about 0.3–0.5 m from a tablet. It shows only about 4–6% relative gain on BUS, and that is on top of a 5-mic beamformer. The sweep calibrates this correctly. With 2 mics at 2.5–6 cm, expect equal or smaller gains.

checked.title: Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence
checked.correct_citation: I. A. McCowan, H. Bourlard, "Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence," IEEE Trans. Speech and Audio Processing 11(6):709–716, Nov. 2003. DOI 10.1109/TSA.2003.818212; earlier version Idiap-RR-40-2001. Generalizes R. Zelinski, ICASSP 1988, pp. 2578–2581; I did not re-check the Zelinski reference online.
checked.applicability_verdict: The description is accurate. Its value here is as theory and background. For 2 mics it is equivalent to the DOA-dependent CDR Wiener gain, and Schwarz & Kellermann place it in the same framework. It needs a steering direction, and 1−Γn becomes ill-conditioned below about 1.9 kHz at 4 cm. Implement the CDR versions instead of a separate McCowan filter. The sweep's numbers (Γn=0.91 at 1 kHz for 4 cm; Γn<0.5 above 4.1, 2.6 and 1.7 kHz) are correct.

checked.title: Multimicrophone signal-processing technique to remove room reverberation from speech signals
checked.correct_citation: J. B. Allen, D. A. Berkley, J. Blauert, "Multimicrophone signal-processing technique to remove room reverberation from speech signals," J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 62(4):912–915, 1977. DOI 10.1121/1.381621.
checked.applicability_verdict: The paper exists. The jontalle.web.engr.illinois.edu PDF link returned HTTP 403 to a direct fetch, so use the DOI. It is a fine 20-line baseline. It was designed for widely spaced mics. At 2.5–6 cm the diffuse field is highly coherent below 0.7–1.7 kHz, so the gain stays near 1 there. The short-time coherence bias (≈0.3–0.5 at λ≈0.7) caps attenuation at a few dB. Schwarz's Table III confirms a gentle effect even at 8 cm (71.7% ASR, PESQ 1.32). It is a low-distortion baseline and reference, not a solution.

checked.title: A Dual-Microphone Speech Enhancement Algorithm Based on the Coherence Function
checked.correct_citation: N. Yousefian, P. C. Loizou, "A Dual-Microphone Speech Enhancement Algorithm Based on the Coherence Function," IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. 20(2):599–609, Feb. 2012 (online July 2011). DOI 10.1109/TASL.2011.2162406; PMC3246289.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Parameters verified:
- 20 mm spacing, 16 kHz, 20-ms frames with 75% overlap, λ=0.6.
- G1 = 1−|Re Γ̂|^P with P=16 below 1 kHz and 2 above.
- The thresholds the sweep did not capture are β_low=−0.1 (≤1 kHz) and β_high=−0.3; µ=0.05.
- Sources at 1.2 m; room 4.3×3.8×2.3 m with T60≈220 ms.
- Maskers were single or few point sources (speech-weighted noise, babble, factory noise) at ≥60°.

The word scores (17→74% and so on) appear only in Figs. 5–6, so treat them as approximate figure readings. The text confirms an average PESQ gain of +0.7. It also confirms the stated limits: no benefit for maskers within 45°, and performance loss in reverberant, less-correlated noise.

The sweep's warning is right. G1 attenuates an endfire target's low band (I compute −12.5 dB at 500 Hz for 20 mm, and about −3.5 dB at 4 cm). Diffuse bus babble is exactly its weak case. The |Im Γ| adaptation for talkers at 0° and 180° is untested. Treat it as an optional directional add-on only.

checked.title: Phase-based dual-microphone robust speech enhancement
checked.correct_citation: P. Aarabi, G. Shi, "Phase-Based Dual-Microphone Robust Speech Enhancement," IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part B 34(4):1763–1773, Aug. 2004. DOI 10.1109/TSMCB.2004.830345 (confirmed via Crossref).
checked.applicability_verdict:
The mask η=1/(1+γθ²) and the geometric-mean multi-pair combination are confirmed. They are reproduced in arXiv:1510.00268 (El-Desoky Mousa, Marchi, Schuller, CHiME-3, Sec. 3.4.1 PEF). I did not verify the Kim et al. Interspeech 2009 smoothing remark. Patent literature citing this method notes high distortion and artifacts.

The physics in the sweep is correct: at 4 cm the IPD is 21° at 500 Hz and 84° at 2 kHz, endfire aliasing starts at 4.3 kHz, and there is a cone of confusion. With two endfire hypotheses it rejects broadside passengers. It cannot reject babble arriving from near the mic axis, or the part of the diffuse field near endfire. Usable only at about 1–4 kHz, as a soft, floored, smoothed secondary mask.

checked.title: Noise Reduction for Dual-Microphone Mobile Phones Exploiting Power Level Differences
checked.correct_citation:
M. Jeub, C. Herglotz, C. M. Nelke, C. Beaugeant, P. Vary, "Noise reduction for dual-microphone mobile phones exploiting power level differences," Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2012, Kyoto, pp. 1693–1696. DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2012.6288223 (ICASSP 2012 Best Paper Award).
Related patent: US 8,903,722 B2, "Noise reduction for dual-microphone communication devices" (Jeub, Nelke, Herglotz, Vary, Beaugeant; Intel Mobile Communications; filed and priority 2011-08-29; granted 2014-12-02).
Hands-free follow-up: C. M. Nelke, C. Beaugeant, P. Vary, ICASSP 2013, pp. 7279–7283, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2013.6639076.
checked.applicability_verdict:
The sweep cited the patent URL; cite the paper by its DOI instead. The patent also claims a coherence-based noise estimate, with Γmax=0.99. It gives no fixed φmin, φmax or smoothing constants. I could not check the detailed three-branch noise-update logic against the paper text.

The applicability analysis is right. The near-field PLD is 0.3–1.1 dB at 0.3–1 m for d=4 cm, below the INMP441 tolerance (±1 dB per unit, so up to about 2 dB between a pair). Keep it as the negative reference that explains why phone PLD tricks fail. Its reusable part is the estimator structure. The lavalier re-wiring idea is valid but changes the product.

checked.title: Audience inter-microphone level difference patents (US 8,345,890 / US 8,867,759; US 8,194,880)
checked.correct_citation:
- US 8,194,880 B2, "System and method for utilizing omni-directional microphones for speech enhancement." Inventor: Carlos Avendano only. Audience; priority 2006-01-30; granted 2012-06-05.
- US 8,345,890 B2 (granted 2013) and its continuation US 8,867,759 B2 (granted 2014-10-21), "System and method for utilizing inter-microphone level differences for speech enhancement." Inventors: Avendano, Watts, Santos. Audience; priority 2006-01-05.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Algorithm details verified: the ILD formulas; λE from T=4 ms; ILD threshold about 0.5; over-subtraction β of 2–3 dB at high ILD and 6–9 dB at low ILD; α=2 expansion below −12 dB; derivative-driven smoothing; Cf/Cb cardioids with Ef/Eb in '880.

Corrections:
- '880 uses 8-ms frames. The 4 ms is the energy-smoothing time constant in '759, not the frame length.
- The claim of use in LG, Pantech and Sharp handsets is unverified. What is documented: the A1026 in the Nexus One (iFixit), reportedly in the iPhone 4, and the eS305 in the Huawei Ascend D1 Quad XL.
- That these patents are 'the basis' of earSmart is inference.

The handset ILD is unusable at 0.3–1 m. Only the patterns transfer: a cue-gated noise tracker, cue-dependent over-subtraction, and fast-attack/slow-release smoothing. The cardioid Ef/Eb ratio needs gain calibration well under 1 dB to be useful at low frequency.

checked.title: Qualcomm phase-based multichannel processing (US 8,620,672 B2; related US 8,724,829 B2)
checked.correct_citation:
- US 8,620,672 B2, "Systems, methods, apparatus, and computer-readable media for phase-based processing of multichannel signal." E. Visser, E. Liu; Qualcomm; priority 2009-06-09; granted 2013-12-31.
- US 8,724,829 B2, "...for coherence detection." E. Visser, I. E. Liu; Qualcomm; priority 2008-10-24; granted 2014-05-13.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Details verified:
- The 700–2000 Hz voice band.
- A mask passband example of ±15° around broadside (75–105°).
- Gain calibration updated only on 'balanced' segments, with α examples 0.8–0.99. The patent notes that 1–2 dB low-frequency mismatch degrades performance.
- Proximity via level difference, said to appear only within about 0.5–1 m.
- Spacing ≤ λmin/2, about 4 cm for 4 kHz.

I did not find the '±3 dB tolerance' claim in the portion I read. Applicability as stated in the sweep is right. Auto-calibration of the INMP441 pair is the most valuable transferable piece. The directional VAD helps only on the bus.

checked.title: Apple multi-mic noise estimation patents (US 9,966,067 B2; US 10,176,823 B2)
checked.correct_citation:
- US 9,966,067 B2, "Audio noise estimation and audio noise reduction using multiple microphones." V. Iyengar, S. V. Dusan; Apple; priority 2012-06-08; granted 2018-05-08.
- US 10,176,823 B2, "System and method for audio noise processing and noise reduction." S. V. Dusan, A. M. Lindahl, A. Kanaris, V. Iyengar; Apple; priority 2014-05-09; granted 2019-01-08.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Numbers verified:
- 8 dB VAD example.
- Comparator of ≥10 dB, 15–22 dB, or about 18 dB.
- Regions 0–3.5 kHz (2-channel), 3.5–5 kHz (1-channel) and >5 kHz.
- About 6 dB separation below 800–900 Hz, against 10–12 dB needed.
- 2–6 dB noise-beam attenuation.
- An occlusion detector that forces the 1-channel estimate.

These are handset designs, with the mouth about 10× closer to the bottom mic. For a tabletop 4-cm pair and a talker at 0.5 m, separation will be a few dB at most. The per-band 'trust the spatial estimate only where measured separation is large' rule is the transferable part. The sweep says this correctly.

checked.title: Augmenting Speech Recognition with a New Split-processing Paradigm (Signia AX Augmented Focus)
checked.correct_citation:
- N. S. Jensen, E. H. Høydal, E. Branda, J. Weber, "Augmenting Speech Recognition with a New Split-processing Paradigm," Hearing Review 28(6):24–27, June 2021.
- B. Taylor, N. S. Jensen, "Evidence Supports the Advantages of Signia AX's Split Processing," Signia white paper, June 2022: https://www.signia-pro.com/en/signia-library/2022-06-evidence-supports-the-advantages-of-signia-ax/
checked.applicability_verdict:
Numbers verified:
- From the 2021 article: SRT80 +3.9 dB with split processing on vs off, n=16 hearing-impaired listeners; 2.1 and 7.3 dB better than two competitors; 48 channels.
- From the 2022 white paper: the KEMAR 6–9 dB and TNT +3 dB figures. The KEMAR 6–9 dB is a phase-inversion output-SNR estimate with the noise placed behind the manikin, the geometry most favorable to a front/back split.

All of these are vendor studies. The device is a per-ear 2-mic beamformer with a binaural link, not '4-mic binaural' (that applies only in the party condition). The numbers do not transfer to a tabletop pair. The architecture is worth copying: a target stream and a residual stream with different gain, compression and NR, then a remix. A mask-based split with a residual at −12 to −20 dB is effectively a gain floor plus separate AGC.

checked.title: OpenSound Navigator (Oticon Opn / Oticon Medical Ponto 4)
checked.correct_citation:
- Primary: N. Le Goff, J. Jensen, M. S. Pedersen, S. L. Callaway, "An Introduction to OpenSound Navigator," Oticon white paper, 2016. I confirmed this only as a reference cited in Hearing Review; I did not retrieve it.
- The URL the sweep gave is a different document: Oticon Medical, "Ponto 4 – a paradigm shift in bone anchored hearing," AudiologyOnline course slides, 06-06-2019.
checked.applicability_verdict:
The 2019 slides verify:
- Analyze: 500×/s over 16 channels, using an omni 'panorama' plus a fixed back-facing cardioid as the noise estimate.
- Balance: null directions placed on dominant noise sources between speech sources, 125×/s.
- Noise removal: 16 bands with centres 155–8750 Hz, in 10-ms steps.

The MVDR claim is unverified, and the sweep correctly hedges it. The 'keep all talkers, remove localized and diffuse noise' philosophy suits the meeting room. With 2 mics there is exactly one adaptive null. The back-cardioid reference needs sub-dB gain matching and loses 6 dB/octave at low frequency.

checked.title: Phonak StereoZoom (binaural 4-mic beamformer)
checked.correct_citation:
- The URL is: Phonak, "Phonak Insight – Binaural directionality: Wireless communication opens the door to a completely new approach in directional multi-microphone systems," July 2010.
- The SRT numbers come from a different source: M. Latzel, "Concepts for binaural processing in hearing aids," Hearing Review, March 2013 (https://hearingreview.com/2013/03/concepts-for-binaural-processing-in-hearing-aids/).
checked.applicability_verdict:
The 2010 PDF does not contain the SRT results, the '3rd order' description or the ±45° nulls. It also says StereoZoom was deliberately kept out of the automatic mode. It does support two points: the ±60° acceptance angle of 2-mic systems, and omni at low frequency / directional at high frequency.

Latzel 2013 supplies:
- SRT80 1.65 dB better than a monaural beamformer and 2.75 dB better than a competitor's directional system.
- 15 subjects with moderate hearing loss; cafeteria noise from 7 loudspeakers.
- A '3rd-order' description with nulls at about ±45°.
- An auto-StereoZoom criterion.

The 'Speech in loud noise' AutoSense OS program came later and is supported by neither document. Use it only to set expectations: 4 mics across the head give about 2 dB over a 2-mic beam. It confirms that a 2.5–6 cm pair is limited to first-order patterns.

checked.title: Conversation Boost (AirPods Pro Transparency mode)
checked.correct_citation: Apple Inc., "Use and customize Transparency mode" (AirPods User Guide, Apple Support). Conversation Boost focuses on the person talking in front of the wearer. The Ambient Noise Reduction slider is a separate control. The feature launched in late 2021 with AirPods Pro firmware 4A400; I did not re-check the firmware number.
checked.applicability_verdict: The support page does not mention beamforming; that wording comes from Apple's 2021 announcement. US 9,516,442 (Dusan, Kanaris, Lindahl; granted 2016-12-06) is a wired-headset patent about earbud position and mic selection. It has front and rear mics plus an accelerometer VAD, but it is not a disclosure of Conversation Boost. No algorithm is disclosed. It is useful only as precedent for a 'focus plus residual slider' UX, so it is low value.

checked.title: anf-generator: Generating coherence-constrained multisensor signals (Python)
checked.correct_citation:
AudioLabs Erlangen / FAU, anf-generator on PyPI: version 0.1.3 released 2026-04-12, MIT, 13 kB wheel, requires numpy≥1.22, scipy≥1.9, matplotlib≥3.6, Python ≥3.8. Methods:
- E. A. P. Habets, I. Cohen, S. Gannot, JASA 124(5):2911–2917, 2008, DOI 10.1121/1.2987429.
- D. Mirabilii, S. J. Schlecht, E. A. P. Habets, JASA 149(3):1425–1433, 2021, DOI 10.1121/10.0003565.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Recommended for controlled tests. Caveats:
(1) Mixing assumes inputs with equal long-term PSDs. In my own 2-channel Cholesky mixing of two different babble sets, the realized coherence missed the target by up to about 0.4 until I spectrally balanced the inputs. Use the package's balanced or smooth options and verify the realized coherence.
(2) A crowded bus is not isotropic. Engine noise is low-frequency and partly coherent, and nearby passengers are point sources at 0.5–2 m. Horizontal babble follows J0 more closely than sinc: at 4 cm the thresholds shift from 1.07/2.59 kHz (sinc above 0.9/0.5) to 0.87/2.08 kHz (J0).
(3) The mic axis must be horizontal. A vertical axis makes horizontal babble broadside and fully coherent.
Complement with real multichannel recordings (DEMAND, CHiME-3 BUS).

missing_key_sources: Y. Hu, P. C. Loizou, "A comparative intelligibility study of single-microphone noise reduction algorithms," J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 122(3):1777–1786, 2007, DOI 10.1121/1.2766778. This is the key reality check: classical single-channel NR (Wiener, LSA, spectral subtraction) generally does not improve intelligibility. The proposed 1-channel stages will improve comfort, not intelligibility.

G. W. Elko, A.-T. Nguyen Pong, "A simple adaptive first-order differential microphone," Proc. IEEE WASPAA 1995, pp. 169–172, DOI 10.1109/ASPAA.1995.482983. The sweep names an 'Elko-style adaptive null' without citing it.

J. Benesty, J. Chen, "Study and Design of Differential Microphone Arrays," Springer, 2013, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-33753-6. Covers first-order DMA design with 2 closely spaced omnis, including white-noise-gain limits.
T. A. Ricketts, "Directional Hearing Aids," Trends in Amplification 5(4):139–176, 2001, DOI 10.1177/108471380100500401. Gives realistic 2-mic directional benefit in reverberant real-world rooms.

K. U. Simmer, J. Bitzer, C. Marro, "Post-Filtering Techniques," in M. Brandstein, D. Ward (eds.), Microphone Arrays, Springer, 2001, pp. 39–60, DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-04619-7_3. The standard review of Zelinski, McCowan and related post-filters.

M. Souden, J. Benesty, S. Affes, "On optimal frequency-domain multichannel linear filtering for noise reduction," IEEE TASLP 18(2):260–276, 2010, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2009.2025790. A 2-mic MVDR/MWF built from PSD matrices; pairs naturally with a CDR-driven speech presence probability, e.g. Taseska & Habets, IWAENC 2012, which I did not re-verify online.

S. Gannot, D. Burshtein, E. Weinstein, "Signal enhancement using beamforming and nonstationarity with applications to speech," IEEE Trans. Signal Process. 49(8):1614–1626, 2001, DOI 10.1109/78.934132. An RTF-based (TF-GSC) 2-mic beamformer that can null one dominant interferer, such as a loud passenger, without knowing the geometry.

S. Doclo, W. Kellermann, S. Makino, S. E. Nordholm, "Multichannel signal enhancement algorithms for assisted listening devices," IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 32(2):18–30, 2015, DOI 10.1109/MSP.2014.2366780. An authoritative overview of hearing-aid and hearable multi-mic processing.

T. Wittkop, V. Hohmann, "Strategy-selective noise reduction for binaural digital hearing aids," Speech Communication 39(1–2):111–138, 2003, DOI 10.1016/S0167-6393(02)00062-6. A hearing-aid coherence/ILD noise reduction scheme, with its documented limits and artifacts in diffuse noise.

M. Jeub, M. Schäfer, T. Esch, P. Vary, "Model-based dereverberation preserving binaural cues," IEEE TASLP 18(7):1732–1745, 2010, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2010.2052156. This is the origin of the 'Jeub' CDR estimator benchmarked by Schwarz and Barfuss. It is a different paper from the Jeub 2012 PLD paper.

Single-channel stages that the sweep names but does not cite:
- R. Martin, IEEE TSAP 9(5):504–512, 2001, DOI 10.1109/89.928915 (minimum statistics).
- I. Cohen, IEEE TSAP 11(5):466–475, 2003, DOI 10.1109/TSA.2003.811544 (IMCRA).
- T. Gerkmann, R. C. Hendriks, IEEE TASLP 20(4):1383–1393, 2012, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2011.2180896 (unbiased MMSE/SPP noise tracking).
- Y. Ephraim, D. Malah, IEEE TASSP 33(2):443–445, 1985, DOI 10.1109/TASSP.1985.1164550 (LSA).

I. Tashev, "Gain self-calibration procedure for microphone arrays," Proc. IEEE ICME 2004, pp. 983–986, DOI 10.1109/ICME.2004.1394367. An industry (Microsoft) mic-mismatch calibration method that complements Qualcomm's.

WPE dereverberation, the main lever for the meeting room, works with 2 channels:
- T. Nakatani et al., "Speech dereverberation based on variance-normalized delayed linear prediction," IEEE TASLP 18(7):1717–1731, 2010, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2010.2052251.
- T. Yoshioka, T. Nakatani, IEEE TASLP 20(10):2707–2720, 2012, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2012.2210879.
- A numpy implementation exists in nara_wpe (L. Drude et al., ITG Speech Communication 2018); I did not re-verify that reference online.

S. Braun et al., "Evaluation and comparison of late reverberation power spectral density estimators," IEEE/ACM TASLP 26(6):1056–1071, 2018, DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2018.2804172. Compares coherence-based and other late-reverb PSD estimators, which is relevant to the 'mild CDR' plan for the meeting room.

K. Kinoshita et al., "A summary of the REVERB challenge," EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. 2016:7, DOI 10.1186/s13634-016-0306-6. Gives 1-, 2- and 8-channel dereverberation results in rooms like the meeting case.

J. Thiemann, N. Ito, E. Vincent, "The Diverse Environments Multi-channel Acoustic Noise Database (DEMAND)," Proc. Meetings on Acoustics 19, 035081, 2013, DOI 10.1121/1.4799597. Real 16-channel array noise including bus, cafeteria and meeting-room environments. The pairs are close to this array's spacing; check the exact geometry. This gives a realistic, non-isotropic bus test.

Real bus recordings from a tablet array, including a 2-channel track:
- J. Barker, R. Marxer, E. Vincent, S. Watanabe, "The third 'CHiME' speech separation and recognition challenge: Dataset, task and baselines," IEEE ASRU 2015, pp. 504–511, DOI 10.1109/ASRU.2015.7404837.
- E. Vincent et al., Computer Speech & Language 46:535–557, 2017, DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2016.11.005 (CHiME-4, which includes the 2-channel track).

R. Scheibler, E. Bezzam, I. Dokmanić, "Pyroomacoustics: A Python package for audio room simulation and array processing algorithms," ICASSP 2018, pp. 351–355, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461310. Provides the RIR simulator the test plan needs, without PyTorch.

Metrics named in the test plan:
- C. H. Taal et al., STOI, IEEE TASLP 19(7):2125–2136, 2011, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2011.2114881.
- J. Le Roux et al., "SDR – half-baked or well done?", ICASSP 2019, pp. 626–630, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2019.8683855 (SI-SDR).

Two-mic time-frequency mask separation by IPD/ILD clustering. Both generalize the Aarabi phase mask to two talkers without fixed TDOA hypotheses:
- O. Yilmaz, S. Rickard, "Blind separation of speech mixtures via time-frequency masking," IEEE Trans. Signal Process. 52(7):1830–1847, 2004, DOI 10.1109/TSP.2004.828896 (DUET).
- M. I. Mandel, R. J. Weiss, D. P. W. Ellis, IEEE TASLP 18(2):382–394, 2010, DOI 10.1109/TASL.2009.2029711 (MESSL).

Z. Chen et al., "Continuous speech separation: dataset and analysis," ICASSP 2020, pp. 7284–7288, DOI 10.1109/ICASSP40776.2020.9053426 (LibriCSS). Real meeting-room replay recordings from a small circular array (radius about 4.25 cm), usable as a test set for the 20-person case.

J.-M. Valin, "A Hybrid DSP/Deep Learning Approach to Real-Time Full-Band Speech Enhancement," IEEE MMSP 2018, DOI 10.1109/MMSP.2018.8547084 (RNNoise; arXiv:1709.08243). A tiny C library that fits the disk and no-PyTorch constraints, as a stage after the spatial post-filter.

A. Kuklasiński, S. Doclo, S. H. Jensen, J. Jensen, "Maximum likelihood PSD estimation for speech enhancement in reverberation and noise," IEEE/ACM TASLP 24(9):1599–1612, 2016, DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2016.2573591. Joint estimation of noise and late reverb for an MWF, from the Oticon/Aalborg line of work.

N. Yousefian, P. C. Loizou, "A dual-microphone algorithm that can cope with competing-talker scenarios," IEEE TASLP 21(1):145–155, 2013. This is the direct follow-up to the coherence algorithm, and it targets the competing-talker weakness. I did not re-verify the citation online because the search budget was exhausted.
verify.notes:
I found all 15 sources, and every one is real. The quoted numbers mostly match the originals. Exceptions:

**1. Wrong source for the Phonak figures.** The Phonak SRT numbers (1.65 dB and 2.75 dB), the '3rd order' description and the ±45° nulls come from Latzel, Hearing Review, March 2013, not from the cited 2010 white paper. That 2010 paper also says StereoZoom was deliberately kept out of the automatic mode.

**2. Audience patents.**
- US 8,194,880 has a single inventor, Avendano.
- '880 uses 8-ms frames. The 4 ms is the energy-smoothing time constant in '759.
- Use in LG, Pantech and Sharp handsets is unverified.

**3. Oticon.** The URL is a 2019 Oticon Medical Ponto 4 course, not the 2016 OSN white paper. The slides do confirm the details: 500/s and 125/s update rates, a back-facing cardioid, and 16 bands at 155–8750 Hz.

**4. Schwarz CDR code.** The lms.lnt.de zip link is dead. Use https://github.com/andreas12345/cdr-dereverb (BSD-2-Clause, MATLAB).

**5. Filterbank.** The paper's 1024-window / 512-FFT filterbank cannot be built with scipy ShortTimeFFT; scipy 1.17.1 raises an error. Use 512/512/128 or a custom WOLA.

**6. Barfuss.** The paper averages diffuseness across mic pairs, not CDR, and uses the 5 forward mics.

**7. Yousefian & Loizou.**
- The Q thresholds are β_low=−0.1 and β_high=−0.3.
- The word-score numbers appear only in figures, so they are approximate.

**8. Schwarz evidence is reverb-only.** It covers single-talker reverberation, no babble, GRID with clean-trained ASR, and 8-cm spacing.

**Overclaims.**

(a) The sweep's '~3–6 dB effective SNR gain against diffuse babble in 1–4 kHz' is optimistic. I ran a numpy check with these conditions:
- Synthetic `say` speech, 16 kHz.
- Ideal spherical-diffuse 8-talker babble at 0 dB SNR, spectrally balanced.
- An anechoic near talker (DRR +6 dB) plus a diffuse reverb tail.
- DOA-independent CDR (eq. 25) with Schwarz's settings, shadow-filtered components.

Results:
- Noise was attenuated 4–6 dB (8–10 dB with λ=0.9), but the target was attenuated 3–4.5 dB (5–7 dB).
- Net SNR gain was about 1–2 dB broadband (2–3.6 dB with λ=0.9) and 0.3–1.5 dB in 1–4 kHz.
- Segmental SNR in 1–4 kHz improved +0.7 to +2.1 dB (+1.3 to +3.1 with λ=0.9).
- Endfire beat broadside by about 0.5–1 dB, and 6 cm beat 2.5 cm by about 0.5 dB.
- Real bus noise, with nearby passengers as point sources and partly coherent engine noise, will do worse. Barfuss's real CHiME-3 BUS data show only 4–6% relative WER gain.

(b) 'Keeps both conversation partners' holds only for partners within about 0.5–0.7 m, i.e. inside the critical distance. At DRR ≈ 0 dB (~1 m) my check gave about 0 dB net gain and negative gain in 1–4 kHz. With µ=1.3, any bin with CDR below −2.2 dB is floored.

(c) The meeting room. The caution against aggressive CDR is justified for listening: a far talker at DRR −8 dB was attenuated 5.6–9 dB with no net SNR gain. Mild settings (µ=0.5, Gmin=0.3) still attenuated the talker by 3.7 dB, again with about 0 net gain, so they are mostly level reduction. The sweep's 'erases far talkers' overstates the ASR case, though: Schwarz found µ=1.3 near-optimal for ASR even at 2–4 m.

(d) The industry SRT figures are vendor lab studies with hearing-impaired listeners: Signia +3.9 dB, Phonak +1.65 dB, and Signia's 6–9 dB KEMAR output-SNR estimate measured with noise from behind. None transfers to a 2-mic tabletop device. Hu & Loizou (2007) show that classical single-channel NR does not improve intelligibility, so expect comfort and quality gains rather than intelligibility gains.

(e) The sinc noise model. Use measured Γn. Horizontal babble behaves more like J0, and the mic axis must be horizontal.

**Process notes.**
- The web-search budget ran out mid-task. I checked the missing-source DOIs by direct Crossref and doi.org lookups, not search. Three citations are flagged as not re-verified: Yousefian 2013, nara_wpe, and Taseska & Habets 2012.
- Simulation script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-chpatel-Library-Application-Support-Claude-scratch-workspaces-7223bc40-0755-4c47-a940-84a904b8ead4-809a743c-126a-440a-9a06-f59818e63020-scratch-2026-11-02-5e756e/c3614d02-9a38-4a14-8dcb-766e8c2e70cf/scratchpad/sim/cdr_check.py. Its audio is in the sibling folder sim/audio.

sweep.angle: Spatial clustering, blind source separation and mask-based beamforming with 2 microphones, including the underdetermined case. Covers DUET, bin-wise clustering with permutation alignment, MESSL, cACGMM/CGMM masks, Souden-form mask-based MVDR (Erdogan/Heymann), GSS (offline, block-online, GPU ablations), the NTT spatial dictionary for online meetings, AuxIVA (offline and low-latency online for hearing aids), ILRMA, FastMNMF (offline and block-online), industry 2-mic ILD clustering (Audience patents), and WPE dereverberation. Libraries: pb_bss, pb_chime5, pyroomacoustics.bss, nara_wpe.

sources.title: Blind Separation of Speech Mixtures via Time-Frequency Masking (DUET). Origin: Jourjine, Rickard & Yilmaz, 'Blind separation of disjoint orthogonal signals: demixing N sources from 2 mixtures', ICASSP 2000. Siemens patent US 6,430,528
sources.authors: Özgür Yılmaz, Scott Rickard (origin paper: Alexander Jourjine, Scott Rickard, Özgür Yılmaz)
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, vol. 52, no. 7, pp. 1830–1847. The citation is confirmed in the reference list of Ito et al., EUSIPCO 2016. Origin paper: ICASSP 2000, vol. 5, pp. 2985–2988
sources.key_idea: W-disjoint orthogonality: in the STFT domain each T-F bin is dominated by at most one talker. So with only 2 mics, N>2 sources can be demixed by binary masks. Each source shows up as one peak in a power-weighted 2-D histogram of relative attenuation and relative delay, computed from the inter-mic ratio X2/X1. Industry origin: the method came from Siemens Corporate Research (patent US 6,430,528, filed 1999, granted 2002, assignee Siemens Corporate Research).
sources.algorithm: 1. STFT X1, X2 (e.g. Hann 1024/256 at 16 kHz). 2. In each bin with ω>0: R=X2/X1, a=|R|, symmetric attenuation α=a−1/a, delay δ=−∠R/ω. 3. Build the histogram H(α,δ)=Σ|X1·X2|^p·ω^q (default p=1, q=0), smooth it with a small kernel and pick the K peaks (α_j,δ_j); the number of peaks is the number of sources. 4. Assign each bin by ML: J(t,f)=argmin_j |a_j·e^{−iωδ_j}·X1−X2|²/(1+a_j²); mask M_j=1[J=j]. 5. Reconstruct ŝ_j=ISTFT(M_j·(X1+a_j·e^{iωδ_j}·X2)/(1+a_j²)). Validity: |ω·δ_max|<π for every ω used. The paper's own example gives d≲2.15 cm at fs=16 kHz. With larger spacing, build the histogram only from f<c/(2d). The forward-model assignment in step 4 still works above that frequency, because the predicted phase e^{−iωδ_j} is never ambiguous.
sources.bus_relevance: A fast, training-free way to find the delays (TDOAs) of the two near talkers. They are loud and have high DRR, so their peaks dominate the power-weighted histogram even in babble. Use those peaks to anchor the classes of a cACGMM or MESSL model, which also fixes the permutation problem. As the final separator it is weak: binary masks cause musical noise, and diffuse babble has no peak, so it is assigned to the nearest talker. You need an explicit noise/garbage class or a coherence/level gate.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not viable as a 20-talker separator with 2 mics. Only a 1-D delay is available (±1.87 samples at 4 cm/16 kHz), sources mirrored about the array axis give the same delay, and RT60 0.5–0.9 s smears the peaks. At best it is a coarse detector of which direction sector is active, which could drive per-sector gain.
sources.two_mic_reality: Echoic office in the paper (RT60≈500 ms, 1.75 cm spacing, 3 talkers at 1.5 m): SIR gain only 4.3–10.6 dB, with PSR 0.56–0.89 and WDO 0.40–0.56, i.e. distorted. Anechoic mixtures of 3–5 sources reached 10–17.7 dB SIR gain. A synthetic 10-source mix kept >12 dB SIR gain but was rated 'very distorted and barely intelligible'. At 2.5/4/6 cm and 16 kHz, delay estimates are phase-ambiguous above 6.9/4.3/2.9 kHz. The near-field ILD (≤1–1.6 dB at 0.3 m, endfire) is about the size of the INMP441's ±1 dB sensitivity mismatch, so calibrate gains before using α. Failure modes: diffuse noise (no peak), reverberant smearing, and broadside or mirror-image talkers that share one delay.
sources.implementation: Write from scratch in numpy, about 120 lines (scipy.signal.stft, np.histogram2d, scipy.ndimage smoothing and peak picking). No maintained Python package found. Runs on Python 3.12–3.14 without extra dependencies.

sources.title: Underdetermined Convolutive Blind Source Separation via Frequency Bin-Wise Clustering and Permutation Alignment
sources.authors: Hiroshi Sawada, Shoko Araki, Shoji Makino (NTT)
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, vol. 19, no. 3, pp. 516–527 (Mar. 2011; citation confirmed in Ito et al. EUSIPCO 2017)
sources.key_idea: Clusters normalized observation vectors separately in each frequency bin with EM. This is robust to reverberation and to spatial aliasing, because no TDOA phase unwrapping is needed. A second stage fixes the per-bin label permutation by aligning the posterior-probability time sequences across frequencies. It works with more sources than mics (2 mics, 3 or more sources). Its normalized-vector feature is the basis of later cWMM/cACGMM clustering.
sources.algorithm: Feature: z_tf=x_tf/‖x_tf‖, phase-normalized to a reference mic, so it lies on the unit hypersphere. In each bin, fit a mixture of K spherical (Watson-like) densities, each with a centroid a_kf and a spread σ_kf; EM gives posteriors P(k|z_tf). Permutation alignment: maximize the correlation of posterior sequences against global centroids, then refine using adjacent and harmonically related bins. Separation: ŷ_k,tf=P(k|z_tf)·x_ref,tf (soft or binary).
sources.bus_relevance: Bin-wise clustering with K=3 (talker A, talker B, noise) avoids DUET's spacing limit, so it works at 4–6 cm and 16 kHz. Aligning by posterior correlation works because the two talkers mostly alternate and so have different activity patterns. The weak spot is low frequencies, where adjacent bins correlate poorly, which is exactly where engine and babble energy sit.
sources.meeting_relevance: Works for a few simultaneous sources only, not 20. Permutation alignment gets worse with more reverberation and more sources, as the MESSL authors also observed. Use it only on overlap segments with 2–3 active talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: In MESSL's binaural reverberant comparison (RT60≈565 ms) this method ranked third. On the example 2-talker mixture it reached 6.87 dB SDR, against 8.32 dB for MESSL and 5.48 dB for DUET. It had trouble unpermuting low-frequency bins, and that got worse with reverberation and with more sources. With 2 mics each bin holds only 2-D vectors. Diffuse noise is highly coherent at low frequency (>0.9 below about 1 kHz at 4 cm), so its cluster overlaps those of broadside talkers.
sources.implementation: numpy from scratch (about 250 lines). Alternatively assemble it from pb_bss: the CWMM/CACGMM models in pb_bss.distribution plus pb_bss.permutation_alignment.DHTVPermutationAlignment (MIT licence).

sources.title: Model-Based Expectation-Maximization Source Separation and Localization (MESSL)
sources.authors: Michael I. Mandel, Ron J. Weiss, Daniel P. W. Ellis
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, vol. 18, no. 2, pp. 382–394, Feb. 2010 (the preprint header reads vol. 17 no. 8, Nov. 2009)
sources.key_idea: Probabilistic spatial clustering of a reverberant, underdetermined 2-channel recording. Each source has a frequency-dependent IPD model, built as a mixture over a grid of candidate ITDs, which removes the phase-wrapping/aliasing ambiguity, plus an ILD model. EM gives soft T-F masks. An extra 'garbage' source absorbs reverberation and noise.
sources.algorithm: For source i and ITD τ on a grid covering ±d/c: IPD residual φ̂(ω,t;τ)=∠(L·R*·e^{−jωτ}) ~ N(ξ_iτ(ω), σ²_iτ(ω)); ILD α(ω,t)=20·log10|L/R| ~ N(μ_i(ω), η²_i(ω)). E-step: posterior z_iτ(ω,t) ∝ ψ_iτ·N(φ̂)·N(α). M-step: weighted means and variances (frequency-dependent or tied) and ITD priors ψ. Mask M_i=Σ_τ z_iτ. Initialize from PHAT-histogram ITD peaks and run about 16 EM iterations. The garbage source and an ILD prior give the largest gains in reverberation.
sources.bus_relevance: Matches the bus need closely using only IPD/ILD: two talker models plus a garbage model for crowd, engine and reverb. The explicit ITD grid handles the aliasing that 4–6 cm spacing causes at 16 kHz. After gain calibration the ILD term adds a weak near-field cue. The soft masks can feed per-talker MVDRs or be applied directly with a floor.
sources.meeting_relevance: Designed for a few sources. With 20 talkers, mirror ambiguity and DRR far below 0 dB at 3–6 m make per-talker clusters unreliable. It could map garbage versus direct-path energy, but far talkers would be labelled garbage, which defeats the goal of capturing everyone.
sources.two_mic_reality: Real classroom, RT60≈565 ms, KEMAR binaural recordings at 1 m, 2–3 talkers: MESSL averaged +1.6 dB SDR and +0.27 PESQ MOS over DUET, Sawada, Mouba-Marchand and TRINICON. On one 2-talker example it reached 8.32 dB SDR, against 5.48 dB for DUET and 12.78 dB for the direct-path oracle. Performance drops when talkers are less than about 40° apart and a second distractor is present. TRINICON reached higher SIR (12.79 dB vs MESSL's 11.07 dB) but added reverberation. The KEMAR head produced large ILDs; a free-field 4 cm pair has almost none, so expect results below the reported ones. 'Bands of ambiguity' remain at frequencies where two ITDs predict the same wrapped IPD.
sources.implementation: Reference code is MATLAB only (github.com/mim/messl); no Python port found. Port it to numpy, roughly 300 lines.

sources.title: Complex Angular Central Gaussian Mixture Model for Directional Statistics in Mask-Based Microphone Array Signal Processing (cACGMM)
sources.authors: Nobutaka Ito, Shoko Araki, Tomohiro Nakatani (NTT)
sources.venue: EUSIPCO 2016, Budapest, pp. 1153–1157 (IEEE Xplore 7760429)
sources.key_idea: Models unit-norm multichannel STFT vectors with a mixture of complex angular central Gaussians. Unlike the complex Watson model, this can represent elliptical spatial clusters, not only rotationally symmetric ones. The EM posteriors are the T-F masks for each source or noise class. This model is the mask estimator inside GSS (CHiME-5 to CHiME-8 systems) and in pb_bss.
sources.algorithm: z_tf=y_tf/‖y_tf‖ (M=2). p(z)=Σ_k α_f^k·A(z;B_f^k), with A(z;B) ∝ det(B)^{-1}·(z^H·B^{-1}·z)^{-M}. E-step: γ_tf^k ∝ α_f^k·det(B_f^k)^{-1}·(z^H·(B_f^k)^{-1}·z)^{-M}. M-step: α_f^k=mean_t γ_tf^k; B_f^k = M·Σ_t γ_tf^k·z·z^H/(z^H·(B_f^k)^{-1}·z) / Σ_t γ_tf^k. Normalize B (trace or eigenvalue) and floor its eigenvalues. Paper settings: 128 ms frames, 32 ms shift, 100 EM iterations, permutation fixed by Sawada's method. In practice 10–20 iterations are enough (GSS gained nothing beyond 5). With speaker activity a_tk known, use time-varying weights α_tfk ∝ α_fk·a_tk.
sources.bus_relevance: The best-documented match to this hardware: the paper itself used two omni mics 4 cm apart with sources 0.6 m and 1.2 m away. For the bus, use K=3 classes (talker A, talker B, noise). Initialize the talker posteriors from the likelihood of each DUET/GCC-PHAT TDOA peak; the predicted phase e^{−jωτ_k} stays unambiguous above c/2d. Initialize the noise class with B ≈ the 2×2 diffuse-coherence matrix. Output the union mask γ_A+γ_B for a post-filter, and the per-talker masks for per-talker MVDRs.
sources.meeting_relevance: A blind 20-class cACGMM on 2 mics is not identifiable. Use it only with guidance, as in GSS (diarization gives 2–3 active classes per segment), or as a coarse direction-sector model.
sources.two_mic_reality: Noise-free simulations with 2 mics at 4 cm, fs 8 kHz, measured room impulse responses (values read from Fig. 2): 2 sources gave about 15.7 dB SDR at RT60 0.13 s, falling to about 8.7 dB at 0.44 s. 3 sources (underdetermined) gave about 8.3 dB falling to about 4.5 dB. That is +1.2 dB over cWMM and +0.9 dB over cBMM. With diffuse babble added, the noise class competes with broadside talkers at low frequency, because 2-mic diffuse coherence at 4 cm is 0.98, 0.91 and 0.68 at 0.5, 1 and 2 kHz. Expect lower numbers than reported. Permutation handling is required: DHTV alignment, or TDOA/activity guidance.
sources.implementation: pb_bss (github.com/fgnt/pb_bss, MIT). Install from git; it compiles Cython, so it needs clang and Cython; dependencies are numpy, scipy and einops. API: CACGMMTrainer().fit(y, num_classes=3 or initialization=..., iterations=10–20, weight_constant_axis=...); CACGMM.predict(y, source_activity_mask=...). Compatibility with numpy 2.x and Python 3.12–3.14 is not stated; test it. Otherwise about 80 lines of numpy using closed-form 2×2 inverses and determinants.

sources.title: Improved MVDR Beamforming Using Single-Channel Mask Prediction Networks (Souden-form mask-based MVDR)
sources.authors: Hakan Erdogan, John R. Hershey, Shinji Watanabe, Michael I. Mandel, Jonathan Le Roux (MERL)
sources.venue: Interspeech 2016, pp. 1981–1985, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2016-552. Builds on Souden, Benesty & Affes, IEEE TASLP 18(2):260–276, 2010, and on Heymann, Drude & Haeb-Umbach, ICASSP 2016 pp. 196–200 (https://ris.uni-paderborn.de/record/11812)
sources.key_idea: Any T-F speech mask, whether from a single-channel enhancer, a spatial clustering model or a neural network, can steer an MVDR without knowing the array geometry or the DOA. The mask gives speech and noise spatial covariance matrices, which go into Souden's steering-free MVDR. Heymann et al. did the same with BLSTM masks plus GEV beamforming with blind analytic normalization (BAN), and showed that mask training does not depend on the number or layout of mics.
sources.algorithm: Φ_N(f)=Σ_t(1−m_tf)·y·y^H/Σ(1−m); Φ_S from mask-weighting, or Φ_Y−Φ_N. Souden MVDR: h(f)=Φ_N^{-1}·Φ_S·e_ref / tr(Φ_N^{-1}·Φ_S). The reference mic is the one with the highest a-posteriori SNR. Best variant: one mask shared by all mics (the max of the per-channel masks), then a post-mask from the reference-channel mask with a minimum floor of 0.3. Alternative GEV: w = principal generalized eigenvector of (Φ_S, Φ_N), followed by BAN. Add diagonal loading for 2×2 stability.
sources.bus_relevance: Turns cACGMM, MESSL or neural masks into a low-distortion linear filter. With 2 mics, though, MVDR has one degree of freedom. It can null one point interferer, or gain only about 0.2–1.7 dB against ideal diffuse babble for broadside talkers (4 cm, ≤3 kHz), up to about 3–6 dB for endfire talkers (superdirective, needs white-noise gain of −10 to −15 dB at ≤500 Hz). A single linear filter that must keep both talkers distortionless has zero degrees of freedom left, so it gives about 0 dB. Instead build one MVDR per talker (Φ_N from the noise class only), pick or blend them per T-F bin by the posteriors, and apply a floor-limited post-mask.
sources.meeting_relevance: A per-utterance MVDR toward the active talker, with masks from GSS or a spatial dictionary, gains a little SNR against HVAC noise and adds mild dereverberation. The noise mask must not label far, reverberant talkers as noise.
sources.two_mic_reality: The paper's results are on the 6-mic CHiME-3 tablet. Real-test SDR rose to 5.52 dB from 1.69 dB unprocessed, and WER was 34.78% against 36.19% for weighted delay-and-sum (mismatched ASR). On the real set, PESQ was slightly better without a post-mask. NTT's mask-based-MVDR exhibition prototype (HSCMA 2017, per NTT's Interspeech 2024 keynote; array size not stated there): WER 40.5% unprocessed, 57.5% with masking alone, 24.1% with mask-based MVDR. Masks on their own add artifacts. With 2 mics expect the MVDR stage to add about 1–3 dB at most; most suppression has to come from the floored mask.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 40 lines (2×2 matrices; diagonal loading ≈1e-3·tr/2). Or pb_bss.extraction.beamformer: get_mvdr_vector_souden, get_gev_vector, blind_analytic_normalization, get_wmwf_vector, get_lcmv_vector_souden. Neural masks need a trained model and there is no PyTorch here. Use cACGMM/CGMM masks instead, or a mask taken from a small single-channel ONNX denoiser: m=min(1,|Ŝ|/|Y|).

sources.title: Online MVDR Beamformer Based on Complex Gaussian Mixture Model With Spatial Prior for Noise Robust ASR
sources.authors: Takuya Higuchi, Nobutaka Ito, Shoko Araki, Takuya Yoshioka, Marc Delcroix, Tomohiro Nakatani (NTT)
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM TASLP, vol. 25, pp. 780–793, doi:10.1109/TASLP.2017.2665341. Online extension of Higuchi et al., ICASSP 2016 pp. 5210–5214, the mask-based MVDR used in NTT's CHiME-3 winning system
sources.key_idea: A time-varying complex Gaussian mixture (speech and noise) on the raw multichannel STFT vectors produces the masks for MVDR. Block-online EM with accumulated statistics makes it streaming. A probabilistic prior on each class's spatial correlation matrix stops the speech class from drifting onto noise or interferers while the target is silent.
sources.algorithm: y_tf | k ~ N_C(0, φ_ktf·R_kf). E-step: γ_ktf ∝ N_C(y; 0, φ·R). M-step: φ_ktf = y^H·R_kf^{-1}·y/M; R_kf = Σ_t γ·y·y^H/φ / Σ_t γ, plus a prior term pulling it toward R_prior. Online: per block, run one or a few EM iterations, initialized from the previous R and regularized by the prior, then MVDR with the principal eigenvector of Φ_S, or Souden's form. R_prior can be a position-specific (enrolled) covariance.
sources.bus_relevance: Fits a streaming bus pipeline. Enroll each talker's spatial correlation as the prior from a few seconds of them speaking. Then compute posteriors online per frame or per block, feeding per-talker MVDR and a post-mask with roughly block latency. The prior is exactly what keeps a talker's class anchored during long silences.
sources.meeting_relevance: Can use a prior or dictionary of seat positions for online processing (see the NTT spatial dictionary). With 2 mics, the priors for mirror-image seats are identical.
sources.two_mic_reality: Online processing performed about as well as batch with a suitable block size. On a conversation task the spatial prior cut WER from 38.4% to 29.2% compared with CGMM without the prior. CHiME-3 evaluation WER went from 8.37% to 8.06% (multi-mic tablet). With M=2, R_k is 2×2, and low-frequency diffuse noise is nearly rank-1, so it is hard to tell apart from broadside speech. Lean on the time-varying power φ (spectral level) as much as on the spatial cue.
sources.implementation: numpy from scratch, about 150 lines. The CGMM-related distribution modules in pb_bss can be adapted. Real-time is easily within reach on the M1 for 2 channels.

sources.title: Front-End Processing for the CHiME-5 Dinner Party Scenario (Guided Source Separation, GSS), plus Block-Online GSS (Horiguchi, Fujita, Nagamatsu, Hitachi, IEEE SLT 2021, arXiv:2011.07791)
sources.authors: Christoph Boeddeker, Jens Heitkaemper, Joerg Schmalenstroeer, Lukas Drude, Jahn Heymann, Reinhold Haeb-Umbach (Paderborn University)
sources.venue: CHiME-5 Workshop 2018, pp. 35–40, doi:10.21437/CHiME.2018-8
sources.key_idea: Speaker-activity (diarization) annotations guide a cACGMM. The activities become time-varying mixture weights, which fixes both the number of sources and the frequency permutation. An always-active noise class and a context window are added, then a mask-based MVDR is computed per utterance. The pipeline is WPE, then GSS, then MVDR, with no neural network. It is the de facto CHiME-6 front end.
sources.algorithm: 1. Dereverberate with WPE; normalize ỹ=y/‖y‖. 2. cACGMM with K = speakers + 1 noise class. Weights π_tfk = π_fk·a_tk / Σ_k' π_fk'·a_tk', where a_tk∈{0,1} comes from diarization and the noise class always has a=1. 3. Run EM (5–20 iterations) on the utterance plus about 15 s of context. 4. Φ_k=Σ_t γ_k·ỹ·ỹ^H/T and Φ_bg=Σ_t(Σ_{k'≠k}γ_k')·ỹ·ỹ^H/T. 5. Souden MVDR h=Φ_bg^{-1}·Φ_k·e_ref/tr(·), then BAN; reference mic chosen by SNR. Block-online variant: 2.4 s blocks with 2.4 s of pre-context, one EM iteration per block, only active speakers updated. It was about 32× faster than offline GSS with nearly the same WER, fast enough for real time.
sources.bus_relevance: If you can label who is talking, GSS-style time-varying weights make the 3-class cACGMM (A, B, noise) much more stable than blind clustering. Labels could come from a 2-speaker diarizer, or even from loudness plus TDOA segmentation, since the two talkers alternate. The block-online version gives about 2–3 s latency.
sources.meeting_relevance: The standard meeting front end (CHiME-6 baseline; CHiME-7/8 systems): for each utterance, extract the active speaker from overlap and noise. With 20 talkers the guidance has to come from speaker-embedding diarization, not from 2-mic spatial cues. With 2 mics, GSS reduces to a 2×2 mask plus MVDR per segment, and it does not even out loudness by itself.
sources.two_mic_reality: In the original CHiME-5 setup (Kinect 4-mic arrays), WPE+GSS+beamforming cut WER by 10.5% relative on the single-array track and 21.1% relative on the multiple-array track. The channel count dominates: see Raj et al. (7 vs 2 channels). Expect only modest gains with 2 mics, mostly in overlapped speech.
sources.implementation: CPU/numpy route: fgnt/pb_chime5 (MIT; the original GSS; depends on nara_wpe, pb_bss, paderbox, dlp_mpi), or re-implement the core (about 200 lines) on top of pb_bss. The popular desh2608/gss package requires CuPy/CUDA, so it will not run on an M1 Mac.

sources.title: GPU-accelerated Guided Source Separation for Meeting Transcription
sources.authors: Desh Raj, Daniel Povey, Sanjeev Khudanpur (JHU / Xiaomi)
sources.venue: Interspeech 2023 (arXiv:2212.05271)
sources.key_idea: A batched GSS implementation, about 300× faster than the original, made systematic ablations on real meeting corpora possible. The number of input channels was the single most important factor. 15 s of context was best, more than 5 EM iterations brought no gain, the noise class matters when there is background noise (AMI), and WPE matters in reverberant conditions (LibriCSS).
sources.algorithm: Same as GSS: WPE, then cACGMM with activity-weighted mixture weights and a noise class, then Souden MVDR per segment. Ablated settings: context 5–25 s (15 s best), BSS iterations (beyond 5 gives no improvement), number of channels, noise class on or off, WPE on or off. For non-oracle segmentation, diarization used spectral clustering of ResNet speaker embeddings, with and without overlap assignment.
sources.bus_relevance: Mostly indirect. It shows the knobs that matter: keep a noise class and a few seconds of context, and adding mics beats a cleverer algorithm.
sources.meeting_relevance: The most directly quantified evidence of what 2 mics can do for meeting extraction. 7 channels gave 50.4% (LibriCSS) and 21.8% (AMI) relative WER reduction compared with 2 channels. With full arrays (7–8 mics), GSS recovered 86.8%, 65.9% and 80.4% of the gap between far-field and close-talk WER on LibriCSS, AMI and AliMeeting. With a real diarizer instead of oracle segments, GSS still cut cpWER by 29.1%, 19.5% and 19.7% relative.
sources.two_mic_reality: Implies that 2-mic GSS will capture only a fraction of those gains. With 20 talkers, diarization quality will matter more than spatial resolution.
sources.implementation: github.com/desh2608/gss (MIT, CuPy/CUDA plus Lhotse) cannot run on Apple M1. Use the pb_chime5/pb_bss CPU path; the repo's recipes are still useful as a reference.

sources.title: Data-driven and Physical Model-based Designs of Probabilistic Spatial Dictionary for Online Meeting Diarization and Adaptive Beamforming (NTT), with the companion online meeting-recognition prototype 'Online Meeting Recognition in Noisy Environments with Time-Frequency Mask Based MVDR Beamforming' (Araki et al., HSCMA 2017)
sources.authors: Nobutaka Ito, Shoko Araki, Tomohiro Nakatani. Prototype: Shoko Araki, Nobutaka Ito, Marc Delcroix, Atsunori Ogawa, Keisuke Kinoshita, Takuya Higuchi, Takuya Yoshioka, Dung Tran, Shigeki Karita, Tomohiro Nakatani (NTT)
sources.venue: EUSIPCO 2017; prototype at IEEE HSCMA 2017 (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/?p=480210); summarized in NTT's Interspeech 2024 keynote (https://interspeech2024.org/wp-content/uploads/IS24_Keynote_Shoko-Araki.pdf)
sources.key_idea: An industry-lab system for a fixed device on a meeting table. It precomputes a 'spatial dictionary': one directional-statistics distribution of normalized observation vectors for each candidate speaker DOA (17 positions around the table), plus one background-noise distribution. Online, only the mixture weights are inferred. That gives online DOA detection, which gives diarization, then masks, then MVDR, with WPE in front. A physical-model (plane-wave) dictionary needs only the array geometry.
sources.algorithm: z_tf=y_tf/‖y_tf‖. For each DOA entry k: p(z|k,f) = complex Watson W(z; a_kf, κ_f), where a_kf is the normalized plane-wave steering vector and κ_f follows an inverse-square law in frequency with one tuned constant. A separate noise entry models background noise. Per block, estimate time-varying weights over the K DOA entries plus noise. Active DOAs are speakers; their masks γ_k drive a Souden MVDR. The live prototype ran with 3–5 s latency at an exhibition.
sources.bus_relevance: The same idea gives a training-free, low-latency bus mode. Build a dictionary over a 1-D TDOA grid plus a noise entry; the two talkers' entries stand out by their weights. No EM over covariance matrices is needed, so it is robust and cheap.
sources.meeting_relevance: The closest published system to the meeting test case: diarization plus per-talker beamforming in noise and reverberation. With 2 mics the dictionary collapses to about 5–9 distinguishable delay bins at 4 cm (±1.87 samples; more with wider spacing), with mirror-image ambiguity. It cannot tell 20 seats apart alone. Combine it with speaker embeddings, and use it to drive per-talker AGC.
sources.two_mic_reality: Reported results used a 4 cm cubic multi-mic array in a room with RT60 500 ms, babble from 10 loudspeakers at 3–15 dB SNR, and 4–6 speakers. WER was 24.1% (data-driven dictionary) and 24.9% (physical-model dictionary), against 40.5% for a single distant mic and 18.8% for headsets. In the keynote, masking alone gave 57.5%, worse than no processing. With 2 mics the dictionary is far less discriminative; expect only a fraction of this.
sources.implementation: numpy from scratch, about 200 lines (a complex Watson or cACG density per grid point; closed-form 2×2 math).

sources.title: Stable and Fast Update Rules for Independent Vector Analysis Based on Auxiliary Function Technique (AuxIVA)
sources.authors: Nobutaka Ono
sources.venue: IEEE WASPAA 2011, pp. 189–192
sources.key_idea: Determined (N=M) frequency-domain BSS. A per-frequency demixing matrix makes the outputs independent, and a spherical (vector) source prior ties all frequencies of one source together, which avoids the permutation problem.
