The auxiliary-function ('iterative projection') updates have no tuning parameters, decrease the objective monotonically, and converge faster than natural gradient.
sources.algorithm: y_tf=W_f·x_tf; r_kt=sqrt(Σ_f|y_ktf|²); V_kf=(1/T)·Σ_t (G'(r_kt)/r_kt)·x·x^H (for a Laplace prior, G'(r)/r=1/r); w_kf ← (W_f·V_kf)^{-1}·e_k; w_kf ← w_kf/sqrt(w^H·V_kf·w). Run 20–100 iterations, then project back to the reference mic. For 2×2 a closed-form 'IP2' update exists. In hearing aids, Kellermann's group used 2-channel BSS as a noise-reference 'blocking matrix' (Reindl, Zheng, Kellermann, ISCCSP 2010, doi:10.1109/ISCCSP.2010.5463317).
sources.bus_relevance: With 2 mics it can separate at most 2 point sources. On the bus the target is both talkers and the crowd is diffuse, so IVA just splits the scene into two outputs that each still carry babble, with no net noise reduction. It helps only to cancel one dominant point interferer (a loud neighbour, a loudspeaker announcement), or as a hearing-aid-style noise reference for a post-filter.
sources.meeting_relevance: Cannot track 20 talkers. It could separate a 2-talker overlap, but STFT-domain IVA degrades when RT60 (0.5–0.9 s) is much longer than the frame, and the outputs' identities are unknown without diarization.
sources.two_mic_reality: Only the determined 2×2 case. Diffuse noise and reverberation leak into both outputs, and the mismatch between frame length and RT60 limits separation in the meeting room.
sources.implementation: pyroomacoustics.bss.auxiva(X, n_src=2, n_iter=20–100, proj_back=True, model='laplace'); this also implements OverIVA. pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 ships universal2 wheels for cp312, cp313 and cp314 (about 1.3 MB).

sources.title: Low-Latency Real-Time Blind Source Separation for Hearing Aids Based on Time-Domain Implementation of Online Independent Vector Analysis with Truncation of Non-Causal Components
sources.authors: Masahiro Sunohara (RION Co., Ltd., hearing-aid maker), Chiho Haruta, Nobutaka Ono
sources.venue: IEEE ICASSP 2017 (IEEE Xplore 7952149)
sources.key_idea: Industry route to hearing-aid latency for BSS. Online AuxIVA runs in the STFT domain; its demixing matrices are converted to time-domain FIR filters, and part of their non-causal taps is truncated, based on a causality analysis of ideal separation filters. Separation then runs with less than 10 ms algorithmic delay.
sources.algorithm: Online AuxIVA: V_kf(t)=α·V_kf(t−1)+(1−α)·(1/r_kt)·x_tf·x_tf^H, with r_kt from the current output, followed by a per-frame IP update w_kf=(W_f·V_kf)^{-1}·e_k and normalization. Periodically convert W_f (after projection back) to FIR demixing filters by IFFT and a circular shift, truncate the non-causal part, and filter in the time domain.
sources.bus_relevance: Shows that 2-channel IVA can run in real time at hearing-aid latency. As with AuxIVA, its value on the bus is limited to point interferers. The FIR-conversion trick, however, can be reused for any frequency-domain spatial filter, such as per-talker MVDRs, when low latency matters.
sources.meeting_relevance: Low: it separates only two point sources.
sources.two_mic_reality: About 7.7 dB SIR with a head-and-torso simulator in a real room, less than 1.4 dB below the conventional frequency-domain implementation. The abstract does not state the mic count. The figure measures interferer suppression (SIR), not diffuse-noise reduction.
sources.implementation: numpy from scratch, about 120 lines on top of an online AuxIVA loop; validate on pyroomacoustics simulations.

sources.title: Determined Blind Source Separation Unifying Independent Vector Analysis and Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (ILRMA)
sources.authors: Daichi Kitamura, Nobutaka Ono, Hiroshi Sawada, Hirokazu Kameoka, Hiroshi Saruwatari
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM TASLP, vol. 24, no. 9, pp. 1626–1641. The citation was confirmed through citing works; the link points to the open-access review by Sawada, Ono, Kameoka, Kitamura & Saruwatari, APSIPA Trans. Signal Inf. Process. 8:e12 (2019), which covers ILRMA
sources.key_idea: AuxIVA with an NMF (low-rank) source-variance model instead of a flat spherical prior. It uses the same iterative-projection demixing update, is usually better than IVA, and is much faster and more stable than full-rank MNMF.
sources.algorithm: Source variance r_ktf=Σ_l t_kfl·v_klt (L bases). V_kf=(1/T)·Σ_t x·x^H/r_ktf; w_kf ← (W_f·V_kf)^{-1}·e_k, then normalize. NMF multiplicative updates (IS divergence) on P_ktf=|y_ktf|², e.g. t ← t·sqrt(Σ_t P·v/r² / Σ_t v/r), and similarly for v; rescale. Run 100–200 iterations, then project back.
sources.bus_relevance: Same determined 2×2 limits as AuxIVA. Speech is only moderately low-rank and babble even less, so the gain over IVA is small. Not a priority for the bus.
sources.meeting_relevance: No: it is determined and gives only 2 outputs.
sources.two_mic_reality: Each source has a rank-1 (point-source) spatial model, so diffuse babble and reverberation cannot be represented. The FastMNMF authors describe ILRMA as suffering a 'severe loss of spatial modeling ability'.
sources.implementation: pyroomacoustics.bss.ilrma(X, n_src=2, n_iter=100, n_components=2–8, proj_back=True).

sources.title: Fast Multichannel Source Separation Based on Jointly Diagonalizable Spatial Covariance Matrices (FastMNMF), with the online follow-ups 'DNN-Free Low-Latency Adaptive Speech Enhancement Based on Frame-Online Beamforming Powered by Block-Online FastMNMF' (arXiv:2207.10934) and the AR-headset system (arXiv:2207.07296)
sources.authors: Kouhei Sekiguchi, Aditya Arie Nugraha, Yoshiaki Bando, Kazuyoshi Yoshii (RIKEN AIP / Kyoto Univ. / AIST). 2022 papers add Mathieu Fontaine and Yicheng Du
sources.venue: EUSIPCO 2019 (arXiv:1903.03237). FastMNMF2: IEEE/ACM TASLP 2020. Online systems: arXiv 2022 (IWAENC/IROS-era papers)
sources.key_idea: A full-rank spatial covariance model, which can represent diffuse noise and reverberant sources and allows more sources than mics. It is made tractable by requiring all sources' covariances in a bin to be jointly diagonalizable by one matrix Q_f, combined with NMF source spectra and ILRMA-like IP updates. It runs an order of magnitude faster than MNMF and separates better. Online version: FastMNMF runs block-wise as a back end and feeds posterior statistics to a frame-online MVDR front end.
sources.algorithm: Model: x_tf ~ N_C(0, Σ_n λ_ntf·Q_f^{-1}·diag(g̃_n)·Q_f^{-H}), with λ_ntf=Σ_c u_ncf·v_nct. MM updates: IP for the rows of Q_f; multiplicative updates for g̃_n, u and v. Per-source Wiener filter W_ntf=Q_f^{-1}·diag(λ·g̃_n/Σλ·g̃)·Q_f. Online dual process: a back end runs WPE plus FastMNMF on blocks of several seconds, initialized from the target direction, and keeps exponential moving averages of W̃_n and the posterior covariances Σ̃_n. A front end applies online WPE, forms frame-wise Γ_n=W̃·x·x^H·W̃^H+Σ̃ and noise Υ=x·x^H−Γ, and computes MVDR w=tr(Υ^{-1}Γ)^{-1}·Υ^{-1}Γ·u_ref. Total latency 22 ms.
sources.bus_relevance: The strongest blind, training-free model for 'two talkers plus a diffuse crowd' with only 2 mics. Set N=3–4: A, B, and 1–2 noise sources with full-rank SCMs; pick the talker outputs by TDOA and energy. The DNN-free dual-process version shows how to make it streaming at 22 ms latency.
sources.meeting_relevance: N≈20 sources with M=2 is hopeless. It could run per diarized segment with N=2–3.
sources.two_mic_reality: The published numbers are multi-mic. On 5-mic CHiME-3 simulations FastMNMF reached about 15–17 dB SDR versus about 11–13 dB for MNMF, at roughly 0.7–3 s per iteration for 8 s of audio on a Xeon CPU; M=2 is far cheaper. On a HoloLens 2 (5 mics, RT60≈0.8 s, 2 talkers plus diffuse noise) the frame-online system beat DNN-mask MVDR by 5.0 WER points at 22 ms latency. With M=2, Q_f is 2×2, so more than 2 sources are told apart only by 2-D nonnegative gain vectors plus NMF spectra. Spatial discrimination is weaker, but this is still the right model for diffuse noise.
sources.implementation: pyroomacoustics.bss.fastmnmf and fastmnmf2(X, n_src=3, n_iter=30–100, n_components=8, mic_index=0). Write the block-online and front-end parts from scratch in numpy (about 250 lines).

sources.title: Adaptive noise reduction using level cues (US 8,718,290 B2) and System and method for utilizing inter-microphone level differences for speech enhancement (US 8,867,759 B2), Audience Inc., maker of the earSmart phone voice processors
sources.authors: Carlo Murgia, Carlos Avendano, Karim Younes, Mark Every, Ye Jiang (US 8,718,290); Carlos Avendano, Lloyd Watts, Peter Santos (US 8,867,759)
sources.venue: US patents granted 6 May 2014 and 21 Oct 2014 (priority 2010 and 2006). Original assignee Audience; Google Patents lists Samsung as current assignee
sources.key_idea: Phone-industry 2-omni-mic noise suppression by T-F clustering of a spatial cue. Per sub-band, the inter-microphone level difference (ILD) is tracked at runtime as separate speech and noise clusters, normalized for mic mismatch, handset and talker position. The cluster decision gates an adaptive null-processing noise canceller and drives a Wiener-type post-filter gain mask. Second patent: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8867759
sources.algorithm: Cochlea-like sub-band analysis of the primary and secondary mics (about 2–20 cm apart; a third 'spread' mic gives stronger level cues). ILD_k(t) is a bounded, normalized energy ratio in [−1,1]. The cluster tracker estimates per-band speech-ILD and noise-ILD and classifies each T-F point as speech or noise. An adaptive NPNS subtraction cascade adapts only where noise dominates. The noise estimate drives a smoothed Wiener post-filter mask before resynthesis. In US 8,867,759, ILD is near 1 when the talker is close to the primary mic, the noise estimator freezes above an ILD threshold, and the example uses 4 ms frames at 16 kHz.
sources.bus_relevance: The productized version of the bus idea: near talkers produce a different level and phase signature than the far crowd. With a 4 cm pair and talkers 0.3–1 m away, the near-field ILD is only about 0.3–1.1 dB (endfire), too weak on its own. Combined with IPD it is still a useful extra cluster feature. It also argues for a hardware change: spread the two mics far apart, e.g. one near each talker at 10–30 cm, so each talker has a large ILD toward 'their' mic.
sources.meeting_relevance: Low. For talkers 1 m or more away, ILD between closely spaced mics is about 0 dB. Level cues favour near over far talkers, which is the opposite of what the meeting needs.
sources.two_mic_reality: Designed for handset close-talk, with the mouth a few cm from the primary mic and a large ILD. For a table device the cue is weak and comparable to the INMP441's ±1 dB sensitivity tolerance, so per-band gain calibration is mandatory. The patents give no published performance figures.
sources.implementation: numpy from scratch, about 150 lines: STFT bands, calibrated ILD and IPD, online 2-cluster GMM/k-means per band, Wiener gain with a floor.

sources.title: NARA-WPE: A Python package for weighted prediction error dereverberation in Numpy and Tensorflow for online and offline processing
sources.authors: Lukas Drude, Jahn Heymann, Christoph Boeddeker, Reinhold Haeb-Umbach (Paderborn University). WPE algorithm: Nakatani et al., IEEE TASLP 2010; Yoshioka & Nakatani, IEEE TASLP 20(10):2707–2720, 2012
sources.venue: 13. ITG Fachtagung Sprachkommunikation (ITG 2018)
sources.key_idea: Blind multichannel linear-prediction dereverberation (WPE). It removes late reverberation while keeping inter-channel cues, which makes it the standard first stage before spatial clustering, GSS or MVDR. It is used in GSS, the NTT meeting system and the FastMNMF online systems. Offline, block-online and frame-online (RLS) versions are provided.
sources.algorithm: STFT 512/128 at 16 kHz. x̂_tf=y_tf−G_f^H·ỹ_{t−Δ,f}, where ỹ stacks K=10 past frames of all M channels after a delay Δ=3. Iterate 3–5 times: λ_t = mean over mics of |x̂_mtf|² (per bin); R_f=Σ_t ỹ·ỹ^H/λ_t; P_f=Σ_t ỹ·y^H/λ_t; G_f=R_f^{-1}·P_f. Online: recursive (RLS) updates of R^{-1} and G with forgetting factor α≈0.9999. These are the values in the repo's example notebooks.
sources.bus_relevance: Low priority. Talkers at 0.3–1 m in an absorptive cabin have estimated DRR of about +7 to −3 dB. WPE would mostly reduce the crowd's reverberant tail and is not needed for a first prototype.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. At 3–6 m with RT60 0.5–0.9 s, talker DRR is about −6 to −14 dB (Sabine estimate for a room of about 360 m³, critical distance about 1.1–1.5 m). WPE is the main tool for making far talkers intelligible and for restoring spatial cues before clustering or beamforming. It works with M=2, and even with M=1.
sources.two_mic_reality: With 2 channels the prediction filter has 2×10 taps per bin, which is fine. Risks: over-whitening and speech distortion with moving talkers or too little context; each estimate needs several seconds. No 2-mic performance figure was confirmed in this session.
sources.implementation: pip install nara_wpe (v0.0.11; pure Python; depends on numpy, soundfile, bottleneck and click; MIT). The README says it was tested on Python 3.7–3.10. bottleneck has arm64 wheels for 3.12–3.14, so it should work; confirm on 3.12.

sweep.takeaways:
A. PHYSICAL LIMITS OF THIS HARDWARE
Computed for 2 omni mics, c=343 m/s, fs=16 kHz. Treat these as design constraints.
(1) Delay range and aliasing. The maximum TDOA is ±1.17, ±1.87 and ±2.80 samples for 2.5, 4 and 6 cm spacing. Spatial aliasing starts above 6.9, 4.3 and 2.9 kHz. DUET's unambiguous-phase condition at 16 kHz needs d≲2.15 cm (Yilmaz & Rickard). So use per-frequency models (cACGMM, MESSL, or likelihoods computed from a predicted phase) instead of unwrapped TDOA.
(2) Diffuse noise looks coherent at low frequency. Coherence at 4 cm is 0.98 at 0.5 kHz, 0.91 at 1 kHz and 0.68 at 2 kHz. Below about 1 kHz, babble and engine noise look spatially like a broadside source, so spatial clusters cannot separate them there; spectral cues have to do it.
(3) Linear filtering gains little against diffuse noise (distortionless 2-mic case). Broadside: ≤0.2 dB at 1 kHz, 0.8 dB at 2 kHz, 1.7 dB at 3 kHz. Endfire: up to about 5–6 dB, but only with white-noise gain of −10 to −15 dB at ≤500 Hz, which amplifies the INMP441's roughly 33 dBA self-noise. A single filter that must keep both bus talkers uses both degrees of freedom and gives about 0 dB. So most suppression must come from time-varying T-F masks; MVDR adds about 0–3 dB.
(4) Near-field ILD is weak. At 4 cm it is 1.1 dB at 0.3 m and 0.3 dB at 1 m (endfire), the same order as the INMP441's ±1 dB unit tolerance. Calibrate per-band gains on diffuse noise first.
(5) Meeting room is reverberation-dominated. For about 360 m³ with RT60 0.5–0.9 s, the Sabine critical distance is about 1.1–1.5 m. DRR is about −6 to −8 dB at 3 m and −12 to −14 dB at 6 m. A 2-mic array gives only a 1-D DOA with mirror ambiguity, about 5–9 resolvable delay bins at 4 cm. Blind spatial separation of 20 talkers is therefore not possible with this array.

B. BUS (two near talkers vs. crowd): ranked
1. Anchored 3-class cACGMM, per-talker MVDR, floor-limited post-mask. Implement first.
- Calibrate the per-band gain between mics.
- STFT 512/128 for streaming, 1024/256 offline.
- Over 5–10 s windows, build a GCC-PHAT/DUET histogram from f<c/2d and take the two TDOA peaks.
- Initialize classes A and B from each peak's predicted-phase likelihood. Initialize the noise class with B equal to the diffuse-coherence matrix.
- Run 10–20 EM iterations (pb_bss).
- Build one Souden MVDR per talker, with Φ_N taken from the noise class only.
- Output ŝ=γ_A·h_A^H·y+γ_B·h_B^H·y, then apply gain max(γ_A+γ_B, g_min) with g_min≈0.1–0.3. Erdogan found a 0.3 floor best for SDR and WER.
Evidence: the same 2-mic, 4 cm geometry (Ito 2016, noise-free) gave about 9–11 dB SDR for 2 talkers at RT60 0.3–0.4 s.
My estimate, not measured: with babble at 0–5 dB SNR, about 3–8 dB SI-SDR/SNR improvement, mostly above 1 kHz, with some musical noise. MVDR contributes ≤1–3 dB of it.
Masking alone hurt ASR in NTT's demo (WER 40.5%→57.5%, while MVDR gave 24.1%), so keep the floor. A limit of roughly 6–10 dB maximum attenuation is my suggestion for listening.
2. Same model, but MESSL-style. Use IPD plus calibrated ILD, an ITD grid, and a garbage class, which makes it explicitly robust to aliasing. MESSL beat DUET and Sawada by about 1.6 dB SDR at RT60≈565 ms. The reference code is MATLAB, so port it.
3. Streaming version. Enroll each talker's spatial covariance as a prior from a few seconds of speech (Higuchi 2017's spatial prior cut WER 38.4%→29.2%), or use an NTT-style TDOA dictionary. Then compute posteriors online in 2.4 s blocks with one EM iteration per block (block-online GSS, 32× faster than offline). Latency is about one block. A frame-online MVDR fed by a block back end reached 22 ms latency (Sekiguchi/Nugraha 2022).
4. Add a coherent-to-diffuse power ratio (CDR) estimate as a noise-class prior. This 2-omni-mic estimator (Schwarz & Kellermann, IEEE/ACM TASLP 23(6):1006–1018, 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03784) suppresses diffuse babble and reverb without needing DOA. Below about 1 kHz, multiply in a spectral speech prior, e.g. the gain of a small single-channel ONNX denoiser, Erdogan/Heymann style.
5. Offline blind baseline: pyroomacoustics fastmnmf2 with n_src=3–4. Pick outputs by TDOA and level, and compare with #1.
6. Not as the main path: AuxIVA/ILRMA give 2 outputs and no diffuse-noise reduction; they help only against one loud point interferer. Online AuxIVA does run at under 10 ms latency with about 7.7 dB SIR (RION). Use DUET masks only to find TDOA anchors.

C. MEETING (20 people, 1–6 m): ranked
1. Do not try to blindly separate 20 talkers; most of the time only one person speaks. Pipeline:
- nara_wpe on 2 channels: taps 10, delay 3, STFT 512/128, 3–5 iterations, or online with α=0.9999.
- MVDR toward the active talker (Souden form).
- Estimate the noise SCM only from non-speech frames, so far, reverberant talkers are not treated as noise.
- Normalize loudness per talker or per segment. The direct-path level differs by about 16–22 dB between 0.5–1 m and 6 m.
Expect only about 1–3 dB from the 2-mic MVDR against HVAC noise. WPE should give the main intelligibility gain for far talkers; no verified 2-mic figure, so measure it.
2. GSS, with speaker activity from speaker-embedding diarization (TDOA as an auxiliary feature), for overlapped speech. Use the CPU route (pb_chime5/pb_bss): 15 s context, ≥5 iterations, noise class on. Expect modest gains. Published GSS gains used 7–8 mics, and going from 2 to 7 channels alone cut WER by 50.4% (LibriCSS) and 21.8% (AMI) relative (Raj 2023).
3. Physical-model spatial dictionary over the 1-D TDOA grid, plus a noise entry, for online 'who/where' and per-direction AGC. Fuse it with speaker embeddings to resolve the mirror ambiguity.
4. Keep floors ≥0.3–0.5 and avoid strong CDR or garbage-class masking. Far talkers look diffuse and would be erased.

D. HARDWARE AND TEST PLAN
- Verify the L/R I2S alignment with claps: broadside should give 0 TDOA, endfire ±d/c. A channel skew would also explain the 2.3 cm vs 4 cm spacing discrepancy. Measure the true spacing from the endfire TDOA.
- Bus: point the mic axis along the line between the two talkers. Both are then endfire, with maximum TDOA separation and a superdirective option. Alternatively spread the mics 10–30 cm apart for large ILD, as in Audience's 'spread mic' patent.
- Meeting: spacing of 10–20 cm gives ±4.7–9.3 samples of TDOA range and better low-frequency DOA resolution; per-bin models handle the aliasing. Adding channels or devices is the biggest single improvement (Raj 2023).
- Benchmark in pyroomacoustics before real recordings: a bus box with 20–40 babble sources plus engine noise, and a 15×8×3 m room at RT60 0.5/0.7/0.9 s with 20 seats plus HVAC noise. Test spacings of 2.5, 4, 6, 10 and 20 cm, and score SI-SDR, PESQ and STOI. Then record real data.
- Everything above runs in numpy/scipy with pb_bss, pyroomacoustics and nara_wpe; no PyTorch needed. The 2×2 versions run comfortably in real time on the M1.

checked.applicability_verdict: Confirmed from the PDF: the spacing limit d ≤ 2.15 cm at 16 kHz is derived as 8.60 cm/4. The echoic office recording (RT60 ≈ 500 ms, 3 sources) gave SIR gains of 4.26, 10.51 and 10.58 dB, PSR 0.56–0.89 and WDO 0.40–0.56. The paper states 1.75 cm spacing and a 1.5 m radius only for the anechoic recordings, not the echoic one. Anechoic 3–5-source SIR gains were 9.8–17.7 dB, so the sweep's lower bound of 10 is slightly high. The 10-source synthetic mix kept an average gain above 12 dB and was rated 'very distorted and barely intelligible'. Overclaim: the sweep says 'diffuse babble has no peak', which is wrong for a 2.5–6 cm pair. Diffuse-field coherence is real-valued and ≥0.9 below about 1 kHz, so babble and engine noise pile up as a broad peak at δ≈0, α≈0. That peak looks like a broadside talker, contradicting the sweep's own takeaway A(2). The forward-model assignment above c/2d is also not ambiguity-free: it breaks down in bands where ω(δA−δB)=2πk, about 4.3 kHz for talkers at opposite endfire with 4 cm spacing. The weak near-field ILD (about 1.1 dB at 4 cm and 1.6 dB at 6 cm, at 0.3 m) is the same size as the INMP441's ±1 dB tolerance. Use DUET only as a TDOA-anchor finder for the bus case. It is useless for the 20-person meeting.

Three speech sources gave 4.2–6.5 dB SDR and four gave 2.6–3.9 dB SDR, at RT60 130–250 ms. At 16 kHz it needed about 3 activity centroids for stable permutation alignment. M. S. Pedersen, D. Wang, J. Larsen, U. Kjems, 'Two-Microphone Separation of Speech Mixtures,' IEEE Trans. Neural Networks 19(3):475–492, 2008, doi:10.1109/TNN.2007.911740. Separates more sources than mics with 2 mics (iterative ICA plus binary masks); Oticon/DTU hearing-aid lineage.

N. Q. K. Duong, E. Vincent, R. Gribonval, 'Under-Determined Reverberant Audio Source Separation Using a Full-Rank Spatial Covariance Model,' IEEE TASLP 18(7):1830–1840, 2010, doi:10.1109/TASL.2010.2050716. Stereo (2-mic) evidence for full-rank spatial covariance models in reverberation, the model family that FastMNMF accelerates.

N. Ito, S. Araki, M. Delcroix, T. Nakatani, 'Probabilistic spatial dictionary based online adaptive beamforming for meeting recognition in noisy and reverberant environments,' ICASSP 2017, pp. 681–685, doi:10.1109/ICASSP.2017.7952242. The core method paper behind the EUSIPCO 2017 and HSCMA 2017 entries.

D. H. Tran Vu, R. Haeb-Umbach, 'Blind speech separation employing directional statistics in an Expectation Maximization framework,' ICASSP 2010, pp. 241–244, doi:10.1109/ICASSP.2010.5495994. Origin of the complex Watson mixture (cWMM) used in NTT's live prototype; the baseline the cACGMM improves on.

S. Araki, H. Sawada, R. Mukai, S. Makino, 'Underdetermined blind sparse source separation for arbitrarily arranged multiple sensors,' Signal Processing 87(8):1833–1847, 2007, doi:10.1016/j.sigpro.2007.02.003. Clustering of normalized phase/level features that tolerates aliasing; the simplest robust 2-mic clustering baseline.

R. Aichner, H. Buchner, F. Yan, W. Kellermann, 'A real-time blind source separation scheme and its application to reverberant and noisy acoustic environments,' Signal Processing 86(6):1260–1277, 2006, doi:10.1016/j.sigpro.2005.06.022. Real-time 2-channel TRINICON; available as pyroomacoustics.bss.trinicon (hard-coded to 2 outputs).

K. Reindl, Y. Zheng, A. Schwarz, S. Meier, R. Maas, A. Sehr, W. Kellermann, 'A stereophonic acoustic signal extraction scheme for noisy and reverberant environments,' Computer Speech & Language 27(3):726–745, 2013, doi:10.1016/j.csl.2012.07.011. Journal version of the 2-channel BSS noise reference plus Wiener post-filter. The sweep's ISCCSP 2010 paper is titled 'Speech enhancement for binaural hearing aids based on blind source separation', pp. 1–6.

T. Taniguchi, N. Ono, A. Kawamura, S. Sagayama, 'An auxiliary-function approach to online independent vector analysis for real-time blind source separation,' HSCMA 2014, pp. 107–111, doi:10.1109/HSCMA.2014.6843261. The online AuxIVA that the hearing-aid paper builds on. Also N. Ono, 'Fast stereo independent vector analysis and its implementation on mobile phone,' IWAENC 2012: the closed-form 2×2 IP2 update running on a phone (cited from memory, not re-verified online).

A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann, 'Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation,' IEEE/ACM TASLP 23(6):1006–1018, 2015, doi:10.1109/TASLP.2015.2418571; and O. Thiergart, G. Del Galdo, E. A. P. Habets, 'On the spatial coherence in mixed sound fields and its application to signal-to-diffuse ratio estimation,' JASA 132(4):2337–2346, 2012, doi:10.1121/1.4750493. CDR appears in the takeaways but not as a source. It becomes ill-conditioned at 4 cm below about 1–1.5 kHz.

I. A. McCowan, H. Bourlard, 'Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence,' IEEE TSAP 11(6):709–716, 2003, doi:10.1109/TSA.2003.818212; and N. Yousefian, P. C. Loizou, 'A dual-microphone speech enhancement algorithm based on the coherence function,' IEEE TASLP 20(2):599–609, 2012, doi:10.1109/TASL.2011.2162406. Coherence-based 2-mic post-filters, the industry-standard alternative or complement to clustering masks.

T. Nakatani, K. Kinoshita, 'A Unified Convolutional Beamformer for Simultaneous Denoising and Dereverberation' (WPD), IEEE SPL 26(6):903–907, 2019, doi:10.1109/LSP.2019.2911179. Joint WPE plus MVDR in a single filter for the reverberant meeting case.

K. Kinoshita et al., 'A summary of the REVERB challenge: state-of-the-art and remaining challenges in reverberant speech processing research,' EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. 2016, doi:10.1186/s13634-016-0306-6; and M. Delcroix et al., 'Strategies for distant speech recognition in reverberant environments,' EURASIP JASP 2015, doi:10.1186/s13634-015-0245-7. 1-, 2- and 8-channel WPE results; they supply the 2-channel dereverberation evidence the sweep could not find.

E. Vincent, S. Watanabe, A. A. Nugraha, J. Barker, R. Marxer, 'An analysis of environment, microphone and data simulation mismatches in robust speech recognition,' Computer Speech & Language 46:535–557, 2017, doi:10.1016/j.csl.2016.11.005. CHiME-4 1-, 2- and 6-channel track analysis: direct evidence of what 2-channel mask-based beamforming loses against 6 channels.

E. A. P. Habets, S. Gannot, 'Generating sensor signals in isotropic noise fields,' JASA 122(6):3464–3470, 2007, doi:10.1121/1.2799929; and R. Scheibler, E. Bezzam, I. Dokmanić, 'Pyroomacoustics: A Python package for audio room simulation and array processing algorithms,' ICASSP 2018, pp. 351–355, doi:10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461310. Needed for the proposed benchmark, so that simulated babble and engine noise have the correct sinc coherence at 2.5–6 cm.

T. Yoshioka, D. Dimitriadis, A. Stolcke, W. Hinthorn, Z. Chen, M. Zeng, X. Huang, 'Meeting Transcription Using Asynchronous Distant Microphones,' Interspeech 2019, pp. 2968–2972, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2019-3088. Supports the advice to add channels or devices for the 20-person room, using ad-hoc consumer devices.
verify.notes:
How this was checked: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after my first query. From then on I ran no search-engine queries. All remaining checks used direct fetches of known URLs:
- author, publisher, EURASIP, ISCA and arXiv PDFs, text-extracted locally;
- Google Patents;
- Crossref lookups of DOIs I already had;
- GitHub raw files and API;
- PyPI JSON.

Sources: all 15 exist and the bibliographic data is mostly right. ILRMA is dropped (keep=false) as redundant with AuxIVA for these test cases.

Physics numbers: all recomputed and correct.
- TDOA range: ±1.17, 1.87 and 2.80 samples (2.5, 4 and 6 cm).
- Spatial aliasing starts at 6.9, 4.3 and 2.9 kHz.
- Diffuse coherence at 4 cm: 0.98, 0.91 and 0.68 at 0.5, 1 and 2 kHz.
- Broadside MVDR gain against diffuse noise: 0.05, 0.19, 0.76 and 1.65 dB at 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz.
- Endfire superdirective: directivity about 6 dB, white-noise gain −15, −9 and −3.6 dB at 250, 500 and 1000 Hz.
- Near-field ILD at 0.3 m: 1.1 dB at 4 cm, 1.6 dB at 6 cm.
- Meeting room (Sabine): critical distance 1.1–1.5 m; DRR −6 to −8 dB at 3 m and −12 to −14 dB at 6 m.

Main corrections and overclaims:
1. Sawada's '6.87 dB, ranked third' comes from MESSL's test of the 2007 WASPAA method on simulated KEMAR binaural mixtures. The 2011 paper's own 2-mic live recordings (5 cm, no diffuse noise) are the realistic prior for this hardware:
   - 3 talkers: 4.2–6.5 dB SDR;
   - 4 talkers: 2.6–3.9 dB SDR.
2. MESSL's mixtures were synthetic (BRIR convolution) and relied on head-sized ITD and ILD cues. A free-field 4 cm pair has far weaker cues.
3. Internal contradiction. The DUET entry says diffuse babble has no histogram peak. At 2.5–6 cm, diffuse coherence is near 1 below 1 kHz, so babble forms a broad 'broadside' peak at δ≈0.
4. The bus estimate of '3–8 dB' has no 2-mic babble evidence behind it. The cited support (Ito 2016) is noise-free, 8 kHz, with sources 80° apart. Treat 8 dB as optimistic. Expect gains mostly above 1–1.5 kHz; below that, spectral (single-channel) suppression has to do the work.
5. Meeting loudness. The direct path differs by 16–22 dB, but the total received level differs by only about 3.5–10 dB between 0.5–1 m and 6 m, because of the reverberant field. Far talkers suffer from low DRR, not low loudness, so AGC alone will not make them intelligible.
6. '1–3 dB MVDR against HVAC' is optimistic. HVAC noise is low-frequency and diffuse, where 4 cm broadside MVDR gives about 0–0.2 dB. Conferencing products handle HVAC with stationary single-channel noise reduction.
7. A CDR prior is ill-conditioned at 4 cm below about 1–1.5 kHz, and nearby babblers that are partly coherent bias it.
8. GSS computes the MVDR covariance matrices from the unnormalized WPE output Y, not the normalized ỹ. Its published results used oracle time annotations. Diarizing 20 talkers from 2 far-field mics is a hard problem in itself.
9. FastMNMF: no M=2 result exists, so 'strongest blind model for 2 mics' is unsupported. The AR-headset paper needs a trainable DNN. The DNN-free system's timings were measured on a V100 GPU.
10. NTT's dictionary and prototype results came from a 4 cm cubic, 3-D multi-mic array. The evaluation babble came from outside the room and a standing audience; the 10-loudspeaker babble was used only for dictionary training data.
11. In the loud bus, superdirective white-noise gain against the 33 dBA mic self-noise hardly matters. The ±1 dB gain mismatch and phase mismatch are the real limit, so calibrate per band first.
12. Tooling:
   - pb_bss also pulls matplotlib, scikit-learn, sympy, pesq, pystoi, mir_eval and srmrpy (from git), and needs a Cython build. A numpy-2 fix was merged in May 2025. Vendoring the pure-numpy cacgmm module is simpler.
   - desh2608/gss fails at install without CuPy.
   - nara_wpe 0.0.11 also needs tqdm and is CI-tested only up to Python 3.10.
   - Online WPE with α=0.9999 has a memory of about 80 s, too slow for 20-talker turn-taking.
   - pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 is confirmed with universal2 wheels for cp312–cp314. It also ships trinicon, a 2-channel time-domain BSS.

Not re-verified:
- Horiguchi's SLT 2021 venue and pages.
- Raj's and Nugraha's final venues.
- Sunohara's RION affiliation.
- The Ono IWAENC 2012 IP2 title.
- Heymann's RIS record number.
- ILRMA's nowpublishers link, which returned HTTP 403.

sweep.angle: Neural speech enhancement that runs on an M1 Mac without PyTorch or TensorFlow (ONNX, C or Rust): single-channel denoisers, multi-channel neural beamformers, and target-speaker or personalized extraction. For each model the entry gives size, license, how to run it from Python 3.12–3.14, how it handles babble, whether it dereverberates, and how likely it is to over-suppress far talkers.

sources.title: A Hybrid DSP/Deep Learning Approach to Real-Time Full-Band Speech Enhancement (RNNoise)
sources.authors: Jean-Marc Valin
sources.venue: IEEE MMSP 2018 (arXiv:1709.08243); code xiph/rnnoise v0.2 (Apr 2024)
sources.key_idea: Hybrid design. A tiny GRU network predicts 22 Bark-band gains (the square root of the ideal ratio mask) and a VAD probability. A classic pitch comb filter then removes noise between harmonics. Cost is about 40 MFLOPS at 48 kHz, roughly 1.3% of one x86 core.
sources.algorithm: 48 kHz, 20 ms Vorbis window, 10 ms hop, 10 ms look-ahead. 42 input features: 22 Bark-frequency cepstral coefficients; first and second temporal derivatives of the first 6; DCT of per-band pitch correlation (6); pitch period; a spectral non-stationarity measure. Network: dense layer plus 3 GRU layers (215 units in total, largest layer 96; 87,503 weights in v0.1). Outputs 22 band gains g_b and a VAD probability. Loss: (g_b^0.5 - ghat_b^0.5)^2 for the gains, cross-entropy for the VAD. Gains are interpolated to FFT bins. Gain smoothing g~_b = max(0.6*g~_b,prev, ghat_b) gives about a 135 ms decay so reverb tails are not chopped. A pitch comb filter with per-band strength follows. Training used random 2nd-order spectral-shaping filters and level augmentation; noise types included crowd, car, train and office. v0.2 was retrained on public data only, adds an optional 'little' model, and can load weights from a blob (rnnoise_model_from_file).
sources.bus_relevance: Use only as a cheap baseline or VAD. It reduces engine/road noise and diffuse 'crowd' noise (the paper shows PESQ gains on babble at moderate SNR) but cannot reject intelligible nearby talkers. On an independent low-SNR benchmark (DPDFNet paper, Table 1): PESQ 1.32->2.36, STOI 83.2->88.5%, against DeepFilterNet3's 2.76 / 90.5%.
sources.meeting_relevance: The gain-decay floor keeps reverberant tails, which helps far talkers, and the VAD output is a usable speech-presence cue. No dereverberation. At low local SNR it attenuates soft talkers, so mix back some of the input if you use it.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel; run it on the beamformer output or per mic. Needs resampling from 16 to 48 kHz; the bands above 8 kHz stay empty, which works but wastes capacity. Expect several dB of reduction on stationary noise, little on babble, and no spatial selectivity.
sources.implementation: C library, BSD-3 (github.com/xiph/rnnoise). ./autogen.sh downloads the model tarball (58.6 MB of C weight sources); then configure and make with clang, and call it via ctypes from Python 3.12–3.14. Alternative: pip pyrnnoise 0.4.5 (Apache-2.0 wrapper; py3-none macosx_26_0 universal2 wheel, 13.4 MB; pulls in matplotlib and audiolab).

sources.title: A Perceptually-Motivated Approach for Low-Complexity, Real-Time Enhancement of Fullband Speech (PercepNet)
sources.authors: Jean-Marc Valin, Umut Isik, Neerad Phansalkar, Ritwik Giri, Karim Helwani, Arvindh Krishnaswamy
sources.venue: Interspeech 2020 (arXiv:2008.04259), Amazon
sources.key_idea: Successor to RNNoise. A conv+GRU network (8M weights, 8-bit) predicts 34 ERB-band gains and a pitch-filter strength per band, followed by an acausal comb filter and an envelope postfilter. The training target keeps early reflections, so only late reverberation is attenuated.
sources.algorithm: 48 kHz, 10 ms frames, 40 ms look-ahead (1x5 and 1x3 conv layers, M=3 future frames). 70 inputs: 34 band magnitudes (with look-ahead), 34 pitch coherences, pitch period and pitch correlation. Per band it outputs a gain (approximating g_b*g_att) and a pitch-filter strength r_b. Attenuation floor n0=0.03 (about 15 dB) inside g_att = sqrt((1+n0-qx^2)/(1+n0-qp^2)). Envelope postfilter. Minimum-decay rule Xr_b(l) = min(max(X_b(l), delta*Xr_b(l-1)), Y_b(l)), with delta equivalent to T60 = 100 ms. Pitch-adaptive high-pass filter. About 800 MMACS, 5.2% of an i7-8565U core. DNS-2020 blind P.808 MOS: synthetic-with-reverb 2.78->3.16 (NSNet baseline 2.64); real recordings 2.97->3.51.
sources.bus_relevance: Not personalized, so it keeps competing nearby talkers. The authors note residual 'roughness' between harmonics in loud car noise. Its ideas (attenuation floor, band gains that avoid musical noise) are more useful here than the model itself.
sources.meeting_relevance: One of the few low-complexity models shown to raise MOS on reverberant speech rather than lower it, thanks to the early-reflection target. That is the property far talkers need, and the 15 dB attenuation floor limits over-suppression.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel, and no official weights exist. 16 kHz input works: the authors up-sampled the 16 kHz DNS data in the STFT domain.
sources.implementation: No official code or weights. An unofficial BSD-3 C++/PyTorch re-implementation (github.com/jzi040941/PercepNet) has no pretrained model, so it would need PyTorch training on another machine. The early-reflection target, the attenuation floor and the min-decay smoothing can be reused in your own numpy post-processing.

sources.title: DeepFilterNet2: Towards Real-Time Speech Enhancement on Embedded Devices for Full-Band Audio (+ DeepFilterNet 1/3 and the Rust 'deep-filter' runtime)
sources.authors: Hendrik Schröter, Alberto N. Escalante-B., Tobias Rosenkranz, Andreas Maier
sources.venue: IWAENC 2022 (arXiv:2205.05474); DF1 ICASSP 2022; DF3 Interspeech 2023 show-and-tell (arXiv:2305.08227)
sources.key_idea: Two-stage perceptual enhancement. Stage 1 predicts 32 ERB-band real gains for the spectral envelope. Stage 2 ('deep filtering') predicts a 5-tap complex filter per bin below about 5 kHz to restore harmonics. A local-SNR head skips or zeroes stages. Training partly removes reverberation because the target uses a decayed room response.
sources.algorithm: 48 kHz, 20 ms window, 10 ms hop, 2-frame look-ahead (40 ms latency). Y_G = X*interp(G_erb). Y(t,f) = sum_{i=0..4} C(t,i,f)*X(t-i+l,f) for the lowest 96 bins (about 4.8 kHz). Local SNR xi in [-15,35] dB: xi < min_db_thresh outputs zeros; xi > max_db_erb_thresh bypasses processing; xi > max_db_df_thresh skips the deep filter. Post-filter: G' = G*sin(pi*G/2), then G <- (1+beta)G/(1+beta+G'). Attenuation limit: S <- (1-lam)*S + lam*X with lam = 10^(-atten_lim/20). VB-DEMAND PESQ/STOI: DF1 2.81/0.942, DF2 3.08/0.943, DF3 3.17/0.944. DF2: 2.31M params, 0.36 GMAC, RTF 0.04 on an i5 notebook. DF3: 2.14M params, 0.35 GMAC. Independent multilingual low-SNR set: DF3 PESQ 1.32->2.76, STOI 83.2->90.5%, SI-SNR 0.4->12.1 dB.
sources.bus_relevance: The strongest ready-to-run fullband denoiser for engine/road noise and diffuse crowd babble. Not personalized, so intelligible nearby passengers survive. Use it as the post-filter after a 2-mic beamformer, with atten_lim around 20–30 dB.
sources.meeting_relevance: Partial dereverberation helps clarity, but the defaults are aggressive. Attenuation is unlimited (100 dB), and local-SNR gating (CLI default -15 dB, library default -10 dB) zeroes frames, which can chop soft or far talkers. Use --atten-lim-db 10-15 and --min-db-thresh around -25, and check the speech-quality score (DNSMOS SIG) per speaker. On DNS4 blind real recordings DF3 does not lower SIG (3.23->3.28), unlike NSNet2, DTLN and GTCRN (DPDFNet paper, Table 3).
sources.two_mic_reality: deep-filter accepts a multi-channel 16 kHz WAV, resamples to 48 kHz internally and shares the ERB mask across channels (--reduce-mask 1=max, 2=mean). That keeps both mics coherent for later beamforming, but the model learns nothing spatial. With 16 kHz input the bands above 8 kHz stay empty, which still works. Expect large stationary-noise reduction, moderate diffuse-babble reduction, and no rejection of a single nearby competing talker.
sources.implementation: MIT/Apache-2.0. No PyTorch needed, four options: (a) GitHub release binary deep-filter-0.5.6-aarch64-apple-darwin (27.9 MB, DF3 embedded; flags --atten-lim-db, --min-db-thresh, --pf, -D), called via subprocess; (b) models/DeepFilterNet3_onnx.tar.gz (8.0 MB) for your own inference loop; (c) pip deepfilternet-slim 0.1.0 (py3-none macOS arm64 wheel, 11.9 MB; C API plus DF3; works from any Python 3.12–3.14 via ctypes); (d) pip deepfilternet-rs 0.1.1 (PyO3 wheels for cp310–cp312 only). Avoid pip 'deepfilternet', which needs torch and numpy<2.

sources.title: Data augmentation and loss normalization for deep noise suppression (NSNet2, Microsoft DNS Challenge baseline, ONNX)
sources.authors: Sebastian Braun, Ivan Tashev
sources.venue: SPECOM 2020 (arXiv:2008.06412); baseline of the ICASSP 2021/2022 DNS Challenges
sources.key_idea: A plain recurrent mask estimator on log-power spectra (dense embedding layer, 2 GRUs, 3 dense layers) with strong SNR, spectral and level augmentation. It targets additive noise only: reverberant speech is the training target, so it does not dereverberate.
sources.algorithm: Released ONNX model: 16 kHz, 20 ms sqrt-Hann window, 10 ms hop (161 bins). Input log10|X|^2 features; output a real per-bin gain G(k,n) (sigmoid). Inference clamps G >= mingain (default -80 dB), then S = G*X with the noisy phase, followed by overlap-add. Paper configuration: 32 ms/16 ms, 255 bins, about 2.8M params. Loss: alpha*|S^c e^{j phi} - Shat^c e^{j phihat}|^2 + (1-alpha)*(|S|^c - |Shat|^c)^2 with c=0.3, alpha=0.3, normalized by active speech level. Independent results: low-SNR set PESQ 2.35, STOI 86.8% (DF3: 2.76 / 90.5%); on VB-DEMAND it lowers STOI from 0.921 to 0.903 (DF2 paper).
sources.bus_relevance: A mediocre denoiser that keeps babble talkers. Its main value: it exposes a clean per-bin real mask at 16 kHz with a built-in floor, which makes it a good mask estimator for 2-mic MVDR/GEV and for conservative suppression.
sources.meeting_relevance: It preserves reverb by design, and the mingain knob (for example -12 dB) gives a hard limit on over-suppression. On the reverberant DNS test set, however, NSNet lowered MOS (2.44->2.16) and STOI (86.6->82.2%) per the DTLN paper, so only use it with a high floor.
sources.two_mic_reality: Native 16 kHz. Run it per mic, average the masks into one shared mask, and use that for covariance estimation. Real-valued mask only.
sources.implementation: nsnet2-20ms-baseline.onnx (10.75 MB) is in the microsoft/DNS-Challenge branch 'icassp2021-final'; a 48 kHz model (24.7 MB) is in branch 'v4dnschallenge_ICASSP2022'. The icassp2021 enhance_onnx.py needs only numpy, onnxruntime and soundfile (the v4 version imports torch). Code MIT, repo CC-BY-4.0. onnxruntime 1.31.1 has macOS arm64 wheels for cp312, cp313 and cp314 (20.9 MB).

sources.title: Dual-Signal Transformation LSTM Network for Real-Time Noise Suppression (DTLN)
sources.authors: Nils L. Westhausen, Bernd T. Meyer
sources.venue: Interspeech 2020 (arXiv:2005.07551)
sources.key_idea: Two stacked LSTM separation cores. Core 1 masks the STFT magnitude; core 2 masks a learned Conv1D basis, which brings in phase implicitly. Under 1M params; one frame in, one frame out.
sources.algorithm: 16 kHz, 32 ms frames, 8 ms shift, 512-point FFT. Core 1: 2xLSTM(128) plus a dense sigmoid mask on |X| (noisy phase), then inverse FFT of the frames. Core 2: Conv1D(256) encoder, instant layer norm, 2xLSTM(128), mask, Conv1D decoder, overlap-add. Negative-SNR loss; trained on 500 h of DNS-1 data at SNR -5..25 dB; 987k params. DNS test set without reverb: PESQ 2.45->3.04, STOI 91.5->94.8%. DNS test set with reverb: PESQ 2.75->2.70, STOI 86.6->84.7%, P.808 MOS 2.44->2.56 (NSNet 2.16). Independent low-SNR set: PESQ 2.14, STOI 88.7%.
sources.bus_relevance: A light, moderate-strength denoiser that runs natively at 16 kHz. Not personalized. Its core-1 STFT mask doubles as a speech-presence mask for 2-mic beamforming.
sources.meeting_relevance: Raises subjective MOS on reverberant and real recordings but slightly lowers objective STOI, so there is a mild risk for far talkers. No explicit dereverberation target and no attenuation-limit knob; add mix-back yourself.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel; use per mic or after beamforming. The ONNX model ran in about 1.13 ms per 8 ms block on a 2012 MacBook Air, so compute on the M1 is negligible.
sources.implementation: MIT (github.com/breizhn/DTLN). pretrained_model/model_1.onnx (1.46 MB) plus model_2.onnx (2.51 MB), with LSTM states handled outside the model. real_time_processing_onnx.py uses numpy and onnxruntime (FFT done outside the model). Works on Python 3.12–3.14 via onnxruntime.

sources.title: GTCRN: A Speech Enhancement Model Requiring Ultralow Computational Resources
sources.authors: Xiaobin Rong, Tianchi Sun, Xu Zhang, Yuxiang Hu, Changbao Zhu, Jing Lu
sources.venue: ICASSP 2024
sources.key_idea: A grouped, simplified DPCRN with ERB band compression, subband feature extraction and temporal recurrent attention. 48.2k params and 33 MMAC/s; outputs a complex ratio mask. A streaming ONNX version exists and ships in sherpa-onnx.
sources.algorithm: 16 kHz STFT (512-point window, 256 hop). ERB compression of the high-frequency bins, subband feature extraction, a grouped temporal-convolution encoder and decoder, a grouped dual-path RNN with temporal recurrent attention, and a complex-ratio-mask output. VB-DEMAND: PESQ 2.87, SI-SNR 18.83, STOI 0.940 (RNNoise PESQ 2.29). DNS3 blind DNSMOS OVRL 2.70 (RNNoise 2.53). Independent low-SNR set: PESQ 2.21, STOI 87.2%, which is below RNNoise's 88.5% STOI and far below DPDFNet.
sources.bus_relevance: Too small to beat babble at low SNR on its own. Its value is as an ultra-cheap mask estimator for beamforming and as the backbone of the dual-channel H-GTCRN.
sources.meeting_relevance: Dereverberation behaviour is not documented. The low capacity raises the risk of gating soft far talkers at low SNR; if you use it, add an attenuation limit.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel ONNX. Dual-mic use needs a retrained model (see H-GTCRN). Streaming RTF 0.07 on an i5-12400.
sources.implementation: MIT (github.com/Xiaobin-Rong/gtcrn), with DNS3 and VCTK checkpoints. The official stream/onnx_models/gtcrn_simple.onnx (0.535 MB, DNS3 checkpoint) is also in the sherpa-onnx release 'speech-enhancement-models'. Install pip sherpa-onnx 2.0.1 (macOS arm64 wheels for cp312/313/314: 2.1 MB plus sherpa-onnx-core 9.5 MB). Usage: sherpa_onnx.OfflineSpeechDenoiser(OfflineSpeechDenoiserConfig(model=OfflineSpeechDenoiserModelConfig(gtcrn=OfflineSpeechDenoiserGtcrnModelConfig(model='gtcrn_simple.onnx'), num_threads=1))); out = sd(samples, 16000).

sources.title: DPDFNet: Boosting DeepFilterNet2 via Dual-Path RNN
sources.authors: Daniel Rika, Nino Sapir, Ido Gus (Ceva Technologies)
sources.venue: arXiv:2512.16420 (v3 Jun 2026; Ceva; journal submission)
sources.key_idea: DeepFilterNet2 plus causal dual-path RNN blocks in the encoder. Adds an over-attenuation (OA) loss that penalizes bins where the output is quieter than clean speech, and an 'always-on' fine-tuning stage. Has 16 kHz-native variants. Released as Apache-2.0 ONNX/TFLite by an audio-IP vendor.
sources.algorithm: 16 kHz, 20 ms Vorbis window, 10 ms hop, same two-stage framework as DeepFilterNet2 (ERB gains plus deep filter), with k in {2,4,8} DPRNN blocks. Loss L = lam_MR*L_MR + lam_OA*L_OA with both weights 500. L_MR is a multi-resolution loss over STFT windows {5,10,20,40} ms with compression c=0.3. L_OA is the same loss restricted to bins where M_i(k,f) = 1{|S_i| > |Y_i|}. Training SNR -5..40 dB. Params/MACs: baseline 2.31M/0.36G; dpdfnet2 2.49M/1.35G; dpdfnet4 2.84M/2.36G; dpdfnet8 3.54M/4.37G. Multilingual low-SNR set: noisy PESQ 1.32, STOI 83.2%, SI-SNR 0.38 dB. DPDFNet-4: 3.18 / 93.0% / 14.1 dB. DPDFNet-8: 3.20 / 93.4% / 14.5 dB. For comparison DF3 2.76 / 90.5% / 12.1 dB, NSNet2 2.35 / 86.8%, GTCRN 2.21 / 87.2%. DNS4 blind: DNSMOS SIG 3.23->3.40 for DPDFNet-8 (no speech degradation).
sources.bus_relevance: The strongest causal single-channel model found here that runs without PyTorch, with the best expected gains in loud everyday noise. Still not personalized, so it keeps intelligible nearby talkers.
sources.meeting_relevance: The OA loss directly targets speech over-attenuation, and the fine-tuning improves recovery when a quiet talker resumes after a long pause. That makes it the safest denoiser in this list for soft or far talkers. It makes no dereverberation claims, so verify it on reverberant far speech.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel. Use it per mic to estimate masks and as the post-filter after the 2-mic beamformer. dpdfnet4 needs about 2.4 GMAC/s, well under real time on an M1 Pro.
sources.implementation: Apache-2.0 (huggingface.co/Ceva-IP/DPDFNet: ONNX, TFLite, .pth). The sherpa-onnx 'speech-enhancement-models' release has dpdfnet_baseline.onnx (8.8 MB), dpdfnet2.onnx (10.2 MB), dpdfnet4.onnx (11.7 MB), dpdfnet8.onnx (14.6 MB) and dpdfnet2_48khz_hr.onnx (10.6 MB). Examples: python-api-examples/offline-speech-enhancement-dpdfnet.py and online-speech-enhancement-dpdfnet.py (streaming). Alternative: pip dpdfnet 0.6.0 (pure Python, but pulls in librosa).

sources.title: A Lightweight Hybrid Dual Channel Speech Enhancement System under Low-SNR Conditions (H-GTCRN)
sources.authors: Zheng Wang, Xiaobin Rong, Yu Sun, Tianchi Sun, Zhibin Lin, Jing Lu
sources.venue: Interspeech 2025 (arXiv:2505.19597)
sources.key_idea: Two mics 4 cm apart. Classical frequency-domain WPE plus AuxIVA produce rough speech and noise estimates. A dual-channel GTCRN takes both noisy channels plus the log-spectra of the IVA speech and noise outputs and predicts a complex mask. 24.4k params, 43 MMAC/s.
sources.algorithm: 16 kHz. Front-end: frequency-domain WPE (rt60 parameter 0.3, 1 iteration), then AuxIVA (20 iterations, 2x2 demixing per bin), then an energy-based choice of which IVA output is speech and which is noise. Features: real and imaginary parts of both mic STFTs, plus log|S_IVA| and log|N_IVA|. Single-encoder GTCRN (grouped temporal convolution, grouped DPRNN, decoder) outputs a complex mask, applied either to mic 0 ('masking on noisy') or to the IVA speech output ('masking on IVA'). Loss: SI-SNR plus compressed complex MSE. Target: mic-0 early speech (first 50 ms of the room response). Training setup: 4 cm linear pair; image-method rooms from 3x3x2.5 to 10x10x3 m; RT60 0.1–0.4 s; distances 0.5–3 m; interferer at least 5 degrees from the target; SNR -10..0 dB; DNS-3 and DCASE noise. STOI (%) at -12.5 / -7.5 / -2.5 dB: noisy 42.0 / 50.5 / 61.1; single-channel GTCRN 47.5 / 61.1 / 72.9; DC-GTCRN 60.2 / 71.3 / 79.7; H-GTCRN 72.4 / 79.0 / 82.0. PESQ at -7.5 dB: 1.05->1.58.
sources.bus_relevance: The closest published match to this hardware and to bus SNRs. At -7.5 dB, the second mic plus IVA adds about 10–18 STOI points over single-channel GTCRN. Caveats: it was tested with a directional interferer, and diffuse babble gives IVA less to work with. It also assumes a single target: with TWO partners, the 2-source IVA may put one partner into the 'noise' output. Test both checkpoints and prefer 'masking on noisy', which is more stable when IVA makes mistakes.
sources.meeting_relevance: It has dereverberation ingredients (WPE, early-reflection target), but its single-target design and training range (RT60 up to 0.4 s, distance up to 3 m) don't cover a 20-person room with RT60 0.5–0.9 s and talkers at 6 m. Low priority for the meeting case.
sources.two_mic_reality: Designed for exactly this setup: 2 omni mics, 4 cm, 16 kHz. Your spacing must be close to the training spacing, and the two mic gains must be matched (calibrate the INMP441's +/-1 dB tolerance). Offline AuxIVA on recorded files is fine.
sources.implementation: MIT (github.com/Max1Wz/H-GTCRN): gtcrn_iva.py and checkpoints masking_on_noisy/best_model_0121.tar and masking_on_iva/best_model_0110.tar (about 0.65 MB each). infer.py needs PyTorch. Without torch, either export ONNX on another machine or Colab and keep WPE/IVA in numpy (nara_wpe, pyroomacoustics AuxIVA, or about 100 lines of your own code), or port the roughly 24k-param forward pass to numpy and read the torch zip checkpoint with zipfile and pickle. Fine-tuning on simulated bus scenes needs PyTorch on another machine.

sources.title: End-to-end Microphone Permutation and Number Invariant Multi-channel Speech Separation (FaSNet with Transform-Average-Concatenate)
sources.authors: Yi Luo, Zhuo Chen, Nima Mesgarani, Takuya Yoshioka
sources.key_idea: A time-domain neural filter-and-sum beamformer. The TAC module (transform each channel, average across channels, concatenate back) makes it invariant to mic order and mic count. DPRNN backbone, 2.9M params.
sources.algorithm: 16 kHz, 16 ms context window (center window 16 or 4 ms). Normalized cross-correlation features between the reference mic and each mic. The network estimates a (2W+1)-tap FIR filter per channel per frame, and the filtered channels are summed. Trained with utterance-level permutation-invariant SI-SNR; target is reverberant clean speech. Data: 2 speakers plus non-speech noise (SNR 10–20 dB), T60 0.1–0.5 s. Ad-hoc arrays, average SI-SNR improvement for 2/4/6 mics: FaSNet+TAC+joint 9.8/11.2/11.7 dB (4 ms window: 10.0/11.5/12.0), against single-channel TasNet-filter 7.8/7.8/8.0 dB. 6-mic, 10 cm circular array: 11.5 dB.
sources.bus_relevance: In principle it separates two talkers from noise, but with 2 mics it gains only about 2 dB over single-channel, and it was evaluated at benign SNRs (10–20 dB), far from bus conditions.
sources.meeting_relevance: A 2-speaker separator, not a tool for capturing 20 talkers at even loudness.
sources.two_mic_reality: At 2.5–6 cm spacing, the cross-correlation and phase cues are weaker than with the paper's randomly placed ad-hoc mics, so expect at most a 2 dB benefit over single-channel. No weights; would need PyTorch training and ONNX export elsewhere.
sources.implementation: github.com/yluo42/TAC has model code and data-generation scripts only: no pretrained weights, license CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (non-commercial). Not recommended for this project.

sources.title: Improved MVDR Beamforming Using Single-Channel Mask Prediction Networks
sources.authors: Hakan Erdogan, John R. Hershey, Shinji Watanabe, Michael I. Mandel, Jonathan Le Roux
sources.venue: Interspeech 2016 (companion: Heymann, Drude, Haeb-Umbach, 'Neural network based spectral mask estimation for acoustic beamforming', ICASSP 2016)
sources.key_idea: Use a single-channel mask network to estimate the speech and noise spatial covariance matrices, then compute an MVDR beamformer. One mask shared across mics, plus post-masking with a minimum floor, worked best. This is how any single-channel ONNX model becomes a 2-mic system without retraining.
sources.algorithm: STFT both mics (e.g., 512/128 at 16 kHz). Mask M(t,f) = mean over mics of the network masks (NSNet2 gain, DTLN core-1 mask, or |S_hat|/|X| from GTCRN, DPDFNet or DF3, clipped to [0,1]). Phi_s(f) = sum_t M*x*x^H / sum_t M. Phi_n(f) = sum_t (1-M)*x*x^H / sum_t (1-M), plus diagonal loading. Souden MVDR: w = Phi_n^-1 Phi_s u / tr(Phi_n^-1 Phi_s), where u selects the reference mic. Alternatively GEV: the principal generalized eigenvector of (Phi_s, Phi_n) with blind analytic normalization. Output y = w^H x, then post-mask y*max(M, M_min) with M_min about 0.1–0.3. Offline, use utterance-level covariances or 2–4 s sliding windows for moving talkers.
sources.bus_relevance: Turns network masks into a distortionless spatial filter. It can null one dominant directional interferer per frequency bin (a loud neighbour, a door or engine opening) while keeping both partners, provided the speech mask covers both. Use a non-personalized network mask or the union of two VoxLock masks, with GEV or a rank-2 multichannel Wiener filter rather than a single steering vector.
sources.meeting_relevance: Little benefit in a diffuse reverberant field with 2 mics and 20 talkers who move, and a far talker whose mask is wrong can get nulled. Use it only against a fixed directional noise source such as a projector fan.
sources.two_mic_reality: For 2 omni mics at 2.5–6 cm, the theoretical diffuse-noise directivity bound is about N^2 = 4 (6 dB, endfire superdirective). In practice expect 1–4 dB in babble. The reason: diffuse-field coherence sin(kd)/(kd) is above 0.9 below about 1 kHz and about 0.7 at 2 kHz for d = 4 cm (first zero at 4.3 kHz), and the INMP441's self-noise forces diagonal loading. Against a single point interferer, 5–15 dB is possible when the masks are good. Calibrate the +/-1 dB inter-mic gain mismatch first.
sources.implementation: numpy/scipy, about 150 lines; the only model needed is the single-channel ONNX mask estimator. Reference beamformer utilities: fgnt/pb_bss (MIT; numpy/scipy/cython).

sources.title: Improving speaker discrimination of target speech extraction with time-domain SpeakerBeam (TD-SpeakerBeam, incl. 2-mic IPD features)
sources.authors: Marc Delcroix, Tsubasa Ochiai, Katerina Zmolikova, Keisuke Kinoshita, Naohiro Tawara, Tomohiro Nakatani, Shoko Araki
sources.venue: ICASSP 2020 (arXiv:2001.08378); builds on SpeakerBeam, Zmolikova et al., IEEE JSTSP 13(4), 2019
sources.key_idea: A Conv-TasNet extractor conditioned, through a multiplicative adaptation layer, on an embedding computed from a short enrollment utterance of the target speaker. Optional 2-mic inter-channel phase difference (IPD) features and a speaker-identification loss.
sources.algorithm: 8 kHz. Conv-TasNet settings N=256, L=20, B=256, H=512, P=3, X=8, R=4. Adaptation layer h' = h * e_s (elementwise), where e_s comes from an auxiliary network (encoder plus 1 conv block) run on the enrollment audio. IPD Phi = angle(Y1/Y2); [cos Phi, sin Phi] from a 32 ms/16 ms STFT, upsampled and fused inside the network. Loss: SI-SNR plus 10 x speaker-ID cross-entropy. MC-WSJ0-2mix (2 of 8 channels, RT60 up to about 600 ms): SDR 11.17 dB single-channel vs 11.45 dB with internal IPD (female-female 9.13->10.17). CSJ-2mix: 17.24->17.81 dB with the speaker-ID loss.
sources.bus_relevance: Shows that 2-mic spatial (IPD) features add only about 0.3 dB on average (about 1 dB for same-gender pairs) to an enrollment-based extractor; the speaker cue does most of the work. That argues for investing in enrollment-based extraction (VoxLock) rather than spatial neural networks to keep the two partners.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not applicable: it extracts one enrolled speaker.
sources.two_mic_reality: With 2.5–6 cm spacing, IPD carries little information below about 1–2 kHz, so expect at most 1 dB from the second mic. Same-gender mixtures are the main failure mode.
sources.implementation: BUTSpeechFIT/speakerbeam (Asteroid/PyTorch, 8 kHz Libri2Mix recipe, license 'Other', no ONNX weights). Not runnable without PyTorch training.

sources.title: VoiceFilter-Lite: Streaming Targeted Voice Separation for On-Device Speech Recognition
sources.authors: Quan Wang, Ignacio Lopez Moreno, Mert Saglam, Kevin Wilson, Alan Chiao, Renjie Liu, Yanzhang He, Wei Li, Jason Pelecanos, Marily Nika, Alexander Gruenstein
sources.venue: Interspeech 2020 (arXiv:2009.04323), Google
sources.key_idea: An LSTM mask on (stacked) log-mel filterbanks, conditioned on the user's speaker embedding. An asymmetric loss penalizes over-suppression, and an adaptive suppression strength is driven by an overlapped-speech detector head. 8-bit TFLite model of 2.2 MB.
sources.algorithm: 3 LSTM layers of 512 (256 for the 2.2 MB model) plus a dense sigmoid mask on 128-dim log-mel features, optionally stacked x4 to 512 dims. Asymmetric L2 loss with alpha = 10 weights over-suppression more heavily than residual noise. A noise-type head f_adapt in [0,1] detects overlapped speech. Runtime suppression strength w(t) = beta*w(t-1) + (1-beta)*(a*f_adapt + b) with beta = 0.8 sets how strongly the filtered features replace the input. On realistic queries, additive speech-noise WER went from 56.5% to 28.8% (49% relative), with no degradation on clean (15.2->15.3) or non-speech noise (21.1->21.3).
sources.bus_relevance: Not open-source, but its two tricks can be implemented directly on top of VoxLock or a denoiser: mixing that avoids over-suppression, and applying target-speaker extraction strongly only when non-target speech is detected. That avoids extraction damage when only engine noise is present.
sources.meeting_relevance: Shows that target filters trained with a plain L2 loss hurt non-speech-noise and reverberant conditions; another warning against personalized filtering for capturing many talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel; the ideas transfer, the model does not.
sources.implementation: No public weights or code. Reuse the w(t) mixing and the asymmetric philosophy in numpy post-processing.

sources.title: Personalized PercepNet: Real-time, Low-complexity Target Voice Separation and Enhancement
sources.authors: Ritwik Giri, Shrikant Venkataramani, Jean-Marc Valin, Umut Isik, Arvindh Krishnaswamy
sources.venue: Interspeech 2021 (arXiv:2106.04129), Amazon
sources.key_idea: PercepNet conditioned on a speaker embedding computed from the same compact perceptual features, plus a personalized VAD output. Real time: 4.7% of a core for the 512-unit model, 17.2% for the 1024-unit model.
sources.algorithm: Speaker embedder trained with the generalized end-to-end loss on VoxCeleb2 using the 68-dim PercepNet features. Conditioned conv+GRU network (512 or 1024 GRU units) outputs 32 band gains, 32 pitch-filter strengths and a target-speaker VAD. Training mixtures: SIR 5–10 dB, SNR 5–35 dB, early-reflection target (late reverb attenuated). Test set (LibriSpeech with an interfering talker plus DEMAND noise, SIR/SNR 3–15 dB), MOS: noisy 2.38, NSNet2 2.54, PercepNet 2.62, 512-unit model 3.13, 1024-unit model 3.21. Embedding analysis showed that the non-personalized models' outputs still contain the interfering talker.
sources.bus_relevance: Quantifies what non-personalized denoising leaves behind (the competing talker) and what enrollment buys: about +0.6 MOS over PercepNet. The personalized-VAD idea can gate each partner's speech covariance in the beamformer.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not suited to 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel and not released. Reported artifact: pitch modulation when target and interferer are close in pitch.
sources.implementation: No public weights (Amazon); ideas only. VoxLock is the runnable analogue.

sources.title: VoxLock: open-source causal target-speaker voice isolation (ONNX), integrated into sherpa-onnx v2.0.1
sources.authors: Arbaz Siddiqui (VoxLock); k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx maintainers (integration)
sources.venue: Open-source release (huggingface.co/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock, github.com/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock); sherpa-onnx v2.0.1 released 2026-10-26
sources.key_idea: A 27.3M-param causal band-split RNN target-speaker extractor. Fine-tuned from the causal BSRNN baseline of the REAL-TSE challenge (WeSpeaker ECAPA embedding) on simulated calls, real AMI meeting crosstalk, long calls, and near/far room conditions. It keeps one enrolled voice and removes other voices; enrollment is at least 3 s, or automatic from the first 15 s.
sources.algorithm: enroll.onnx computes the speaker conditioning from a 3 s, 16 kHz voice sample; from a longer sample it uses the loudest 3 s within the first 30 s. chunk*.onnx processes 16 kHz audio in 20–80 ms chunks and carries the LSTM state between chunks. Algorithmic latency 24 ms plus chunk length. Precisions: int8, int8-full, fp16, fp32. Self-reported results: on the Krisp Voice Isolation benchmark (265 real recordings), WER 23.21%->4.95% and leaked background words 66.48->0.11 per minute. On AMI with the headset wearer as target, WER 33.03%->10.12% and leakage 78.34->2.12 words per minute. Single-thread RTF on a Xeon: 1.10 with 20 ms chunks, 0.61 with 80 ms chunks.
sources.bus_relevance: The only ready-to-run target-speaker extractor that needs no PyTorch, and it removes other passengers' voices that denoisers keep. For TWO partners, run it twice (voice sample A, voice sample B) and take the union: the max of the two time-frequency ratio masks applied to the input or beamformer output. Or feed the union as the beamformer's speech mask. Auto-enrollment would lock onto ONE partner and suppress the other, so always pass explicit samples. Real conversational extraction is still brittle: REAL-TSE baselines reach token error rates of 0.65–0.84, and the far-field mic scored worst (arXiv:2607.15198). Partners at 0.3–1 m are the favourable near-field case.
sources.meeting_relevance: Unsuitable: it keeps one target, so it would suppress 19 of 20 talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel model. Failure modes: partners with similar voices, enrollment contaminated by babble, overlapped speech between the two partners, and far or reverberant targets. The second mic helps only through a beamformer placed before it or a mask union after it.
sources.implementation: Apache-2.0. Two routes without torch: (a) pip sherpa-onnx 2.0.1 (macOS arm64, cp312/313/314) plus sherpa-onnx-voxlock-int8.tar.bz2 (72.5 MB) from the k2-fsa 'speech-enhancement-models' release, using sherpa_onnx.OfflineSpeechDenoiserVoxLockModelConfig(enroll_model, chunk_model, voice_sample); (b) pip voxlock 1.3.0 (pure Python; numpy, onnxruntime, huggingface_hub, soundfile, soxr) with voxlock.VoxLock().isolate(..., sample=...). Model downloads are 47–94 MB depending on precision.

sources.title: ICASSP 2023 Deep Noise Suppression Challenge (5th DNS: personalized, headset and speakerphone)
sources.authors: Harishchandra Dubey, Ashkan Aazami, Vishak Gopal, Babak Naderi, Sebastian Braun, Ross Cutler, Alex Ju, Mehdi Zohourian, Min Tang, Hannes Gamper, Mehrsa Golestaneh, Robert Aichner
sources.venue: ICASSP 2023 Signal Processing Grand Challenge (arXiv:2303.11510), Microsoft
sources.key_idea: Benchmark for joint denoising, dereverberation and suppression of neighbouring talkers, with 10–30 s enrollment per primary talker, headset and speakerphone tracks, and personalized P.835 listening tests. Findings: speech quality (SIG) degraded for most models, personalized models sometimes suppressed the primary talker, and the winners improved the challenge score by only +0.145 (headset) and +0.141 (speakerphone) over noisy audio.
sources.algorithm: Evaluation protocol: personalized ITU-T P.835 (SIG/BAK/OVRL) plus ASR word accuracy. The DNS-Challenge repo publishes non-intrusive DNSMOS P.835 models (DNSMOS/DNSMOS/sig_bak_ovr.onnx, model_v8.onnx for P.808) and a personalized version (DNSMOS/pDNSMOS/sig_bak_ovr.onnx) with dnsmos_local.py. These score SIG, BAK and OVRL from the processed audio alone, with no clean reference.
sources.bus_relevance: Confirms that removing neighbouring talkers needs enrollment (or headset-like direct-to-reverberant cues) and that even winning systems trade speech quality for suppression. Industry counterpart: Microsoft Teams 'voice isolation', a personalized model driven by a voice profile stored on the device (learn.microsoft.com/microsoftteams/voice-isolation). Use pDNSMOS to score bus outputs without clean references.
sources.meeting_relevance: The speakerphone track is close to far-field, and models struggled there; the personalized approach is unsuitable for many talkers. Use non-personalized DNSMOS SIG per speaker to catch over-suppression of far talkers.
sources.two_mic_reality: The benchmark is single-channel; its scoring tools work on any of your outputs.
sources.implementation: DNSMOS ONNX models and dnsmos_local.py in github.com/microsoft/DNS-Challenge (repo CC-BY-4.0, code MIT); run with onnxruntime on cp312–cp314. The P.808 path computes mel features; reimplement in numpy if you want to avoid librosa.

sources.title: Using deep learning to improve the intelligibility of a target speaker in noisy multi-talker environments for people with normal hearing and hearing loss
sources.authors: Iordanis Thoidis, Tobias Goehring
sources.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (JASA) 2024, doi:10.1121/10.0028007
sources.key_idea: A quasi-causal, speaker-informed (enrollment-based) deep network that extracts a target talker from mixtures of 1–3 competing talkers in restaurant noise. In double-blind listening tests it improved sentence recognition by 17% for normal-hearing listeners and 31% for listeners with hearing loss.
sources.algorithm: An enrollment utterance identifies the target speaker, and the network conditioned on it extracts that speaker from the mixture. It generalized to unseen speakers, speaker counts, relative levels and corpora. Architecture details are in the paper; only the abstract was checked here.
sources.bus_relevance: The only human-listener evidence in this survey that enrollment-based extraction raises intelligibility, not just quality, in restaurant-like multi-talker noise. Directly supports adding target-speaker extraction (two passes, one per partner) for the bus case.
sources.meeting_relevance: Not applicable to capturing 20 talkers (single target).
sources.two_mic_reality: Single-channel: the gains come from speaker cues, not spatial cues, so they transfer to this device. Expect smaller gains when the target is far or reverberant.
sources.implementation: No public ONNX model found (not checked in depth). Use VoxLock via sherpa-onnx as the runnable analogue.

sources.title: Revolutionary Speech Understanding with Spheric Speech Clarity (Phonak Audéo Sphere Infinio, DEEPSONIC DNN chip)
sources.authors: Henning Hasemann, Alena Krylova (Phonak/Sonova)
sources.venue: Phonak Insight white paper, June 2024
sources.key_idea: Hearing aid with a 4.5M-parameter DNN running on a dedicated chip (DEEPSONIC, about 7.7 GOPS). It is engaged only in the 'Speech in Loud Noise' scene, and only after spatial preprocessing (fixed directional mic by default). The DNN takes a 64-bin complex spectrum and outputs a 64-band speech/noise mask. Manufacturer claim: up to 10 dB SNR improvement in complex group conversations.
sources.algorithm: Signal chain: AutoSense OS scene classifier, then a directional beam (fixed directional by default), then a 64-bin STFT (real and imaginary parts, 128 inputs), then the DNN mask (64 values) applied to the spectrum, then normal hearing-aid gain processing. Trained on 22 million sound samples. Models were selected with a learned 'Audio Quality Estimator' DNN trained on about 1M human ratings (30,000 files, 9 ratings each, about 350 raters) predicting noise, sound-quality and overall MOS. Phonak's test setup (Phonak audiology blog): speech at 0 degrees, realistic scenes from the ARTE database played from 12 loudspeakers all around.
sources.bus_relevance: The industry template for the bus case: beam first, then a DNN mask, engaged only when noise is loud. It also shows the value of a learned quality estimator for tuning; DNSMOS can stand in for it. The numbers are manufacturer claims, not independent measurements.
sources.meeting_relevance: Phonak keeps the DNN off in calm scenes to avoid artifacts; mirror this by scaling suppression with the measured noise level. Its beam assumes a talker in front, which doesn't fit a 360-degree meeting table.
sources.two_mic_reality: Uses a compact hearing-aid mic array (geometry not given in the paper), and the DNN, not the beam, supplies most of the benefit. Emulate it with a 2-mic MVDR/differential beam followed by DPDFNet (2.5–3.5M params, similar scale). Expect less than 10 dB.
sources.implementation: Proprietary. Emulate with open parts: a numpy beamformer, a DPDFNet or DeepFilterNet3 post-filter, and DNSMOS P.835 ONNX as the quality estimator.

sweep.takeaways:
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THIS HARDWARE. Everything needed runs without PyTorch in under 150 MB on Python 3.12–3.14:
- **sherpa-onnx 2.0.1** (macOS arm64 wheels for cp312/313/314, about 12 MB) bundles GTCRN (0.5 MB), DPDFNet (9–15 MB) and VoxLock target-speaker extraction (72 MB int8).
- The **deep-filter 0.5.6 arm64 binary** (28 MB) runs DeepFilterNet3.
- **onnxruntime 1.31** (21 MB) runs NSNet2, DTLN and DNSMOS.

No ready-made model learns from the two mics. The second mic has to be used through DSP driven by neural-network masks, or by porting H-GTCRN.

Babble, as a rule of thumb:
- Diffuse many-voice babble behaves like noise. Every DNS-trained model reduces it, and DPDFNet and DeepFilterNet3 do so better than RNNoise or GTCRN.
- A few intelligible nearby voices are kept by every non-personalized model (Personalized PercepNet embedding analysis; DNS-2023 report). Only enrollment-based target-speaker extraction or spatial nulling removes them.
- On real DNS4 recordings, NSNet2 (3.23→3.08), DTLN (3.10) and GTCRN (3.15) lower DNSMOS SIG, while DeepFilterNet3 (3.28) and DPDFNet-8 (3.40) don't (DPDFNet paper, Table 3). Prefer the latter two whenever speech fidelity matters.

TEST CASE 1, CROWDED BUS (ranked):
1. **Build first: a 2-mic beamformer driven by network masks, with a neural post-filter.** This follows Erdogan/Heymann 2016 and Phonak's beam-then-DNN chain.
   - Run DPDFNet-4 on each mic, or NSNet2 for a cheap real mask, and average into one shared mask.
   - Beamform with GEV or Souden MVDR, using diagonal loading and 2–4 s covariance windows.
   - Post-filter with DPDFNet-4 (native 16 kHz) or DeepFilterNet3, with an attenuation limit of 20–30 dB.
   - Expected gain from the post-filter alone on low-SNR everyday noise (DPDFNet Table 1): about +12–14 dB SI-SNR, STOI 83→91–93%, PESQ 1.3→2.8–3.2.
   - The spatial stage adds roughly 1–4 dB against diffuse babble (6 dB is the theoretical limit for two omni mics), and more against one dominant directional talker.
   - Gains on babble specifically will be lower than these figures.
2. **Then add enrollment-based extraction for nearby non-partner voices.**
   - Run VoxLock through sherpa-onnx twice, once with a 3–10 s sample of each partner.
   - Combine as the union (max) of the two time-frequency masks, or use that union as the beamformer's speech mask.
   - Apply it adaptively, following VoiceFilter-Lite: strong only when non-target speech is detected, mixing the input back otherwise.
   - Expected: much less leaked chatter. VoxLock's self-reported results: 66.5→0.11 leaked words per minute, WER 23.2→4.95% on 265 real recordings. Human evidence for enrollment-based extraction: +17% sentence intelligibility for normal-hearing listeners in restaurant noise (Thoidis & Goehring 2024).
   - Risks: auto-enrollment locks onto ONE partner and suppresses the other; partners with similar voices; noisy enrollment samples. Real-world extraction is still brittle (REAL-TSE baselines reach token error rates of 0.65–0.84), but partners at 0.3–1 m are the favourable case.
3. **Research track: port H-GTCRN** (MIT; 24k params; exactly 2 mics at 4 cm, 16 kHz).
   - Published STOI at -7.5 dB is 50.5→79.0%, against 61.1% for single-channel GTCRN.
   - That was measured with a single point-source interferer and one target. Validate with two partners plus diffuse babble before fine-tuning, which needs PyTorch on another machine.

Skip:
- **FaSNet-TAC:** no weights, non-commercial license, only about +2 dB over single-channel with 2 mics.
- **SpeakerBeam:** no weights, and 2-mic IPD features add only +0.3 dB on average.
- **PercepNet, Personalized PercepNet and VoiceFilter-Lite:** no public weights; reuse their ideas.
- **RNNoise:** baseline or VAD only.

TEST CASE 2, 20-PERSON MEETING (ranked):
1. **Conservative, non-personalized noise suppression after classical WPE dereverberation.**
   - Use DPDFNet-2/4 (its over-attenuation loss protects speech), or DeepFilterNet3 with --atten-lim-db 10–15 and --min-db-thresh around -25. Its default local-SNR gating zeroes frames below -15 dB.
   - Mixing the input back in this way is also what Iwamoto et al. 2022 (arXiv:2201.06685) found reduces the artifacts that hurt speech recognition.
   - Expected: a large comfort gain on HVAC and projector noise (DNSMOS BAK +1.5 to +2.4 on the DNS4 and low-SNR sets) but little or no intelligibility gain for far, reverberant talkers.
   - Aggressive settings make far talkers worse. On the DNS reverberant test set, STOI fell 86.6→84.7% with DTLN and to 82.2% with NSNet, and NSNet's MOS fell 2.44→2.16.
2. **Get even loudness from diarization, not from noise suppression.**
   - Run sherpa-onnx offline speaker diarization (pyannote-segmentation-3.0 ONNX, 7 MB, plus a speaker-embedding ONNX model).
   - Then normalize each speaker's loudness, capping the gain at about +20 dB and keeping a noise floor.
3. **Never use target-speaker or personalized suppression here** (VoxLock, Teams-style voice isolation). By design they remove voices that aren't enrolled, and DNS-2023 found personalized models even suppress the enrolled talker.
4. **2-mic mask-based MVDR:** use it only against a fixed directional noise source; otherwise expect under 2 dB in the diffuse reverberant field.
5. **Quality check:** score every setting per diarized speaker with DNSMOS P.835 ONNX, and reject any setting that lowers SIG for far talkers.

HARDWARE HINTS FROM THIS ANGLE:
- Fix and measure the mic spacing. About 4 cm matches H-GTCRN's training geometry and puts spatial aliasing above 4.3 kHz.
- Match the gains of the two INMP441s (±1 dB tolerance) before any mask-based beamforming or dual-channel network.
- Stay at 16 kHz and prefer 16 kHz-native models (NSNet2, DTLN, GTCRN, DPDFNet, VoxLock) over 48 kHz ones (RNNoise, DeepFilterNet3).
- Everything above runs faster than real time offline on the M1 Pro. VoxLock is the heaviest: RTF 0.6–1.1 on one Xeon thread, so use two or more threads.

checked.correct_citation: Z. Wang, X. Rong, Y. Sun, T. Sun, Z. Lin, J. Lu, "A Lightweight Hybrid Dual Channel Speech Enhancement System under Low-SNR Conditions," Proc. Interspeech 2025 (arXiv:2505.19597). Code: github.com/Max1Wz/H-GTCRN (MIT). 'H-GTCRN' is the repo's name; the paper labels it 'Proposed'.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified against the paper:
- Setup: 4 cm pair at 16 kHz; rooms 3x3x2.5 to 10x10x3 m; RT60 0.1-0.4 s; distances 0.5/1/2/3 m; target-interferer DOA difference >5 degrees; SNR -10..0 dB; 50 ms early-reflection target.
- Size: 24.39k params, 43.2 MMAC/s.
- STOI at -12.5 / -7.5 / -2.5 dB: noisy 42.0 / 50.5 / 61.1; GTCRN 47.5 / 61.1 / 72.9; DC-GTCRN 60.2 / 71.3 / 79.7; proposed 72.4 / 79.0 / 82.0.
Verified in the code: FD-WPE (rt60=0.3, 1 iteration) and AuxIVA (20 iterations) run inside the torch forward pass; infer.py imports torch; checkpoints are 647,958 B each.
OVERCLAIM RISK: AuxIVA ALONE scores STOI 62.5 / 70.2 / 73.4, already beating single-channel GTCRN at -12.5 and -7.5 dB. Most of the 2-mic gain therefore comes from a 2x2 IVA separating ONE directional interferer, the case IVA solves well. Diffuse multi-talker bus babble is not that case, so expect much smaller gains. Two partners plus babble exceed IVA's 2-source model, and one partner can land in the 'noise' output.
Port notes: WPE and IVA use complex torch ops, so ONNX export requires moving them to numpy. Spacing must be about 4 cm and mic gains matched.
Verdict: a good research track for the bus; not for the meeting case (RT60 up to 0.4 s, distances up to 3 m, single target).
