checked.title: Improved MVDR Beamforming Using Single-Channel Mask Prediction Networks
checked.correct_citation: H. Erdogan, J. R. Hershey, S. Watanabe, M. I. Mandel, J. Le Roux, "Improved MVDR Beamforming Using Single-Channel Mask Prediction Networks," Proc. Interspeech 2016, pp. 1981-1985, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2016-552. Companion: J. Heymann, L. Drude, R. Haeb-Umbach, "Neural network based spectral mask estimation for acoustic beamforming," Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2016, pp. 196-200, doi:10.1109/ICASSP.2016.7471664.
checked.applicability_verdict:
The method is described correctly; the paper's best variant uses one shared mask with minima-limited post-masking. The physics checks out: for d=4 cm, diffuse-field sinc coherence is 0.91 at 1 kHz and 0.68 at 2 kHz, the first zero is at 4.29 kHz, and N^2=4 (6 dB) is the endfire superdirective limit.
OVERCLAIM (bus): 'null one dominant interferer while keeping both partners via rank-2 MWF/GEV' is not possible with M=2.
- Two mics give one spatial degree of freedom. Keeping two partners from different directions undistorted AND nulling a third source needs at least 3 mics.
- With both partners inside the 2-4 s covariance window, the rank-2 MWF/GEV degenerates to near-spectral filtering.
Workable 2-mic alternatives:
- (a) Short covariance windows that re-steer to whichever partner is talking (exploits turn-taking).
- (b) Orient the mic axis along the partner-partner line and use a first-order dipole or back-to-back cardioids. These keep both endfire partners and attenuate broadside crowd (DI about 4.8 dB; less in practice because of mismatch and white-noise gain).
'5-15 dB against a point interferer' holds mainly in low reverberation. In a bus cabin only the direct path is nulled, so expect roughly 3-8 dB. The +/-1 dB INMP441 mismatch limits null depth, so calibration is mandatory.
The meeting-case verdict (little benefit) is correct.

checked.correct_citation: M. Delcroix, T. Ochiai, K. Zmolikova, K. Kinoshita, N. Tawara, T. Nakatani, S. Araki, "Improving Speaker Discrimination of Target Speech Extraction With Time-Domain SpeakerBeam," Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2020, pp. 691-695, doi:10.1109/ICASSP40776.2020.9054683 (arXiv:2001.08378).

Verified (Table 2/3):
- MC-WSJ0-2mix (2 of 8 channels, RT60 up to about 600 ms), average SDR: 11.17 -> 11.45 dB with internal IPD (11.11 with input IPD); female-female 9.13 -> 10.17.
- CSJ-2mix: 17.24 -> 17.81 with the SI-loss.

Mild over-reach: generalizing to 'spatial neural networks aren't worth it' rests on one 2020 fusion design tested on noise-free simulated 2-speaker mixtures. The direction is nonetheless consistent with the physics of a 2.5-6 cm pair (about 0.73 rad maximum IPD at 1 kHz for 4 cm).
No usable weights (BUTSpeechFIT/speakerbeam, license 'Other', PyTorch). Keep as evidence only.

checked.correct_citation: R. Giri, S. Venkataramani, J.-M. Valin, U. Isik, A. Krishnaswamy, "Personalized PercepNet: Real-time, Low-complexity Target Voice Separation and Enhancement," Proc. Interspeech 2021 (arXiv:2106.04129).

checked.title: VoxLock: open-source causal target-speaker voice isolation (ONNX), integrated into sherpa-onnx v2.0.1
checked.correct_citation:
A. Siddiqui, VoxLock (Apache-2.0).
- Model card: huggingface.co/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock.
- Code: github.com/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock (repo created 2026-10-11).
- pip voxlock 1.3.0 (2026-10-31).
- Integrated in k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx v2.0.1 (GitHub release 2026-10-26; PyPI wheels 2026-10-27). Asset: sherpa-onnx-voxlock-int8.tar.bz2 (72.5 MB) in the 'speech-enhancement-models' release.

checked.applicability_verdict:
Model-card facts confirmed:
- 27.3M-param causal BSRNN with a WeSpeaker ECAPA base, fine-tuned from the REAL-TSE causal TFMAP baseline; trained on LibriSpeech and AMI.
- Voice sample of at least 3 s, or the first 15 s by default. Files: enroll.onnx plus chunk models; int8 74 MB, fp16 47 MB, fp32 94 MB. 24 ms algorithmic latency.
- Krisp benchmark: WER 23.21 -> 4.95%, leaked words 66.48 -> 0.11 per minute. AMI: WER 33.03 -> 10.12%, leakage 78.34 -> 2.12 per minute.

Skeptical notes:

- The training/eval domain is calls and AMI headset wearers (target very near the mic), not a 2-MEMS device at 0.3-1 m in 0 dB babble.

Target-conversation extraction (Chen et al. 2024) fits the 'two partners' problem more directly. Never use it in the meeting case.

checked.title: ICASSP 2023 Deep Noise Suppression Challenge (5th DNS: personalized, headset and speakerphone)
checked.correct_citation: H. Dubey, A. Aazami, V. Gopal, B. Naderi, S. Braun, R. Cutler, A. Ju, M. Zohourian, M. Tang, H. Gamper, M. Golestaneh, R. Aichner, "ICASSP 2023 Deep Noise Suppression Challenge," ICASSP 2023 Signal Processing Grand Challenge (arXiv:2303.11510). Confirmed:

- The DNSMOS/pDNSMOS ONNX files exist as listed.
Nuance: the paper attributes SIG drops to 'suppression of primary talker's speech and/or leakage of interfering talker and noise' across models (most entries were personalized). The sweep's 'personalized models even suppress the enrolled talker' is therefore loosely supported; Eskimez et al. 2022 (TSOS metric) is the direct evidence.
The Microsoft Teams voice-isolation page is confirmed: a personalized model using a voice profile stored on the user's device.
Using DNSMOS SIG per diarized speaker is a reasonable screen, but DNSMOS is a learned predictor trained on DNS-style data. Pair it with ASR WER and short listening checks.

checked.title: Using deep learning to improve the intelligibility of a target speaker in noisy multi-talker environments for people with normal hearing and hearing loss
checked.correct_citation: I. Thoidis, T. Goehring, "Using deep learning to improve the intelligibility of a target speaker in noisy multi-talker environments for people with normal hearing and hearing loss," J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 156(1), 706-724 (2024), doi:10.1121/10.0028007, PMID 39082692.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Confirmed: a quasi-causal, enrollment-based extractor with 1-3 competing talkers in restaurant noise, giving +17% intelligibility for normal-hearing and +31% for hearing-impaired listeners in double-blind tests.
Important omission in the sweep: the abstract states that the speaker-informed method improved intelligibility where UNINFORMED (non-personalized) enhancement methods FAILED. This directly undercuts expecting DPDFNet/DF3 alone to raise intelligibility in bus babble.
Caveats: single-channel, laboratory mixtures, no public model; gains will shrink for distant or reverberant targets.
Strong, peer-reviewed support for speaker-informed extraction in the bus case.

checked.title: Revolutionary Speech Understanding with Spheric Speech Clarity (Phonak Audéo Sphere Infinio, DEEPSONIC DNN chip)
checked.correct_citation: H. Hasemann, A. Krylova, "Revolutionary Speech Understanding with Spheric Speech Clarity," Phonak Insight (Sonova AG), June 2024, doc. 028-2684-02. The 10 dB SNR claim is cited to S. Raufer et al., Phonak Field Study News (2024), a manufacturer publication.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified in the PDF:
- 4.5M-param DNN; 7,700 million ops/s; 22 million training samples.
- Input: 64 complex bins (128 values); output: a 64-band mask.
- Runs only on the 'Speech in Loud Noise' path, after spatial preprocessing (default 'fixed directional').
- Audio Quality Estimator trained on about 350 raters x 30,000 files (about 1M ratings, 9 per file).
- 'Up to 10 dB' SNR improvement: a manufacturer claim.
NOT in the white paper:
- The 'ARTE database, 12 loudspeakers' test setup (unverified; it cannot be traced to this source).
- 'The DNN, not the beam, supplies most of the benefit' (an inference).
The paper also claims benefit 'from any direction' (Wright et al. 2024), which softens the 'beam assumes talker in front' point.
Verdict: the architecture template (fixed beam, then a single-channel DNN mask, engaged only in loud noise) is a valid industry pattern to emulate. Expect far less than 10 dB with 2 MEMS mics. For peer-reviewed DNN hearing-aid intelligibility evidence, cite Diehl et al. 2023.

missing_key_sources: T. Chen, M. Itani, S. E. Eskimez, T. Yoshioka, S. Gollakota, "Hearable devices with sound bubbles," Nature Electronics 7, 1047-1058 (2024), doi:10.1038/s41928-024-01276-z. On-device neural 'sound bubble' with a programmable 1-2 m radius that keeps up to 2 nearby talkers and suppresses everything outside, the most direct match to the bus case. Uses up to 6 headset mics plus head shadow, so a 2-MEMS port will be weaker.

K. Patterson, K. Wilson, S. Wisdom, J. R. Hershey, "Distance-Based Sound Separation," Proc. Interspeech 2022, pp. 901-905 (arXiv:2207.00562). Single-mic near/far separation (+4.4 dB SI-SNRi for 1 near talker against 4 far talkers in reverberant simulation). Shows distance (DRR) cues alone can keep nearby partners and reject a distant crowd.

T. Chen, Q. Wang, B. Wu, M. Itani, S. E. Eskimez, T. Yoshioka, S. Gollakota, "Target conversation extraction: Source separation using turn-taking dynamics," Proc. Interspeech 2024, pp. 3550-3554, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2024-225 (arXiv:2407.11277; code github.com/chentuochao/Target-Conversation-Extraction). Extracts ALL participants of a conversation from one enrolled speaker, a principled alternative to running VoxLock twice and taking the mask union for the two partners.

G. Hu, M. Itani, T. Chen, S. Gollakota, "Proactive Hearing Assistants that Isolate Egocentric Conversations," Proc. EMNLP 2025 (arXiv:2511.11473). Infers conversation partners from turn-taking, anchored on the wearer's own speech, with no explicit enrollment. Relevant if the device owner is one of the two bus talkers.

B. Veluri, M. Itani, T. Chen, T. Yoshioka, S. Gollakota, "Look Once to Hear: Target Speech Hearing with Noisy Examples," Proc. ACM CHI 2024 (arXiv:2405.06289). Enrollment from under 5 s of NOISY binaural audio (about 7 dB gain). Addresses VoxLock's main bus failure mode: babble-contaminated enrollment.

K. Tan, X. Zhang, D. Wang, "Real-Time Speech Enhancement for Mobile Communication Based on Dual-Channel Complex Spectral Mapping," Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2021. The canonical neural design for dual-mic phones (causal DC-CRN, structured pruning). A blueprint for training a true 2-mic model for this array. The journal extension (IEEE/ACM TASLP 2021) was not re-verified here.

K. Tesch, T. Gerkmann, "Spatially Selective Deep Non-linear Filters for Speaker Extraction," Proc. IEEE ICASSP 2023 (arXiv:2211.02420). A steerable joint spatial-spectral neural filter conditioned on target direction. Follow-up: "Multi-channel Speech Separation Using Spatially Selective Deep Non-linear Filters" (arXiv:2304.12023).

S. E. Eskimez, T. Yoshioka, H. Wang, X. Wang, Z. Chen, X. Huang, "Personalized Speech Enhancement: New Models and Comprehensive Evaluation," arXiv:2110.09625 (ICASSP 2022). Defines the target-speaker over-suppression (TSOS) metric, the direct evidence and test for the 'personalized model suppresses the enrolled talker' risk.

P. U. Diehl, Y. Singer, H. Zilly, U. Schönfeld, P. Meyer-Rachner, M. Berry, H. Sprekeler, E. Sprengel, A. Pudszuhn, V. M. Hofmann, "Restoring speech intelligibility for hearing aid users with deep learning," Scientific Reports 13, 2719 (2023), doi:10.1038/s41598-023-29871-8. Peer-reviewed human-intelligibility evidence for DNN denoising in hearing aids; Phonak's white paper cites it. The independent counterpart to the manufacturer claims.

A. Vinnikov et al., "NOTSOFAR-1 Challenge: New Datasets, Baseline, and Tasks for Distant Meeting Transcription," Proc. Interspeech 2024 (arXiv:2401.08887). Real far-field meetings (30 rooms, 4-8 attendees, single- and multi-channel devices) with an open baseline (continuous speech separation, ASR, diarization). Realistic evaluation data and a reference pipeline for the meeting case.

W. Rao, Y. Fu, Y. Hu, X. Xu, Y. Jv, J. Han, Z. Jiang, L. Xie, Y. Wang, S. Watanabe, Z.-H. Tan, H. Bu, T. Yu, S. Shang, "INTERSPEECH 2021 ConferencingSpeech Challenge: Towards Far-field Multi-Channel Speech Enhancement for Video Conferencing," arXiv:2104.00960. A far-field multi-channel conferencing enhancement benchmark.

K. Kinoshita, M. Delcroix, H. Kwon, T. Mori, T. Nakatani, "Neural Network-Based Spectrum Estimation for Online WPE Dereverberation," Proc. Interspeech 2017, pp. 384-388, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2017-733. DNN-driven WPE, the neural route to dereverberating distant meeting talkers, which the sweep leaves to classical WPE.

A. Plaquet, H. Bredin, "Powerset multi-class cross entropy loss for neural speaker diarization," Proc. Interspeech 2023, pp. 3222-3226 (arXiv:2310.13025). The pyannote segmentation-3.0 model behind the sherpa-onnx diarization that the meeting plan's per-speaker leveling depends on.

K. Iwamoto, T. Ochiai, M. Delcroix, R. Ikeshita, H. Sato, S. Araki, S. Katagiri, "How Bad Are Artifacts?: Analyzing the Impact of Speech Enhancement Errors on ASR," Interspeech 2022 (arXiv:2201.06685). Cited in the takeaways but not listed as a source; verified. Its evidence is about ASR, not human intelligibility.
verify.notes:
VERIFICATION SUMMARY

All 17 sources exist. Every numeric table claim I checked matched the primary sources: arXiv PDFs, repos, PyPI, GitHub release assets, and the Phonak PDF. The defects are below.

CORRECTIONS
- DPDFNet venue: accepted in Speech Communication (v3, 16 Jun 2026), not a "journal submission".
- NSNet2 entry and meeting takeaways: the reverberant MOS 2.44→2.16 and STOI 86.6→82.2 belong to NSNet v1 (Xia et al., ICASSP 2020; the DTLN paper's baseline), not NSNet2. Valid NSNet2 evidence: VB-DEMAND STOI 0.921→0.903 and DNS4 DNSMOS SIG 3.23→3.08.
- Personalized PercepNet training ranges: SNR −5..35 dB and SIR −5..10 dB. The pitch-modulation artifact appears during target/interferer overlap, not because voices are close in pitch.
- REAL-TSE baseline TER: 0.651–0.773, not up to 0.84.
- GTCRN complexity: the paper reports 23.7K params / 39.6 MMAC/s; 48.2K / 33.0 are the repo's later figures.
- DF3 author order: Schröter, Rosenkranz, Escalante-B., Maier.
- Phonak: the "ARTE / 12 loudspeakers" test setup is not in the white paper and could not be verified. "DNN gives most of the benefit" is an inference.
- DNS-2023: "personalized models suppress the enrolled talker" is only loosely supported. Eskimez 2022 (the TSOS metric) is the direct evidence.

PACKAGING (all confirmed)
- sherpa-onnx 2.0.1 (GitHub release 2026-10-26) has macOS arm64 wheels for cp312, cp313 and cp314.
- The VoxLock, GTCRN and DPDFNet configuration classes and the example scripts exist.
- Release assets: voxlock-int8 72.5 MB; dpdfnet 8.8–14.6 MB; gtcrn 0.54 MB.
- onnxruntime 1.31.1 has cp312–cp314 arm64 wheels (macOS 14+).
- deepfilternet-rs supports only cp310–cp312.
- pyrnnoise 0.4.5 is a macOS-26 wheel.
- The deep-filter CLI defaults are as claimed and it resamples internally.
- H-GTCRN runs WPE and IVA inside torch, so it needs a numpy port.
- The VoxLock repo is only about 3 weeks old (created 2026-10-11).

CROSS-CUTTING OVERCLAIMS (2 omni MEMS, 2.5–6 cm, 16 kHz)

1) Bus post-filter gains are overstated. "+12–14 dB SI-SNR, STOI →91–93%" comes from synthetic additive, non-reverberant mixtures scored with clean references. Thoidis & Goehring 2024 found that non-personalized enhancement FAILED to improve intelligibility in multi-talker restaurant noise. Expect quality/comfort gains, and treat intelligibility gains as unproven until tested on real bus recordings.

2) Two mics give one spatial degree of freedom. A rank-2 MWF/GEV cannot keep two partners in different directions undistorted and also null an interferer; that needs at least 3 mics.
- Practical 2-mic options: short-window steering to whichever partner is talking (they mostly take turns), or align the mic axis with the partner-partner line and use a dipole or back-to-back cardioids.
- Realistic spatial gain in diffuse babble: about 1–3 dB, at most 6 dB in theory.
- Gain against one point interferer in a bus cabin: roughly 3–8 dB, not up to 15.
- Matching the ±1 dB sensitivity and phase of the two INMP441s is mandatory.

3) H-GTCRN's 2-mic gain is largely IVA separating ONE point interferer: IVA alone scores STOI 70.2 against 61.1 for single-channel GTCRN at −7.5 dB. Diffuse babble removes most of that advantage.

4) Partners at 0.3–1 m: my rough estimate puts the bus critical distance near 0.6–0.8 m (about 66 m³, RT60 about 0.5 s). The 0.3 m case is favourable; the 1 m case is marginal for VoxLock and for distance-based extraction.

MEETING-CASE REALITY CHECK (the neural angle understates this)
- Estimated critical distance in a 240 m³ room at RT60 0.7 s is about 1–1.5 m. A talker at 6 m then has a direct-to-reverberant ratio of about −12 to −15 dB.
- No single-channel network, and no 2-mic beamformer at 2.5–6 cm, will make such talkers evenly intelligible. Per-speaker gain from diarization raises reverberation and noise by the same amount, so the speech-to-noise ratio does not change.
- WPE, classical or DNN-WPE, gives modest late-reverberation reduction.
- The INMP441's 33 dBA self-noise penalizes superdirective beams in a quiet room, so keep a white-noise-gain constraint.
- The realistic fix is hardware: several distributed ESP32 two-mic nodes along the table, or a larger array. Evaluate on NOTSOFAR-1-style real meetings.

LIMITS OF THIS CHECK
The web-search budget ran out near the end, so these remain unverified:
- the deep-filter reduce-mask semantics (1=max, 2=mean);
- the Tan, Zhang & Wang IEEE/ACM TASLP journal version (only the ICASSP 2021 version was confirmed);
- the Phonak ARTE claim.
Every missing source I listed was confirmed on arXiv, ISCA, OpenAlex or publisher pages.

sweep.angle: Capturing MANY talkers in a LARGE REVERBERANT MEETING ROOM with one 2-mic device: room physics (critical distance, DRR vs distance, what 2 omnis can and cannot do), WPE dereverberation (offline/online), coherence/CDR postfiltering, GCC-PHAT/SRP-PHAT talker tracking, Dugan gain-sharing automixing, noise-capped/position-aware AGC and EBU R128 loudness, conferencing-industry DSP (Shure, Biamp, Sennheiser, Poly, Nureva, Teams Rooms, Owl/Jabra), and lessons from Microsoft meeting research, LibriCSS, CHiME-6/GSS and AliMeeting.

sources.title: Room Acoustics (6th ed.): critical distance (reverberation radius) and direct-to-reverberant ratio vs distance
sources.authors: Heinrich Kuttruff
sources.venue: CRC Press / Taylor & Francis textbook (ISBN 978-1-4822-6043-4). Formula cross-checked in the pyrato.parametric.critical_distance docs, which cite Kuttruff (4th ed.)
sources.key_idea: In a diffuse reverberant room, direct sound falls 6 dB per doubling of distance while the reverberant level stays roughly constant. The two are equal at the critical distance r_c. Beyond r_c the microphone signal is mostly reverberation (DRR < 0 dB). A directional pickup with directivity factor γ stretches r_c by sqrt(γ).
sources.algorithm: r_c ≈ 0.057·sqrt(γ·V/T60) m, with V in m³, T60 in s, γ=1 omni, ≈3 cardioid, ≈4 hypercardioid. DRR(r) ≈ 20·log10(r_c/r) dB. Total received power ∝ 1/r² + 1/r_c². Values computed for this project: V=210-288 m³ and T60=0.5-0.9 s give r_c ≈ 0.9-1.4 m. DRR is about +3…0 dB at 1 m, −7…−11 dB at 3 m and −13…−17 dB at 6 m. Classical theory predicts the total level drops only ≈3-4 dB from 1 m to 6 m, while DRR drops ≈15 dB. A bus cabin (assumed ≈66 m³, T60 0.3-0.5 s) gives r_c ≈ 0.65-0.85 m.
sources.bus_relevance: The two target talkers (0.3-1 m) are inside or near r_c (DRR ≈ +7…−2 dB), while other passengers are far beyond it. Directness (coherence/DRR) is therefore a physically valid cue for keeping the pair and suppressing the crowd.
sources.meeting_relevance: Far talkers sound distant rather than quiet. AGC alone cannot fix this because it scales reverberation together with speech. Only dereverberation or a shorter talker-to-mic distance (more nodes) changes DRR. Use these numbers to set expectations and to configure simulations.
sources.two_mic_reality: Two omnis barely move r_c. With d=4 cm, broadside delay-and-sum DI is only ≈0.2/0.8/1.7/2.7 dB at 1/2/3/4 kHz (computed). Endfire differential patterns reach γ≈3-4 (DI 4.8-6 dB), but only toward the two axis directions and with a heavy low-frequency white-noise penalty. Most of 20 talkers around a table get ≤0-3 dB of spatial DRR gain.
sources.implementation: One line of numpy, or pyrato.parametric.critical_distance(volume, reverberation_time). Feed the same V/T60 into pyroomacoustics (inverse Sabine) to build the test rooms.

sources.title: Speech dereverberation based on variance-normalized delayed linear prediction (WPE), with its MIMO generalization (Yoshioka & Nakatani 2012) and the NARA-WPE implementation (Drude et al. 2018)
sources.authors: T. Nakatani, T. Yoshioka, K. Kinoshita, M. Miyoshi, B.-H. Juang (2010); T. Yoshioka, T. Nakatani (2012); L. Drude, J. Heymann, C. Boeddeker, R. Haeb-Umbach (2018)
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. ASLP 18(7):1717-1731 (2010); IEEE Trans. ASLP 20(10):2707-2720 (2012); ITG Speech Communication 2018 + GitHub fgnt/nara_wpe (MIT)
sources.key_idea: Blind, linear dereverberation. In every STFT bin, WPE predicts the late reverberation of the current frame from delayed past frames of all mics and subtracts it. The predictor is the maximum-likelihood solution under a time-varying-variance speech model, solved by iteratively reweighted least squares. The 2012 MIMO generalization (blind MIMO impulse-response shortening) dereverberates every channel jointly and keeps the direct path and early reflections. Inter-channel cues therefore survive for later DOA, beamforming and CDR stages.
sources.algorithm: STFT 512/128 at 16 kHz. Per bin, stack ỹ(t)=[y(t−Δ),…,y(t−Δ−K+1)] over D mics (dimension D·K). Iterate 3-5 times: λ(t)=mean_d|x_d(t)|², optionally averaged over ±psd_context frames; R=Σ ỹỹᴴ/λ; P=Σ ỹyᴴ/λ; G=R⁻¹P; x(t)=y(t)−Gᴴỹ(t). nara_wpe defaults: taps=10, delay=3, iterations=3; the example notebook uses 16 kHz, size 512, shift 128, iterations 5. Online class OnlineWPE does an RLS/Kalman update of R⁻¹ and G with forgetting factor alpha (example 0.9999) and a buffer of taps+delay+1 frames. Suggested sweep for RT60 0.5-0.9 s: taps ∈ {10,15,20}, delay ∈ {2,3}.
sources.bus_relevance: Low. Bus capture is noise-limited with a short RT, and the target pair already has high DRR. WPE's signal model ignores additive noise.
sources.meeting_relevance: Core tool. It is the only blind, artifact-free way to raise DRR for all 20 talkers without knowing their positions. As a linear filter it does not raise the noise floor. It is the standard first stage in the CHiME-6/GSS pipelines and in NTT's REVERB system.
sources.two_mic_reality: Works with D=2: 20×20 matrices per bin at 10 taps, so it is cheap. The filters depend on talker position and need several seconds of one talker to converge. One filter estimated over a whole 20-talker meeting is wrong. Run it offline per VAD/DOA segment with context, or online with a shorter memory plus per-position filter memory. My suggestion (to be tuned) is alpha≈0.995-0.998, about 2-4 s at an 8 ms hop. Expect partial, not studio-dry, tail reduction for 4-6 m talkers.
sources.implementation: pip install nara_wpe: v0.0.11 (Sep 2024), a pure-Python wheel. The core wpe.py imports only numpy and click. The declared dependencies are tqdm, soundfile, bottleneck and click; use --no-deps if no bottleneck wheel exists for 3.14. The README states tests on Python 3.7-3.10. Use wpe/wpe_v8 on Y[F,D,T] and OnlineWPE(taps, delay, alpha, channel=2, frequency_bins=257).step_frame. Offline processing of one hour of 2-channel audio takes minutes on an M1; online processing is real-time feasible.

sources.title: Adaptive multichannel dereverberation for automatic speech recognition (Google online WPE), deployed in 'Acoustic Modeling for Google Home'
sources.authors: J. Caroselli, I. Shafran, A. Narayanan, R. Rose (Google); companion paper: B. Li, T. N. Sainath, A. Narayanan, J. Caroselli et al.
sources.venue: Interspeech 2017 (both papers); Google patents US10762914 / US11699453
sources.key_idea: A causal, frequency-domain RLS version of multichannel WPE for a 2-microphone smart speaker: mics about 70 mm apart (71 mm in simulation), 16 kHz. It gives gains similar to non-causal WPE on large real far-field datasets. This is the closest industry analog to our hardware.
sources.algorithm: Per bin: Ỹ = N delayed frames (starting Δ back) from both mics; output Ŷ=Y−WᴴỸ. Power-weighted RLS: Kalman gain K=SỸ/(αΛ²+ỸᴴSỸ), with S updated by the matrix inversion lemma and Λ² a running power estimate. α=0.9999. N=10 taps; more than about 10 degraded ASR. Google Home used Δ=2 frames and reset taps to zero at each utterance. Taps need roughly 2 s to adapt. Both papers cite Yoshioka et al., ICASSP 2009, 'Adaptive dereverberation of speech signals with speaker-position change detection', for handling talker moves.
sources.bus_relevance: Low to moderate. It shows 2-mic online dereverberation is affordable in real time, but the bus problem is noise, not reverberation.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Quantified expectation for exactly 2 omnis in far field (simulated rooms with RT60 0-900 ms, 1-8 m): WER 20.2→19.2% (≈5% relative) on rerecorded data and 32.2→29.5% (≈8% relative) on rerecorded-noisy data. The Google Home paper shows up to ≈7% relative (32.2→30.1%) with no loss on clean speech.
sources.two_mic_reality: Directly applicable, but gains are single-digit percent relative WER. Each new talker gets about 1-2 s of less-dereverberated speech while the taps re-adapt. For 20 alternating talkers, my adaptation is to keep a filter state per DOA cluster and restore it on talker change.
sources.implementation: numpy RLS in about 80 lines, vectorized over 257 bins (20-dimensional state for 2 mics × 10 taps); real-time on M1. Alternatively nara_wpe.OnlineWPE(channel=2, taps=10, delay=2, alpha=0.999x).

sources.title: Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation (plus the coherence postfilter evaluated on real CHiME-3 data, including BUS)
sources.authors: A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann; follow-up by H. Barfuss, C. Huemmer, A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM Trans. ASLP 23(6):1006-1018 (arXiv:1502.03784); MATLAB code github.com/andreas12345/cdr-dereverb (BSD-2); Barfuss et al., arXiv:1604.03393 (v4, 2017)
sources.key_idea: The short-time complex coherence between two omni mics lets you estimate, per time-frequency bin, the ratio of coherent (direct) to diffuse (late reverberation plus diffuse noise) power. This CDR is turned into a Wiener-like gain. Unbiased estimators need either the DOA or only the diffuse-coherence model. The DOA-independent one does blind dereverberation of any talker.
sources.algorithm:
Φ_ij(l,f)=λΦ_ij(l−1,f)+(1−λ)X_iX_j*, with λ=0.68 (hop 128 at 16 kHz); Γ_x=Φ12/sqrt(Φ11Φ22). Diffuse model Γ_n=sin(2πfd/c)/(2πfd/c), which needs the spacing d. Direct model Γ_s=e^{j2πfΔt} for the DOA-dependent variants. CDR comes from the unbiased estimators (estimate_cdr_nodoa.m, estimate_cdr_unbiased.m, estimate_cdr_robust_unbiased.m). Channels are combined as Y=sqrt((|X1|²+|X2|²)/2)·e^{j∠X1}. Gain G=max(Gmin, 1−sqrt(µ/(CDR+1))) with µ=1.3 and Gmin=0.1. Filterbank: window 1024, FFT 512, hop 128.

Results with 2 mics 8 cm apart, T60 0.6-3.5 s, sources at 1-4 m: ASR accuracy 62.2→77.6% (DOA-independent) or 81.5% (DOA-dependent); ELR50 6.1→9.4/10.8 dB; PESQ 1.27→1.42/1.48. In a 5×3.5×3 m meeting room (T60 0.6 s): 63.9→80.2/81.9%. As a beamformer postfilter on real CHiME-3 data (6-mic tablet): 7-8% relative WER reduction overall, and BUS WER 18.53→17.42-17.71%.
sources.bus_relevance: High. Crowd babble and road noise are roughly diffuse, while the two talkers at 0.3-1 m are coherent. The CDR gain is therefore a cheap, physics-based near-talker gate that needs no DOA. Run it more aggressively (µ 1.3-2) with a gain floor. Add an HPF and stationary NS for engine rumble, where the gain is weak.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. It gives blind (DOA-independent) suppression of late reverberation and diffuse HVAC noise for all 20 talkers. Cascade it after WPE with mild settings (µ≈1-1.3, Gmin≈0.1-0.3) to avoid musical noise. The per-utterance mean CDR is also a distance (DRR) proxy for position-aware AGC.
sources.two_mic_reality: A native 2-mic method, but its frequency range depends on d. Diffuse coherence falls below 0.7 only above ≈3.1/1.9/1.3/1.0 kHz for d=2.5/4/6/8 cm (sinc model, computed). At the user's ≈4 cm it acts mainly above about 2 kHz. It needs an accurate d (use the user's diffuse-coherence fit) and phase-matched mics. The ±1 dB INMP441 gain mismatch does not bias coherence magnitude. It is nonlinear: over-suppression produces musical noise.
sources.implementation: Port the MATLAB to numpy, about 100-150 lines (only auto/cross PSDs per bin); real-time is trivial.

sources.title: A summary of the REVERB challenge: state-of-the-art and remaining challenges in reverberant speech processing research
sources.authors: K. Kinoshita, M. Delcroix, S. Gannot, E. Habets, R. Haeb-Umbach, W. Kellermann, V. Leutnant, R. Maas, T. Nakatani, B. Raj, A. Sehr, T. Yoshioka
sources.venue: EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. 2016:7 (open access), doi:10.1186/s13634-016-0306-6
sources.key_idea: Benchmark of 25 enhancement and 49 ASR systems on simulated and real reverberant speech. RealData: RT60≈0.7 s, near≈1 m, far≈2.5 m, 8-ch circular array of 20 cm diameter. Many 1/2/8-channel systems reduced perceived reverberation. Overall quality was reliably improved mainly by multichannel (2-ch and 8-ch) systems. Linear processing (WPE-type inverse filtering, beamforming) helped without unnatural nonlinear distortion; 1-channel nonlinear methods often traded reverberation for artifacts. ASR: the 8-ch WPE-based front end gave more than 30% relative WER reduction; delay-and-sum gave about 10%.
sources.algorithm: Evaluation lessons rather than one algorithm. Objective measures: CD, SRMR, LLR, FWSegSNR, PESQ, plus a MUSHRA-style (BS.1534) listening test of perceived reverberation and overall quality.
sources.bus_relevance: Low (reverberation-focused). General lesson: aggressive nonlinear suppression costs naturalness.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Justifies the order 'linear 2-ch WPE first, mild nonlinear postfilter second' and sets realistic expectations for 1-2.5 m talkers in a 0.7 s room.
sources.two_mic_reality: 2-ch systems were a separate category and many significantly improved overall quality. For our 2 mics, expect clearly audible but partial reverberation reduction; 8-ch-level ASR gains are out of reach.
sources.implementation: Reuse the metrics: SRMR (non-intrusive), and PESQ/ESTOI in simulation. No code is needed from the paper.

sources.title: The generalized correlation method for estimation of time delay (GCC with PHAT weighting), with SRP-PHAT for multi-node fusion
sources.authors: C. H. Knapp, G. C. Carter (1976); J. H. DiBiase (PhD thesis, Brown University, 2000)
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. ASSP 24(4):320-327, doi:10.1109/TASSP.1976.1162830; DiBiase, 'A high-accuracy, low-latency technique for talker localization in reverberant environments using microphone arrays'
sources.key_idea: The TDOA between two sensors is the peak of a frequency-weighted cross-correlation. PHAT weighting whitens the cross-spectrum so the direct-path peak stays sharp in reverberation; it is the workhorse of conferencing talker localization. SRP-PHAT sums pairwise GCC-PHAT over a spatial grid. For one 2-mic node it equals GCC-PHAT, but it is the way to fuse several nodes.
sources.algorithm: C(f)=X1X2*/(|X1X2*|+ε), averaged over 0.1-0.5 s of speech frames. Weight frames and bins by speech probability and by high CDR to favour direct-path-dominant bins. r(τ)=IFFT with ×16 zero-padding for sub-sample resolution. τ̂=argmax over |τ|≤d/c; θ=arccos(cτ̂/d). Restrict to about 200 Hz up to min(4 kHz, c/2d). Track talkers by clustering τ̂ per speech segment (histogram or online k-means). Declare a talker change when the dominant cluster switches for more than 200-300 ms.
sources.bus_relevance: Medium to high. Locates the two conversation partners so an angular fence or beam can be built toward them. In dense babble, use only high-CDR frames, otherwise the estimate wanders.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Provides the 'position' key for per-talker gain memory (Nureva idea), per-position WPE filter memory, speaker-change detection, and optional mild beam steering.
sources.two_mic_reality: One pair gives one angle relative to the array axis, with mirror (cone) ambiguity. Maximum TDOA is ±1.2/±1.9/±2.8 samples at 16 kHz for 2.5/4/6 cm, so interpolation is mandatory. Resolution degrades toward endfire. Beyond r_c (DRR −8…−15 dB) single-frame estimates are unreliable, so accumulate over time. Realistically about 10-15 separable angular clusters in 180° (my estimate); neighbouring seats merge.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 30-40 lines. pyroomacoustics.doa provides SRP (SRP-PHAT), MUSIC, NormMUSIC, TOPS, CSSM, WAVES and FRIDA for multi-node experiments.

sources.title: Automatic microphone mixer: Dugan gain-sharing automixing (US Patent 3,992,584)
sources.authors: Daniel W. Dugan
sources.venue: US Patent 3,992,584 (filed 9 May 1975, granted 16 Nov 1976); preceded by US 3,814,856 (ambient-sensing control apparatus) and an AES 1974 presentation
sources.key_idea: Hold total system gain constant by giving each input a gain equal to its share of the total level. Each channel is attenuated by as many dB as its level lies below the level of the sum of all inputs. With one talker, his channel stays near 0 dB and the others drop strongly; with two equal talkers, each is about −3 dB. With N noise-only channels, each is −10·log10(N) dB, so the mix carries the noise and reverberation of only one open mic. There is no 3 dB-per-doubling build-up from the number of open mics, and no gating clicks.
sources.algorithm: Per channel k: band-limited (about 300-4000 Hz) envelope power P_k with about 10-50 ms smoothing. g_k = P_k/Σ_j P_j, equivalently g_k[dB] = L_k − L_sum. Optional per-channel bias/priority and last-mic-hold. Smooth the gains (attack about 5-20 ms, release about 100-300 ms). Output y = Σ g_k·x_k.
sources.bus_relevance: Medium. Mix two back-to-back endfire beams aimed at the two partners, so the active talker dominates while the summed background stays at one channel's level.
sources.meeting_relevance: High once several capture nodes are used (recommended). It automatically favours the node nearest the active talker, which shrinks the effective talker-to-mic distance. Biamp Parlé sums its tracked beams through such a gain-sharing automixer, and Shure offers gain-sharing and gating modes.
sources.two_mic_reality: Inside one 2-mic node the 'channels' (beams) are strongly correlated (DI ≤ ≈5 dB), so the benefit is small. Across multiple ESP32 nodes it is the most robust combiner, because it needs no sample-accurate synchronization, unlike beamforming across independent USB clocks.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 20 lines; real-time.

sources.title: WebRTC Audio Processing Module: AGC2 adaptive digital gain controller, noise suppressor and HPF (Python access via LiveKit)
sources.authors: WebRTC project (Google et al.); Python binding by LiveKit (livekit.rtc.AudioProcessingModule)
sources.venue: Open-source C++ (BSD), main branch as accessed; PyPI livekit 1.2.0 (Oct 2026)
sources.key_idea: A production AGC built not to amplify noise. Speech level is estimated only from frames the RNN-VAD is confident about. The gain brings that level to a target below full scale, is slew-limited, and is capped so the estimated noise floor after gain stays below a ceiling. A limiter follows. The module also includes a mature stationary noise suppressor and an HPF.
sources.algorithm:
AdaptiveDigital defaults: headroom_db=5, max_gain_db=50, initial_gain_db=15, max_gain_change_db_per_second=6, max_output_noise_level_dbfs=−50. target_gain = clamp(−headroom − speech_level, 0, max_gain). LimitGainByNoise: gain ≤ max(−50 − noise_dBFS, 0). A frame counts as speech when VAD probability ≥0.95 for ≥12 consecutive 10 ms frames. The level estimator needs about 400 ms of speech to become confident. The adaptive gain is reduced when the limiter level exceeds −1 dBFS. NS levels: kLow, kModerate (default), kHigh, kVeryHigh.

Alternative: the SpeexDSP preprocess AGC (agc_level 8000 ≈ −12 dBFS RMS, max gain 30 dB, +12 dB/s up and −40 dB/s down, adapts only when speech probability > 0.5). Its NS default is −15 dB, and its dereverb switch is a no-op in current code (marked FIXME).
sources.bus_relevance: High. The noise cap and VAD-gated adaptation stop the AGC from pumping crowd noise up between utterances. NS removes stationary engine and road hum, and the AGC evens out the two talkers.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Evens loudness without lifting HVAC/projector noise. Limitation: it is talker-agnostic and slews at ≤6 dB/s, so after a loud near talker a quiet far one stays under-amplified for seconds. Add per-position gain memory (see the Nureva entry).
sources.two_mic_reality: A mono stage, applied after the 2-channel spatial processing. With the INMP441 at −26 dBFS for 94 dB SPL, speech at the mic (about 55-60 dB SPL) lands near −60…−65 dBFS, so about +35-40 dB of gain is needed. Keep 24-bit/float and apply a fixed pre-gain of about +20 dB before the int16 APM. With 35-45 dBA HVAC, the −50 dBFS noise cap, not the AGC, will bound how loud far talkers get unless NS runs first.
sources.implementation: pip install livekit (1.2.0; macOS arm64 wheel 9.3 MB, py3-none, Python ≥3.9). AudioProcessingModule(noise_suppression=True, high_pass_filter=True, auto_gain_control=True); its C++ shim enables gain_controller2 with adaptive_digital at default parameters, which cannot be changed from Python. Call process_stream() on exactly-10 ms int16 AudioFrames (16 kHz works). For tunable or position-aware AGC, port AGC2's roughly 200 lines of logic to numpy. webrtc-noise-gain (rhasspy, AGC1-style dBFS target) ships Linux wheels only, so macOS needs an sdist build. The speexdsp Python bindings date from 2018.

sources.title: EBU R 128: Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals (measured with ITU-R BS.1770), plus pyloudnorm
sources.authors: European Broadcasting Union; ITU-R (BS.1770); C. J. Steinmetz & J. D. Reiss (pyloudnorm, AES 150th Convention 2021)
sources.venue: EBU R 128 v5.0 (Nov 2023), EBU Tech 3341/3342; ITU-R BS.1770; ITU-T P.56 (active speech level, current edition 07/2026)
sources.key_idea: Level audio by perceived loudness, not peaks. Integrated programme loudness target is −23 LUFS (±0.5 LU; ±1 LU live), maximum true peak −1 dBTP, plus a Loudness Range descriptor. Momentary (400 ms) and short-term (3 s) loudness allow per-segment and per-talker measurement. ITU-T P.56 'active speech level' is the telephony counterpart that measures speech-only level.
sources.algorithm: BS.1770: K-weighting, mean square in 400 ms blocks with 75% overlap, absolute gate −70 LUFS, relative gate −10 LU, giving integrated loudness. Three uses here: (1) evaluation metric: per-talker integrated loudness on diarized/VAD segments, reporting the spread (max−min LU) across the 20 talkers before and after processing; (2) final offline normalization to −23 LUFS (or another chosen target) with a −1 dBTP true-peak limiter; (3) definition of the AGC target.
sources.bus_relevance: Medium. Verifies that both partners end up at similar loudness. Measuring loudness in speech vs pause segments quantifies background suppression.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Turns 'evenly loud' into a number. For example, a goal of ≤±2-3 LU spread across talkers; this is a design target, not a published result.
sources.two_mic_reality: Measurement only, independent of mic count. Gating does not tell speech from noise, so measure on speech segments.
sources.implementation: pip install pyloudnorm (0.2.0, Jan 2026, pure Python): pyln.Meter(16000).integrated_loudness(x). The ITU-T P.56 reference C code is in the ITU-T G.191 STL (SV-P56 module).

sources.title: Conferencing arrays in practice: Shure MXA920 (Automatic Coverage, Autofocus, IntelliMix AGC/automixer/denoiser), Biamp Parlé Beamtracking, Sennheiser TeamConnect Ceiling 2
sources.authors: Shure Inc.; Biamp Systems; Sennheiser
sources.venue: Shure MXA920 user guide (2026 edition); Biamp Cornerstone support docs for the Parlé series; Sennheiser TCC2 product page and newsroom
sources.key_idea:
What the DSP in these products actually does:
(1) Talker tracking. Shure Autofocus refines lobes in real time within up to 8 coverage areas. Biamp Parlé runs a separate speech-band tracking path that localizes talkers and steers one beam per 90° zone, and freezes tracking while the far end talks. Sennheiser TCC2 (28 capsules) uses patented automatic dynamic beamforming that follows the active talker, with exclusion and priority zones and 4 ms latency.
(2) Automixing of lobes/beams. Either gain-sharing (system gain equal to one open channel) or gating with off-attenuation, maximum open channels, last-mic-lock and priority. Biamp sums its beams with a gain-sharing automixer.
(3) Per-channel AGC placed after the automix gate, so it never acts on gated-off noise. Shure suggests −37 dBFS as a starting target, with max boost and max cut limits.
(4) Adaptive denoiser and AEC.
The MXA920 is rated for talkers up to 4.9 m away.
sources.algorithm: Chain worth copying: speech-band localization path → steer or select beams/nodes → AEC (if a loudspeaker is present) → denoise → automix (gain-sharing, or gating with off-attenuation and last-mic-lock) → post-gate AGC with max boost/cut → limiter and delay. Our analog: GCC-PHAT tracker → per-node or per-beam channels → WPE + CDR → NS → Dugan gain sharing → position-aware AGC (post-gate) → limiter.
sources.bus_relevance: Medium. Exclusion/priority zones and 'track only speech-band energy' map to an angular gate around the two partners. Off-attenuation in pauses keeps the crowd down.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Confirms the architecture (track → automix → post-gate AGC) and the distance ceiling: even 28-100+ capsule arrays are specified to about 5 m.
sources.two_mic_reality: We can copy the control logic, not the spatial selectivity. Their lobes come from 8-100+ capsules; two omnis give about 0-6 dB DI depending on direction. Tracking mainly helps us choose per-talker gains and filters, not reject sound spatially.
sources.implementation: numpy re-implementation of the control logic, about 200 lines in total.

sources.title: Talker-position-based gain control (Nureva HDL300/HDL310/HDL410, 'Microphone Mist')
sources.authors: Nureva Inc.
sources.venue: Nureva technical blog, originally published in audioXpress. The year is inferred from page assets. Nureva describes 'patented algorithms' but gives no patent numbers.
sources.key_idea: Conventional AGC treats the signal as a whole: lifting a quiet or far talker also lifts room noise, and gain swings between talkers cause 'noise pumping'. Nureva uses the measured talker position to choose the gain strategy, raising each talker's level while keeping the ambient noise level constant.
sources.algorithm: My implementable interpretation; the vendor gives no numbers. Keep a table from position to speech level. Position = (GCC-PHAT TDOA cluster, mean-CDR/DRR distance proxy, optional speaker-embedding ID). Per position, keep a leaky average of active-speech level (BS.1770/P.56 style, ≥400 ms of confident speech). Gain g_p = clamp(target − L_p, −10, +40 dB), capped by the AGC2 noise rule. On a confirmed talker change (≥200-300 ms), cross-fade to g_p in about 50-100 ms instead of slewing at 6 dB/s. During pauses, hold a single room gain so the noise floor does not move. Optionally apply the extra talker gain only to speech-dominant time-frequency bins (mask-weighted) to keep noise constant.
sources.bus_relevance: Medium. Two stable per-talker gains with a constant background.
sources.meeting_relevance: High. Matches the 'all 20 talkers evenly loud, noise not boosted' requirement and fixes the slow cross-talker adaptation of standard AGCs.
sources.two_mic_reality: Position from 2 mics is coarse: one angle with mirror ambiguity plus a noisy distance proxy, giving perhaps 10-15 usable clusters. Adjacent or mirrored seats merge, which is acceptable when they are at similar distances; otherwise add a small speaker-embedding model. It degrades gracefully to plain AGC2 behaviour.
sources.implementation: numpy, about 100 lines on top of GCC-PHAT, CDR and an AGC2-style level estimator.

sources.title: HP Poly Audio Innovations: NoiseBlockAI and Acoustic Fence
sources.authors: HP Inc. / Poly
sources.venue: HP technical brochure PDF c09038815. It is undated; the HP Poly branding implies 2024 or later.
sources.key_idea: NoiseBlockAI uses machine-learning speech/non-speech classification to remove non-voice noise in conversational gaps (auto-mutes non-verbal noise); it also reduces reverberation. Acoustic Fence defines a pickup zone as an angle from the video bar (beamforming) and suppresses voices outside it as a 'smart mute'. More separated mics make the fence more precise, and desk phones use a reference mic for background. M-mode turns AGC and NS off for music.
sources.algorithm: Our analogs. (1) NoiseBlock ≈ a VAD-gated downward expander/gate: after more than 200 ms of non-speech, ramp to −10…−20 dB; release within 20 ms at speech onset (look-ahead offline). (2) Acoustic Fence ≈ a DOA-sector soft mask: per time-frequency bin, compute the phase-implied TDOA; weight 1 inside the allowed sectors (the two bus partners, or the table area) and Gmin outside, with temporal smoothing. Or gate whole frames on the GCC-PHAT dominant DOA.
sources.bus_relevance: High. The fence maps to keeping only the two partners' directions, and the noise block keeps crowd noise low between utterances.
sources.meeting_relevance: Medium. Speech-gated attenuation keeps HVAC/projector noise down in pauses, and a fence can exclude a door or corridor direction.
sources.two_mic_reality: A 2-mic fence is only a cone around the array axis with front/back ambiguity, and per-bin phase in diffuse babble is noisy. Expect a few dB of extra rejection; hard masks create artifacts. ML noise blocking needs a model (covered by other angles).
sources.implementation: numpy, about 60 lines each; VAD via WebRTC VAD or an ONNX VAD.

sources.title: Teams Rooms certified systems and peripherals: recommended maximum microphone-to-talker distance (with tabletop analogs Owl Labs Meeting Owl 3 and Jabra PanaCast 50)
sources.authors: Microsoft (Teams Rooms certification); Owl Labs; Jabra (GN)
sources.venue: Microsoft Learn (page updated Oct 2026); Teams device certification spec packages V4 (2019) and V5 (2023); vendor spec pages
sources.key_idea:
Certified practice caps talker distance:
- Focus room (2-4 people): 1.5 m.
- Small (4-6 people): 2.0 m.
- Medium (6-12 people): 2.4 m.
- Large (12-16 people, 4.5×9.75 m): 3 m; the 3 m also applies to each satellite microphone.
Tabletop 8-mic devices: Meeting Owl 3 claims an 18 ft (5.5 m) pickup radius with mics that equalize speaking volume, plus 2.5 m per expansion mic. Jabra PanaCast 50 (8-mic beamforming) is certified for rooms up to 4.5×6 m.
sources.algorithm: Deployment rule: every talker within about 2.4-3 m of some microphone node. Number of nodes ≈ ceil(table length / 4-5 m), placed on the table centreline and combined with a gain-sharing automix.
sources.bus_relevance: Low, except that talkers at 0.3-1 m are well inside even the 1.5 m focus-room distance.
sources.meeting_relevance: Very high for setting expectations. Twenty people with talkers up to 6 m from one device is about twice Microsoft's guidance for 12-16-person rooms. Industry solves this with ceiling arrays or satellite mics, not DSP alone.
sources.two_mic_reality: One 2-mic node cannot meet the guidance for 4-6 m talkers; 2-4 nodes can approach it.
sources.implementation: N/A (deployment rule). The V5 spec ZIP from Microsoft contains the detailed audio test procedures.

sources.title: Meeting Transcription Using Virtual Microphone Arrays
sources.authors: T. Yoshioka, Z. Chen, D. Dimitriadis, W. Hinthorn, X. Huang, A. Stolcke, M. Zeng (Microsoft)
sources.venue: arXiv:1905.02545 (Microsoft Research)
sources.key_idea: Several unsynchronized consumer devices (laptops, phones) spread around the table become a 'virtual microphone array' through continuous stream alignment, blind beamforming and system combination. With 7 streams, WER is 22.3%, within 3% of close-talk WER on non-overlapped speech. Speaker-attributed WER improves 14.8/20.3/22.4% relative with 3/5/7 devices compared with a single device.
sources.algorithm: (1) Coarse alignment of streams by cross-correlation, with periodic re-alignment to track clock drift. (2) Blind beamforming (mask/MVDR) or channel selection. (3) Diarization and system combination. Cheap version for us: N ESP32 2-mic nodes → per-node WPE+CDR → GCC-PHAT alignment on speech every few seconds → Dugan gain-sharing mix (tolerant of residual drift) → AGC.
sources.bus_relevance: Low; the bus case uses a single device.
sources.meeting_relevance: Very high. The strongest lever for capturing all 20 people is shrinking talker-to-mic distance with several cheap nodes; the paper shows double-digit relative gains from 3 or more devices.
sources.two_mic_reality: Each node is our 2-mic array. Nodes are not sample-synchronized (separate USB streams and clocks), so beamforming across nodes needs drift compensation; selection or gain sharing does not.
sources.implementation: numpy: alignment about 50 lines, automix about 20 lines; multiple USB streams on the Mac.

sources.title: Continuous speech separation: dataset and analysis (LibriCSS)
sources.authors: Z. Chen, T. Yoshioka, L. Lu, T. Zhou, Z. Meng, Y. Luo, J. Wu, X. Xiao, J. Li (Microsoft)
sources.venue: ICASSP 2020; arXiv:2001.11482
sources.key_idea: Real meeting-room replays with a 7-ch circular array, loudspeaker-to-mic distances of 33-409 cm and 0-40% overlap. Even without overlap, far-field WER (11.7-11.8%) is more than twice the anechoic WER (4.9-5.1%). 7-channel mask-based MVDR brings it to 8.3-8.4%. Single-channel separation degrades non-overlapped speech (no-separation 15.4% vs 17.6% WER at 0S), and with 3 mics separation gave no meaningful improvement for non-overlapped speech.
sources.algorithm: Sliding-window (e.g., 1.2-0.8-0.4 s) PIT-trained BLSTM mask estimation followed by MVDR per output stream; Kaldi ASR evaluation protocol; py-webrtcvad for segmentation.
sources.bus_relevance: Low to medium. Two overlapping partners are the 2-speaker CSS case, but neural separation is neither feasible nor useful here with 2 mics.
sources.meeting_relevance: High as a reality check. With 2 mics the meeting problem is reverberation and level, not separation, so don't spend effort on separation. The dataset is usable for tests by taking 2 adjacent channels.
sources.two_mic_reality: Separation gains scale with mic count. With 2 mics expect none on non-overlapped speech, and possible degradation; skip CSS.
sources.implementation: Use the dataset for evaluation only; the separation models need PyTorch, which is out of scope.

sources.title: CHiME-6 Challenge: Tackling multispeaker speech recognition for unsegmented recordings, read with the GPU-GSS ablations and AliMeeting/M2MeT
sources.authors: S. Watanabe et al. (CHiME-6, 2020); D. Raj et al. (GPU-accelerated guided source separation, 2022); F. Yu et al. (M2MeT/AliMeeting, ICASSP 2022)
sources.key_idea:
The state-of-the-art classical multi-talker front end is WPE (nara_wpe) plus guided source separation across arrays: dev WER 51.8% vs 69.8% for WPE + weighted delay-and-sum (BeamformIt).
GSS ablations: the number of channels is the single most important factor. Seven vs two channels gives 50.4% (LibriCSS) and 21.8% (AMI) relative WER reduction. WPE matters most on reverberant meeting-room replay, and 15 s context is best.
AliMeeting puts an 8-ch array on the table, with talkers at 0.3-5 m in 13 rooms of 8-55 m². The same near-field-trained ASR model gets 9.9% CER near-field vs 49.0% far-field, and far-field training only brings far CER to about 33-37%.
sources.algorithm: WPE (taps about 10, delay 2-3) → cACGMM spatial mixture model guided by speaker activity, ±15 s context, ≤5-20 EM iterations → mask-based MVDR.
sources.bus_relevance: Low. One lesson carries over: 2 channels give limited spatial separation of overlapping speech.
sources.meeting_relevance: Medium to high. Confirms (a) WPE as the standard first stage, (b) small spatial gains with only 2 channels, and (c) that extra channels or devices are worth more than algorithmic sophistication.
sources.two_mic_reality: GSS can technically run on 2 channels, but the ablation shows it loses most of its benefit, and it also needs diarization. Not a priority for this hardware.
sources.implementation: desh2608/gss uses CuPy/PyTorch on GPU, so it is not usable under the disk and framework constraints. Take the lessons only.

sources.title: Pyroomacoustics: A Python package for audio room simulations and array processing algorithms (test harness, plus DNSMOS P.835 for real recordings)
sources.authors: R. Scheibler, E. Bezzam, I. Dokmanić; DNSMOS P.835: C. K. A. Reddy, V. Gopal, R. Cutler
sources.venue: ICASSP 2018 (arXiv:1710.04196); DNSMOS P.835 arXiv:2110.01763 with ONNX models in github.com/microsoft/DNS-Challenge
sources.key_idea: Simulate both test cases with the exact 2-mic geometry: image-source (plus ray-tracing) RIRs for polyhedral rooms with many sources, and reference DOA (SRP-PHAT, MUSIC, NormMUSIC, …) and beamforming implementations. This gives reproducible, labelled data (clean direct/early reference, known per-talker levels) for tuning WPE, CDR and AGC before real recordings. DNSMOS P.835 gives non-intrusive SIG/BAK/OVRL scores on real recordings.
sources.algorithm:
Meeting: rooms 12×8×3 m and 10×7×3 m, absorption from inverse Sabine for RT60 0.5/0.7/0.9 s. Two mics with d ∈ {2.5,4,6,8} cm at table centre, 0.75 m high. Twenty talkers at 1.2 m height and 1-6 m distance, with levels randomized ±6 dB. Diffuse/pink HVAC noise at 35-45 dBA.
Metrics: DRR/ELR, ESTOI against a direct+50 ms reference, per-talker BS.1770 loudness spread, DOA error.
Bus: 12×2.5×2.2 m, RT60 0.3-0.5 s, 2 talkers at 0.3-1 m, 20-40 babble sources plus low-frequency engine noise.
Add ±1 dB gain mismatch and a small phase mismatch to mimic the INMP441.
sources.bus_relevance: High as a test harness.
sources.meeting_relevance: High as a test harness.
sources.two_mic_reality: Simulation idealizes diffuse noise, mic matching and source directivity, so confirm conclusions on real ESP32 recordings.
sources.implementation: pip install pyroomacoustics (0.10.1, May 2026; macOS arm64 wheels for CPython 3.10-3.14, about 1.1 MB). For DNSMOS: onnxruntime 1.31.1 (macOS arm64 wheel about 21 MB, Python ≥3.11) with DNSMOS/DNSMOS/sig_bak_ovr.onnx (1.16 MB).

sweep.takeaways:
BOTTOM LINE: the meeting case is limited by physics, not algorithms.
- In a 20-person room (V≈200-300 m³, RT60 0.5-0.9 s) the critical distance is only ≈0.9-1.4 m (Kuttruff formula, my calculation).
- A talker at 3 m arrives with DRR ≈ −7…−11 dB; at 6 m, ≈ −13…−17 dB.
- Total level at 6 m is only ≈3-4 dB below 1 m, so far talkers sound distant rather than quiet. AGC alone just amplifies the room.
- Industry never asks one device to cover 6 m: Teams Rooms ≤3 m per mic even in 12-16-person rooms; Shure MXA920 ≤4.9 m with a ceiling array; Owl 5.5 m radius and Jabra 4.5×6 m rooms with 8 mics.
- Two omnis 4 cm apart add only ≈0.2/0.8/1.7 dB DI at 1/2/3 kHz for broadside talkers, and ≤4.8-6 dB toward the two endfire directions (computed).
- Realistic target for ONE node: talkers within 2-3 m clear and level-matched; talkers at 4-6 m intelligible but audibly distant.

MEETING — what to build and test, in rank order
1. Build the test harness first: pyroomacoustics simulation of the exact geometry (add ±1 dB mic mismatch, 20 talkers at 1-6 m with ±6 dB voice spread, HVAC noise) plus real recordings.
   - Metrics: per-talker BS.1770 loudness spread (pyloudnorm), ELR/DRR and ESTOI in simulation, DNSMOS P.835 and listening on real audio.
2. HPF (80-100 Hz), then 2-channel MIMO WPE (nara_wpe): STFT 512/128, taps 10 (also try 15-20), delay 2-3, 3-5 iterations.
   - Run it per VAD/DOA segment offline, or online with the Google RLS recipe (10 taps, delay 2) plus per-talker filter memory.
   - Expected: audible tail reduction with no musical noise. In Google's 2-mic (70 mm) far-field system, about 4-8% relative WER reduction. In REVERB listening tests, 2-channel linear dereverberation improved overall quality, which 1-channel nonlinear methods mostly did not.
3. CDR coherence postfilter (DOA-independent, µ≈1.0-1.3, Gmin≈0.1-0.3) on the WPE output.
   - Published with 2 mics at 8 cm: ELR50 +3.3…+4.7 dB, PESQ +0.15…+0.21, ASR accuracy 62→78-82% (Schwarz & Kellermann).
   - In their 0.6 s meeting room: 64→80-82%.
   - At ≈4 cm the effect is confined to roughly 2 kHz and above, which is a reason to give the meeting unit 6-8 cm spacing.
4. Stationary noise suppression for HVAC/projector before any gain: WebRTC NS via `livekit` APM, or Speex NS (default −15 dB).
5. Position-aware, noise-capped AGC.
   - AGC2 logic: level from confident speech only; max gain ≥40 dB, because INMP441 speech sits near −60…−65 dBFS; ≤6 dB/s within one talker; output-noise cap ≈ −50 dBFS.
   - Add Nureva-style per-position gain memory, keyed by GCC-PHAT TDOA cluster plus mean CDR as a distance proxy, with a fast cross-fade at talker changes.
   - Hold gain in pauses and apply −6…−10 dB off-attenuation (Shure gating, Poly NoiseBlock).
   - Finish with a −1 dBTP limiter and offline normalization to −23 LUFS.
   - Target to verify (no published number exists): per-talker loudness spread from roughly 10-15 dB raw down to ≤±2-3 LU, with a noise floor that stays put across talkers.
6. Deployment — the largest single gain:
   - Put the device at the table centre with the array axis along the table, so the farthest (table-end) talkers are near endfire, where a 2-mic beam has its best DI.
   - Mount the mic ports within a few mm of the tabletop to avoid comb notches from the table reflection.
   - For 20 people, add 2-3 more ESP32 2-mic nodes so every talker is within about 3 m of a node (Teams rule), and mix them with Dugan gain-sharing, which needs no clock sync.
   - Moving the farthest talkers from 6 m to 2.5 m raises their DRR by ≈7.6 dB, more than all 2-mic DSP combined.
   - Published support: 14.8/20.3/22.4% relative speaker-attributed WER gains for 3/5/7 devices (Yoshioka 2019); GSS gains 50%/22% relative going from 2 to 7 channels (Raj 2022).
7. Skip:
   - Neural continuous speech separation, GSS or other separation with 2 channels: in LibriCSS, 1-channel separation degraded non-overlapped speech and 3 mics gave no meaningful gain.
   - Elaborate 2-mic beam steering: ≤0-3 dB for most seats.

BUS — what this angle contributes, in rank order
1. Noise-capped, speech-gated AGC with off-attenuation (AGC2 / NoiseBlock style), so the crowd is never boosted in pauses.
   - Add Dugan gain-sharing between two back-to-back endfire beams aimed at the two partners, with the array axis pointing at them.
2. CDR coherence postfilter as a near-talker gate.
   - In a bus, r_c ≈ 0.65-0.85 m (assumed cabin), so partners at 0.3-1 m are coherent while the crowd is diffuse.
   - Run it more aggressively (µ 1.3-2, Gmin 0.1), plus HPF and stationary NS for engine/road rumble below about 1.5-2 kHz, where coherence cannot discriminate at 4 cm.
   - Evidence is modest: on real CHiME-3 BUS data, a coherence postfilter after a 6-mic beamformer cut WER only from 18.53% to 17.42-17.71%.
   - My estimate for 2 mics: about 3-6 dB of extra babble reduction above 2 kHz.
3. GCC-PHAT 'acoustic fence': learn the two partners' TDOAs on high-CDR frames and softly attenuate other directions. Expect a few dB; hard masks create artifacts.
4. Skip WPE on the bus: the reverberation is short and the problem is noise.
This angle alone will not remove loud babble; combine it with the noise-focused (neural/MMSE) methods from other angles.

SPACING AND SIGNAL CHAIN
- Measure d exactly: with a clap at endfire, TDOA = d/c.
- Meeting use favours 6-8 cm: CDR works down to about 1-1.3 kHz and TDOA resolution is finer. Restrict the GCC band below c/2d.
- Differential beams for the bus tolerate smaller d.
- A single compromise build: about 5-6 cm.
- Keep the 24-bit audio as float end-to-end, since about 35-40 dB of digital gain is needed.
- Every stage (numpy WPE-RLS, CDR, GCC-PHAT, AGC, LiveKit APM) is real-time feasible on the M1.

checked.title: Room Acoustics (6th ed.): critical distance and direct-to-reverberant ratio vs distance
checked.correct_citation: H. Kuttruff, Room Acoustics, 6th ed., CRC Press (Taylor & Francis), Boca Raton, 2016. ISBN 978-1-4822-6043-4 (hbk), eISBN 978-1-315-37215-0, doi:10.1201/9781315372150. The pyrato.parametric.critical_distance docstring uses d_c = 0.057·sqrt(V/T60) and cites the 4th edition.
checked.applicability_verdict:
I recomputed the numbers and they are correct.
- r_c = 0.87–1.37 m for 210–288 m³ and T60 0.5–0.9 s.
- DRR is −6.8…−10.8 dB at 3 m and −12.8…−16.8 dB at 6 m.
- Total level drops 2.4–4.4 dB from 1 m to 6 m.
- Bus r_c = 0.65–0.85 m.
- Broadside delay-and-sum DI at 4 cm is 0.19/0.76/1.65/2.71 dB at 1/2/3/4 kHz.

Small errors: DRR at 1 m is +2.7…−1.2 dB, not +3…0. The bus pair (0.3–1 m) spans about +9…−4 dB, not +7…−2.

Caveats the angle omits:
- Sabine diffuse-field theory fits a long, low, passenger-packed bus cabin and a furnished meeting room poorly. Barron & Lee's revised theory has the reverberant level falling with distance, so far talkers drop somewhat more than 3–4 dB.
- Talker directivity (Q≈2 frontal) raises r_c by about 1.4× for talkers facing the device and lowers it for talkers facing each other (the bus pair) or facing away.

Consequence for the bus: the partner at ~1 m is at or beyond r_c. 'Directness' therefore separates direct from diffuse sound, not the conversation pair from bystanders 1–2 m away. Keep it as expectation-setting physics.

checked.title: WPE dereverberation (Nakatani 2010; Yoshioka & Nakatani 2012 MIMO; NARA-WPE 2018)
checked.correct_citation:
- T. Nakatani, T. Yoshioka, K. Kinoshita, M. Miyoshi, B.-H. Juang, 'Speech dereverberation based on variance-normalized delayed linear prediction,' IEEE Trans. ASLP 18(7):1717-1731, Sep 2010, doi:10.1109/TASL.2010.2052251.
- T. Yoshioka, T. Nakatani, 'Generalization of multi-channel linear prediction methods for blind MIMO impulse response shortening,' IEEE Trans. ASLP 20(10):2707-2720, Dec 2012, doi:10.1109/TASL.2012.2210879.
- L. Drude, J. Heymann, C. Boeddeker, R. Haeb-Umbach, 'NARA-WPE: A Python package for weighted prediction error dereverberation in Numpy and Tensorflow for online and offline processing,' ITG Speech Communication 2018.
- Software: nara_wpe 0.0.11 (PyPI, 2024-09-10).
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- nara_wpe 0.0.11 is a py3-none-any wheel. It declares numpy, tqdm, soundfile, bottleneck and click; wpe.py itself imports only numpy and click. The README says it is tested on Python 3.7–3.10.
- Defaults are taps 10, delay 3, iterations 3. The notebooks use 16 kHz, STFT 512/128, 5 iterations, and α=0.9999 online.
- OnlineWPE(taps, delay, alpha, channel, frequency_bins).step_frame exists, with a buffer of taps+delay+1 frames.

Two-channel MIMO WPE is valid and cheap. 'The only blind, artifact-free way' overstates it:
- WPE ignores additive noise, so HVAC noise lowers its gain.
- Short per-segment estimates and online filters that are mis-adapted after a talker change leave residual tails and over-whitening.
- Alternatives exist: statistical late-reverb PSD suppression and Kalman-filter multichannel linear prediction.

The α≈0.995–0.998 plus per-DOA filter-memory scheme is the agent's own untested design; the precedent is Yoshioka et al., ICASSP 2009. Expect only partial tail reduction for 3–6 m talkers. Low bus relevance is correct.

checked.title: Google online (RLS) WPE: Caroselli et al. 2017 + Acoustic Modeling for Google Home
checked.correct_citation:
- J. Caroselli, I. Shafran, A. Narayanan, R. Rose, 'Adaptive Multichannel Dereverberation for Automatic Speech Recognition,' Proc. Interspeech 2017, pp. 3877-3881, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2017-1791.
- B. Li, T. N. Sainath, A. Narayanan, J. Caroselli, M. Bacchiani, A. Misra, I. Shafran, H. Sak, G. Pundak, K. Chin, K. C. Sim, R. J. Weiss, K. W. Wilson, E. Variani, C. Kim, O. Siohan, M. Weintraub, E. McDermott, R. Rose, M. Shannon, 'Acoustic Modeling for Google Home,' Proc. Interspeech 2017, pp. 399-403, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2017-234.
- Google LLC, 'Adaptive multichannel dereverberation for automatic speech recognition': US 10,762,914 B2 (granted 2020-09-01) and US 11,699,453 B2 (granted 2023-07-11).
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- Two mics, about 70 mm apart (71 mm in simulation).
- α=0.9999, Δ=2, N=10; more than about 10 taps degraded WER; taps need about 2 s to converge and are zeroed at each new utterance.
- WER (Caroselli): clean 11.2→11.1, rerecorded 20.2→19.2, rerecorded-noisy 32.2→29.5.
- WER (Li): rerecorded-noisy 32.2→30.1, about 6.5% relative.
- Both papers cite Yoshioka 2009.

Corrections:
- The simulated training distances were 1–7 m (Caroselli) and 1–8 m (Li).
- The quoted WERs come from real rerecorded sets, not from the simulated rooms.

Limits on what the numbers mean:
- The gains are ASR WER with acoustic models retrained on WPE output and with joint neural beamforming; the authors say gains are 'much more significant' when the model is trained with WPE. They show nothing about perceived quality for human listeners.
- 71 mm is wider than the user's 25–60 mm, so there is less diversity between the two channels.
- α=0.9999 (about 100 s of memory at a 10 ms hop) and per-utterance resets do not fit a continuous 20-talker meeting. The per-DOA state-restore idea is unvalidated.

It is still the closest industry analog to this hardware.

checked.title: Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio estimation (Schwarz & Kellermann 2015) + coherence postfilter on CHiME-3 (Barfuss et al.)
checked.correct_citation:
- A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann, 'Coherent-to-Diffuse Power Ratio Estimation for Dereverberation,' IEEE/ACM Trans. ASLP 23(6):1006-1018, Jun 2015, doi:10.1109/TASLP.2015.2418571 (arXiv:1502.03784). Code: github.com/andreas12345/cdr-dereverb (BSD-2-Clause).
- H. Barfuss, C. Hümmer, A. Schwarz, W. Kellermann, 'Robust coherence-based spectral enhancement for speech recognition in adverse real-world environments,' Computer Speech & Language 46:388-400, 2017, doi:10.1016/j.csl.2017.02.005 (arXiv:1604.03393).
checked.applicability_verdict:
All quoted numbers match the source tables.
- Schwarz & Kellermann Table III, mean: ASR 62.2→77.6/81.5%, ELR50 6.08→9.37/10.80 dB, PESQ 1.27→1.42/1.48. Meeting room MR2: 63.9→80.2/81.9%.
- Parameters: λ=0.68, µ=1.3, Gmin=0.1, filterbank 1024/512/128.
- Barfuss Table 3, BUS: 18.53→17.71/17.42%; overall 7.0/8.2% relative.

Correction: T60 was about 0.4–3.5 s (Room A 0.4, B 1.0, C 3.5, plus REVERB RIRs at 0.5–0.8 s). Distances were 1/2/4 m plus about 0.5/2 m, not '0.6–3.5 s, 1–4 m'.

Limits of the evidence:
- Noise-free reverberant convolutions with 8 cm spacing.
- GRID small-vocabulary task, scored with PocketSphinx and a clean-trained model.
- Oracle TDOA for the DOA-dependent estimator.
- The real-BUS gain came after a 6-mic BeamformIt beamformer, with diffuseness averaged over all mic pairs, and a near (tablet-held) talker.

Bus overclaim: CDR separates direct from diffuse sound, not near from far talkers.
- Bystanders within about 1–2 m are coherent point sources and pass through.
- The partner at about 1 m has DRR ≈ −1.4…−3.7 dB by the angle's own r_c. With µ=1.3–2, G=1−sqrt(µ/(CDR+1)) is about Gmin except at direct-dominant onsets.
- The '3–6 dB extra babble reduction above 2 kHz' is unsupported.

At 4 cm the useful band is above about 2 kHz (sinc calculation verified). Meeting use with mild settings after WPE is reasonable.

checked.title: A summary of the REVERB challenge
checked.correct_citation: K. Kinoshita, M. Delcroix, S. Gannot, E. A. P. Habets, R. Haeb-Umbach, W. Kellermann, V. Leutnant, R. Maas, T. Nakatani, B. Raj, A. Sehr, T. Yoshioka, 'A summary of the REVERB challenge: state-of-the-art and remaining challenges in reverberant speech processing research,' EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. 2016:7 (online 18 Jan 2016), doi:10.1186/s13634-016-0306-6.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- 27 papers, covering 25 enhancement and 49 ASR systems.
- RealData: RT60 ≈ 0.7 s, talkers at about 1 m and 2.5 m, 8-channel circular array of 20 cm diameter.
- Listening tests: many multichannel systems reduced perceived reverberation and also improved overall quality, with similar trends for 2-ch and 8-ch. Among 1-ch systems, only one improved both.
- Linear spatial filtering avoids unnatural nonlinear distortion.

Caveat: '>30% for 8-ch WPE vs ~10% for delay-and-sum' merges different systems and back-ends. NTT's 8-ch dereverberation gave >30% with a DNN acoustic model. In another system, delay-and-sum gave about 10% and dereverberation only a few percent.

The ordering lesson (linear 2-ch processing first, mild nonlinear processing after) is well supported. The ASR magnitudes do not transfer to a 2-mic node with 4 cm spacing.

checked.title: GCC-PHAT (Knapp & Carter 1976) and SRP-PHAT (DiBiase 2000)
checked.correct_citation:
- C. H. Knapp, G. C. Carter, 'The generalized correlation method for estimation of time delay,' IEEE Trans. ASSP 24(4):320-327, Aug 1976, doi:10.1109/TASSP.1976.1162830.
- J. H. DiBiase, 'A high-accuracy, low-latency technique for talker localization in reverberant environments using microphone arrays,' Ph.D. thesis, Brown University, 2000.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- Knapp & Carter via Crossref.
- DiBiase thesis via the pyroomacoustics reference list.
- pyroomacoustics.doa provides SRP, MUSIC, NormMUSIC, CSSM, WAVES, TOPS and FRIDA.
- The maximum-lag figures (±1.17/1.87/2.80 samples) are correct.

Overclaim: '10–15 separable clusters in 180°' is optimistic.
- A 2.5–6 cm aperture at DRR −7…−17 dB gives a broad DOA spread, compressed further toward endfire.
- A linear pair has cone (mirror) ambiguity, so seats facing each other across the array axis map onto the same TDOA.
- Twenty talkers therefore collapse to at most ~10 cones, and realistically ~5–8 stable clusters.

Restricting GCC to frequencies below c/(2d) is unnecessary: PHAT with a lag search limited to |τ|≤d/c tolerates per-bin aliasing. The restriction discards the high band that carries most TDOA resolution; for 6 cm the cut would be at 2.9 kHz.

Bus: frames dominated by babble bias the peak, so selecting high-CDR frames is the right mitigation.

checked.title: Dugan gain-sharing automatic microphone mixer (US 3,992,584)
checked.correct_citation:
- D. W. Dugan, 'Automatic microphone mixer,' US Patent 3,992,584 (application 05/575,951, filed 9 May 1975, granted 16 Nov 1976).
- Earlier gating system: D. Dugan, 'Control apparatus for sound reinforcement systems,' US 3,814,856 (1974).
- The AES presentation was not verified. The usually cited paper is D. Dugan, 'Automatic Microphone Mixing,' JAES 23(6):442-449, 1975; not re-verified here.
checked.applicability_verdict:
The mechanism is verified from the patent text:
- Each channel's gain is its level divided by the level of the sum.
- Two equal talkers each sit at −3 dB.
- N equal inputs each sit at −10·log10 N, so total gain stays constant.

Correction: US 3,814,856 is an adaptive-threshold gating patent titled 'Control apparatus for sound reinforcement systems', not an 'ambient-sensing' apparatus.

Applicability:
- Inside one 2-mic node the 'channels' are highly correlated beams, so the gain is small (the agent agrees).
- Across ESP32 nodes, gain-sharing still sums the signals. Independent crystals drift by tens of ppm, which is tens to over 100 ms per hour. Two nodes at comparable gain then produce comb filtering or echo.
- 'Needs no sample-accurate sync' holds only if the streams are coarsely aligned and drift-compensated (as Yoshioka 2019 does), or if hard best-node selection is used instead.

The Shure and Biamp mode claims were not independently verified.

checked.title: WebRTC APM (AGC2 adaptive digital, NS, HPF) via LiveKit Python; SpeexDSP preprocess as alternative
checked.correct_citation:
- WebRTC Audio Processing Module (BSD): api/audio/audio_processing.h and modules/audio_processing/agc2/* (main branch, fetched 2026-11-02).
- Python binding: livekit 1.2.0 on PyPI (released 2026-10-27; macOS arm64 wheel 9.33 MB, py3-none, Python ≥3.9), class livekit.rtc.AudioProcessingModule. The C++ shim is livekit/rust-sdks webrtc-sys include/livekit/apm.h.
- SpeexDSP: xiph/speexdsp libspeexdsp/preprocess.c.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified in source:
- AdaptiveDigital: headroom 5 dB, max_gain 50 dB, initial 15 dB, 6 dB/s, max_output_noise −50 dBFS.
- VAD threshold 0.95, 12 adjacent frames, 400 ms to confidence; limiter threshold −1 dBFS.
- NS levels kLow…kVeryHigh, default kModerate.
- The LiveKit shim enables gain_controller2 and adaptive_digital at defaults and leaves NS at kModerate. The Python API needs exactly 10 ms frames.
- webrtc-noise-gain 1.3.0 ships Linux-only wheels; speexdsp on PyPI is 0.1.1 (2018), sdist only.
- Speex defaults: agc_level 8000, max_gain 30, +12/−40 dB/s, NS −15 dB, adaptation when Pframe>0.5; the dereverb flag is stored but unused.

Correction: AGC2's target also adds the saturation-protector headroom (initially 20 dB). Speech therefore converges near −25 dBFS, not at '−headroom'.

Bus overclaim: an RNN speech VAD fires on crowd babble. 'Speech-gated' AGC and off-attenuation will track bystanders' voices and open on them, so they cannot keep the crowd down by themselves. A target-specific activity signal (proximity, DOA or CDR) is needed. For the meeting room, where HVAC noise is non-speech, the approach is sound.

checked.title: EBU R 128 / ITU-R BS.1770 / ITU-T P.56 loudness + pyloudnorm
checked.correct_citation:
- EBU R 128 v5.0, 'Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals' (EBU, 21 Nov 2023), with EBU Tech 3341/3342.
- ITU-R BS.1770 (measurement algorithm).
- ITU-T P.56, 'Objective measurement of active speech level', edition 07/2026 (in force, prepublished; previous edition 12/2011).
- C. J. Steinmetz, J. D. Reiss, 'pyloudnorm: A simple yet flexible loudness meter in Python,' 150th AES Convention, 2021. Software: pyloudnorm 0.2.0 (PyPI, 2026-01-04).
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- −23 LUFS target.
- Relative gate of −10 LU (since v2.0).
- Version history up to v5.0.
- P.56 07/2026 edition.
- pyloudnorm version and citation.

This is a measurement tool, so the applicability claims are modest and acceptable.

Practical caveats:
- Per-talker integrated loudness needs several seconds of speech per talker. Use VAD or diarized segments, or the P.56 active speech level.
- For the bus case, report the level of the target pair versus bystanders, not only the level in pauses.

checked.title: Conferencing arrays: Shure MXA920, Biamp Parlé Beamtracking, Sennheiser TeamConnect Ceiling 2
checked.correct_citation:
- Shure MXA920 Ceiling Array Microphone: user guide at shure.com/en-US/docs/guide/MXA920 and product page at shure.com/en-US/products/microphones/mxa920.
- Biamp Parlé family page: biamp.com/products/families/parle.
- Sennheiser TeamConnect Ceiling 2 (article 509161): sennheiser.com product page.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Partly verified.

Shure MXA920 (product page):
- Default coverage area 30×30 ft (9×9 m); up to 8 coverage areas; IntelliMix AI AEC, AI Denoiser and AI Deverb.
- The claim 'rated for talkers up to 4.9 m' was not found. The 9×9 m area implies about 4.6 m to its edge and 6.4 m to its corner, horizontally.

- The gain-sharing automix of beams and the freeze of tracking during far-end audio were not verified.

Sennheiser TCC2: 28 capsules, patented automatic dynamic beamforming, exclusion and priority zones, and 4 ms latency are confirmed.

The control-logic architecture is a reasonable template. The spatial selectivity of these large arrays does not transfer to two omnis (the agent agrees).

checked.title: Nureva position-based gain control ('Microphone Mist')
checked.correct_citation: Nureva Inc., 'A groundbreaking approach to gain control that cuts conference call annoyance,' Nureva blog, posted 27 Feb 2020. It originally appeared in audioXpress as part of a Microphone Mist series. It mentions 'patented' algorithms but gives no patent numbers.
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified, as vendor marketing with no dB or ms figures.

The article itself says position-based gain control raises the noise floor 'only slightly' and keeps it 'relatively constant', not fixed.

Nureva localizes talkers with a wide-aperture array ('thousands of virtual microphones'). A 4 cm pair gives only one mirror-ambiguous angle plus a noisy DRR proxy, and head orientation changes CDR about as much as distance does. Per-position gain memory will therefore mostly degrade to per-cluster AGC.

The fast cross-fade design is the agent's own and untested: a reasonable idea with low evidence.

checked.title: HP Poly Audio Innovations: NoiseBlockAI, Acoustic Fence, M-mode
checked.correct_citation: HP Inc., 'HP Poly Audio Innovations' Solution Brief, document c09038815, dated JUL 2026 (© 2026 HP Development Company), 5 pp.
checked.applicability_verdict:
The content is verified:
- NoiseBlockAI uses machine learning to block non-voice noise in conversational gaps and also reduces reverberation.
- The Acoustic Fence zone is 'selected as an angle from the video bar' and becomes more precise with physically separated mics.
- Desk phones use the speakerphone mic as a reference.
- M-mode turns off AGC and NS and keeps only echo cancellation.

Correction: the brochure is dated July 2026, not undated or 2024.

Applicability:
- The fence makes outside voices 'less prominent'; it does not remove them.
- A 4 cm pair yields a wide cone with front/back ambiguity.
- NoiseBlock-style gating relies on a speech/non-speech decision. In a crowded bus the babble is speech, so it cannot separate targets from bystanders. It is fine for HVAC and projector noise in meetings.

checked.title: Teams Rooms certified hardware: recommended maximum mic-to-talker distance (+ Meeting Owl 3, Jabra PanaCast 50)
checked.correct_citation:
- Microsoft Learn, 'Teams Rooms certified systems and peripherals', page updated 2026-10-16. Its table gives 'Recommended maximum distance from microphone to speaker': Focus 3×2.7 m, 2–4 people, 1.5 m; Small 4.87×4.87 m, 4–6, 2.0 m; Medium 5.5×6 m, 6–12, 2.4 m; Large 4.5×9.75 m, 12–16, 3 m, also applying to each satellite microphone.

checked.title: Meeting Transcription Using Virtual Microphone Arrays (Microsoft, 2019)
checked.correct_citation:
- T. Yoshioka, Z. Chen, D. Dimitriadis, W. Hinthorn, X. Huang, A. Stolcke, M. Zeng, 'Meeting Transcription Using Virtual Microphone Arrays,' arXiv:1905.02545 / MSR-TR-2019-11, 2019.
