checked.applicability_verdict:
Numbers verified:
- With 7 streams, WER is 22.3%, within 3% of close-talk WER on non-overlapped speech.
- SAWER is 26.7%, with 14.8/20.3/22.4% relative gains for 3/5/7 mics.
- DER is 13.6%.

This strongly supports multi-node capture. However:
- Their pipeline relies on continuous cross-correlation alignment with 'global' and 'local' (clock-drift) lag correction, plus neural mask-based blind beamforming, diarization and system combination.
- The gains are ASR and speaker-attribution metrics, not evenness of perceived loudness.

The cheap 'GCC alignment + Dugan mix' adaptation is plausible, but it still has to handle drift.

checked.title: Continuous speech separation: dataset and analysis (LibriCSS)
checked.correct_citation: Z. Chen, T. Yoshioka, L. Lu, T. Zhou, Z. Meng, Y. Luo, J. Wu, X. Xiao, J. Li, 'Continuous Speech Separation: Dataset and Analysis,' Proc. ICASSP 2020, pp. 7284-7288, doi:10.1109/ICASSP40776.2020.9053426 (arXiv:2001.11482).
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- 7-channel circular array, loudspeaker-to-mic distances 33–409 cm.
- Utterance-wise, no separation: 11.8/11.7% vs 4.9/5.1% anechoic. 7-channel MVDR: 8.4/8.3%.
- Continuous input at 0S: no separation 15.4% vs 1-channel separation 17.6%; at 0L, 11.5 vs 16.3%.

'Skip separation with 2 mics' is a fair extrapolation.

Notes:
- The data are loudspeaker replays: fixed 'talkers' with no head movement.

checked.title: CHiME-6 + GPU-GSS ablations + M2MeT/AliMeeting
checked.correct_citation:

Verified:

- AliMeeting: 13 venues of 8–55 m², talkers at 0.3–5.0 m. A near-trained model gets 9.9% CER near-field vs 49.0% far-field. Far CER is 33.3–37.5% with added far/external data and 29.7–34.3% for far-trained serialized-output (SOT) models.

Corrections:
- The GSS paper is Interspeech 2023, not 2022.
- CHiME-6 appeared at the CHiME 2020 workshop.

Caveats:
- The CHiME-6 GSS front end used multiple arrays, while BeamformIt used only the reference array, so the comparison is confounded by channel count.
- AliMeeting far-field CER includes about 34% overlapped speech, so the 9.9→49.0 gap is not a pure distance penalty.
- GPU GSS needs CuPy/CUDA and cannot run on the Mac. fgnt/pb_bss offers numpy cACGMM/MVDR if this is ever needed.

checked.title: Pyroomacoustics (simulation harness) + DNSMOS P.835 (non-intrusive scoring)
checked.correct_citation:
- R. Scheibler, E. Bezzam, I. Dokmanić, 'Pyroomacoustics: A Python Package for Audio Room Simulation and Array Processing Algorithms,' Proc. ICASSP 2018, pp. 351-355, doi:10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461310 (arXiv:1710.04196).
- C. K. A. Reddy, V. Gopal, R. Cutler, 'DNSMOS P.835: A Non-Intrusive Perceptual Objective Speech Quality Metric to Evaluate Noise Suppressors,' Proc. ICASSP 2022, pp. 886-890, doi:10.1109/ICASSP43922.2022.9746108 (arXiv:2110.01763).
- Model file: github.com/microsoft/DNS-Challenge, DNSMOS/DNSMOS/sig_bak_ovr.onnx (1,157,965 bytes).
checked.applicability_verdict:
Verified:
- pyroomacoustics 0.10.1, released 2026-05-01. Its macOS wheels are universal2 for CPython 3.9–3.14 (not arm64 for 3.10–3.14), about 1.1 MB.
- The DOA algorithm list and inverse_sabine are present.
- onnxruntime 1.31.1, released 2026-10-26: macOS arm64 wheel about 20.9 MB, Python ≥3.11, macOS ≥14.

Caveats:
- pyroomacoustics has no built-in spatially diffuse noise. Use the Habets–Gannot generator or real multichannel noise (DEMAND TBUS, PCAFETER and OMEETING, recorded with 5 cm minimum spacing) to get correct inter-mic coherence. Otherwise CDR and coherence methods look better than they are.
- DNSMOS P.835 was trained on noise-suppressor outputs. It is not validated for dereverberated far-field speech, and it cannot tell the target pair from babble; it may reward suppressing everything but one voice.
- For the bus case, use intrusive per-source metrics in simulation, such as target-vs-bystander level and ESTOI or SI-SDR of the pair.

missing_key_sources: G. W. Elko, A.-T. Nguyen Pong, 'A simple adaptive first-order differential microphone,' Proc. IEEE WASPAA 1995, pp. 169-172, doi:10.1109/ASPAA.1995.482983. This is the standard adaptive null-steering design for two mics (back-to-back cardioids) used in hearing aids and phones. It applies to the bus (a null toward the dominant interferer) and to endfire beams along a table. It needs gain calibration for the INMP441 ±1 dB tolerance.

H. Cox, R. M. Zeskind, T. Kooij, 'Practical supergain,' IEEE Trans. ASSP 34(3):393-398, 1986, doi:10.1109/TASSP.1986.1164847. This gives superdirective beamforming with a white-noise-gain constraint, needed to trade DI against INMP441 self-noise amplification at 2.5–6 cm spacing.

I. A. McCowan, H. Bourlard, 'Microphone array post-filter based on noise field coherence,' IEEE Trans. Speech Audio Process. 11(6):709-716, 2003, doi:10.1109/TSA.2003.818212. This is the classic diffuse-noise coherence postfilter, a baseline or alternative to CDR.

O. Thiergart, G. Del Galdo, E. A. P. Habets, 'On the spatial coherence in mixed sound fields and its application to signal-to-diffuse ratio estimation,' J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 132(4):2337-2346, 2012, doi:10.1121/1.4750493.

E. A. P. Habets, S. Gannot, I. Cohen, 'Late reverberant spectral variance estimation based on a statistical model,' IEEE Signal Process. Lett. 16(9):770-773, 2009, doi:10.1109/LSP.2009.2024791. Together with S. Braun, A. Kuklasinski, O. Schwartz, O. Thiergart, E. A. P. Habets, S. Gannot, S. Doclo, J. Jensen, 'Evaluation and comparison of late reverberation power spectral density estimators,' IEEE/ACM TASLP 26(6):1056-1071, 2018, doi:10.1109/TASLP.2018.2804172. These are cheap spectral dereverberation alternatives, benchmarked including dual-mic estimators.

T. Nakatani, K. Kinoshita, 'A unified convolutional beamformer for simultaneous denoising and dereverberation' (WPD), IEEE Signal Process. Lett. 26(6):903-907, 2019, doi:10.1109/LSP.2019.2911179. It combines WPE with a steered beamformer per talker.

T. Yoshioka, H. Tachibana, T. Nakatani, M. Miyoshi, 'Adaptive dereverberation of speech signals with speaker-position change detection,' Proc. ICASSP 2009, pp. 3733-3736 (verified via the reference lists of both Google 2017 papers). It is the precedent for switching WPE filters per talker in a multi-talker meeting.

S. Braun, E. A. P. Habets, 'Linear prediction-based online dereverberation and noise reduction using alternating Kalman filters,' IEEE/ACM TASLP 26(6):1119-1129, 2018. This online multichannel linear prediction method is more robust to additive noise and talker changes than RLS-WPE. The citation is from memory; the DOI was not re-verified.

M. Barron, L.-J. Lee, 'Energy relations in concert auditoriums. I,' J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 84(2):618-628, 1988, doi:10.1121/1.396840. Its revised theory has the reverberant level decaying with distance, which refines the classical critical-distance and level-drop estimates.

C. Blandin, A. Ozerov, E. Vincent, 'Multi-source TDOA estimation in reverberant audio using angular spectra and clustering,' Signal Processing 92(8):1950-1960, 2012, doi:10.1016/j.sigpro.2011.09.032. It benchmarks GCC-PHAT variants for clustering several talkers' TDOAs with two mics.

A. Vinnikov et al., 'NOTSOFAR-1 Challenge: New Datasets, Baseline, and Tasks for Distant Meeting Transcription,' arXiv:2401.08887, 2024. It has 315 real meetings in 30 conference rooms with 4–8 attendees each, recorded by single tabletop devices. It is the closest real benchmark to 'one device on the table'.

J. Carletta et al., 'The AMI Meeting Corpus: A pre-announcement,' MLMI 2005, LNCS 3869, pp. 28-39, Springer 2006, doi:10.1007/11677482_3. It contains real meetings recorded with tabletop arrays plus headset references.

J. Thiemann, N. Ito, E. Vincent, 'The Diverse Environments Multi-channel Acoustic Noise Database (DEMAND),' Proc. Meetings on Acoustics 19:035081, 2013, doi:10.1121/1.4799597. It is real 16-channel noise with 5 cm minimum spacing, including TBUS, PCAFETER and OMEETING. Also: E. A. P. Habets, S. Gannot, 'Generating sensor signals in isotropic noise fields,' JASA 122(6):3464-3470, 2007, doi:10.1121/1.2799929, and E. A. P. Habets, I. Cohen, S. Gannot, 'Generating nonstationary multisensor signals under a spatial coherence constraint,' JASA 124(5):2911-2917, 2008, doi:10.1121/1.2987429, for simulating babble and HVAC noise with correct inter-mic coherence.

J. Barker, R. Marxer, E. Vincent, S. Watanabe, 'The third CHiME speech separation and recognition challenge: Dataset, task and baselines,' Proc. IEEE ASRU 2015, pp. 504-511, doi:10.1109/ASRU.2015.7404837. It provides real BUS and CAF recordings from a 6-mic tablet with a near talker, which suits testing the bus case.

T. Gburrek, J. Schmalenstroeer, R. Haeb-Umbach, 'On synchronization of wireless acoustic sensor networks in the presence of time-varying sampling rate offsets and speaker changes,' Proc. ICASSP 2022. Code: github.com/fgnt/paderwasn (MIT, numpy), which estimates sampling-rate offsets (WACD) and resamples. This is needed before summing several ESP32 nodes.

N. Yousefian, P. C. Loizou, 'A dual-microphone speech enhancement algorithm based on the coherence function,' IEEE TASLP 20(2):599-609, 2012, doi:10.1109/TASL.2011.2162406. It is a hearing-aid-oriented two-mic coherence filter for a frontal target against diffuse noise or babble, relevant to the bus case.
fgnt/pb_bss (GitHub, MIT): numpy implementations of cACGMM and mask-based MVDR/GEV. It is a CPU path for GSS-style processing, since the GPU GSS package needs CuPy/CUDA.
verify.notes:
VERIFICATION SUMMARY
- All 17 sources exist; none were fabricated, and none are dropped.
- Citation corrections:
  - Barfuss et al. is Computer Speech & Language 46:388-400 (2017).
  - The GPU-GSS paper is Interspeech 2023 (pp. 3507-3511), not 2022.
  - CHiME-6 appeared at the CHiME 2020 workshop (pp. 1-7).
  - Yoshioka 2019 has a peer-reviewed Interspeech 2019 version.
  - The HP brochure is dated July 2026.
  - Dugan's earlier patent US 3,814,856 is titled 'Control apparatus for sound reinforcement systems'.
  - Google WPE training simulations used 1-7 m (Caroselli) and 1-8 m (Li), and the quoted WERs are on real rerecorded sets.
  - The Schwarz & Kellermann rooms had T60 0.4-3.5 s at 0.5-4 m.
  - pyroomacoustics macOS wheels are universal2 for CPython 3.9-3.14.
  - The AGC2 speech target includes the saturation-protector headroom of about 20 dB, so speech settles near −25 dBFS.
- Every quantitative claim I could reach matched the primary tables exactly.
- I recomputed the physics (r_c, DRR, level drop, delay-and-sum DI, sinc thresholds); it is correct apart from small nits.

COULD NOT VERIFY
- Shure MXA920 'rated to 4.9 m'. The product page instead gives a default 30×30 ft (9×9 m) coverage area with up to 8 areas.
- Shure −37 dBFS AGC starting target and the 'post-gate AGC' ordering.
- Biamp gain-sharing automix and freezing tracking during far-end audio.
- Teams V4/V5 certification spec packages.
- A 1974 AES presentation by Dugan.

MAIN APPLICABILITY OVERCLAIMS
1. Bus: speech-gated AGC, off-attenuation and NoiseBlock analogs cannot tell crowd babble (which is speech) from the two targets. The RNN-VAD fires on bystanders, so a target-specific cue is required (proximity, DOA cone, or CDR combined with level).
2. CDR is a direct-vs-diffuse cue, not a near-vs-far cue.
   - Passengers 1-2 m away are coherent and pass through.
   - The partner at ~1 m is at or beyond the bus r_c, and with µ=1.3-2 gets G≈Gmin most of the time.
   - Published 2-mic CDR evidence is noise-free, 8 cm spacing, GRID with clean-trained PocketSphinx, and oracle TDOA. The real-BUS gain (18.53→17.4-17.7% WER) came after a 6-mic beamformer.
   - The '3-6 dB babble reduction' is unsupported.
3. WPE is not 'the only artifact-free' option. Google's 5-8% relative gains are ASR WER with acoustic models retrained on WPE output, from 71 mm spacing.
4. '10-15 GCC-PHAT clusters' is optimistic. Mirror (cone) ambiguity merges seats facing each other across the array axis; expect about 5-8 stable clusters.
5. Summing several ESP32 nodes with Dugan gain-sharing needs coarse alignment plus sampling-rate-offset compensation (crystals differ by tens of ppm), or else hard best-node selection.
6. Spacing advice is incomplete. A first-order delay-and-subtract cardioid has an on-axis null at c/(2d): 4.3 kHz at 4 cm, 2.9 kHz at 6 cm, 2.1 kHz at 8 cm. A '5-6 cm compromise' therefore needs band-split processing (differential beam only below ~1.5-2 kHz, omni/CDR above), or ≤3-4 cm spacing for differential beams.
7. DNSMOS is not valid for judging dereverberation or target-vs-babble selection.
8. Several 'evidence' gaps are confounded:
   - AliMeeting near/far CER includes ~34% overlap.
   - CHiME-6 GSS used more arrays than BeamformIt.
   - REVERB's 30%/10% figures come from different systems.

USEFUL EXTRA
sherpa-onnx 2.0.1 (PyPI, Oct 2026, macOS arm64 wheels ~2 MB) offers ONNX VAD and speaker embeddings without PyTorch, suitable for per-talker gain memory.

METHOD
The shared WebSearch budget ran out after 2 searches. I continued with direct fetches only:
- arXiv and ISCA PDFs through pdftotext.
- The Springer page.
- Crossref DOI and ISBN lookups.
- PyPI JSON.
- GitHub raw source for WebRTC, LiveKit, nara_wpe, pyrato, SpeexDSP and pyroomacoustics.
- Vendor pages and Google Patents.

sweep.angle: How to test both scenarios rigorously in simulation, without field recordings. Covers image-source room simulation (pyroomacoustics), spatially correct diffuse noise and babble for a 2.5–6 cm pair (Habets/ANF generators, real 5 cm DEMAND recordings), realistic levels for a bus and a meeting room (published dBA levels and Lombard SNR data, INMP441 self-noise), the choice of speech sources (real speech instead of TTS), and metrics: SI-SDR, PESQ, ESTOI, DNSMOS P.835, component-wise or phase-inversion SIR/leakage, and industry-style per-talker level tests. Ends with a reproducible protocol (SNR sweep, many seeds, paired statistics, sim-to-real checks) and a small-disk toolchain.

sources.title: Image method for efficiently simulating small-room acoustics
sources.authors: Jont B. Allen, David A. Berkley
sources.key_idea: Models the room impulse response (RIR) between two points in a rectangular room as a sum of delayed, attenuated impulses from mirror-image sources. The result is exact when the walls are rigid. Convolving dry speech with one RIR per microphone gives multi-mic signals that are physically consistent for any array geometry: correct TDOAs, direct-to-reverberant ratio (DRR) and reverberation.
sources.algorithm: Shoebox Lx x Ly x Lz with wall reflection coefficients beta. Image sources sit at R_p+R_m, with p in {0,1}^3 (mirror parity) and m in Z^3 (lattice of 2L). h(t)=sum_p sum_m [product of beta^(number of reflections)] * delta(t-|R_p+R_m|/c)/(4*pi*|R_p+R_m|). Truncate by reflection order or by time (at least RT60). Implement each delay as a windowed-sinc fractional delay; the original rounded to the nearest sample and then high-passed. Compute one RIR per (source, mic) pair; mic signal = sum_i s_i * h_i,mic. Pick wall absorption for a target RT60 with Sabine: T60 = 0.161 V / sum(S_i alpha_i), alpha = 1 - beta^2. Known artifacts: specular reflections only, frequency-independent walls unless octave-band coefficients are used, sweeping/flutter echoes in symmetric boxes (fix by randomizing image positions), and poor low-frequency modal accuracy.
sources.bus_relevance: Approximate the cabin as a long narrow box (about 12 x 2.5 x 2.3 m) with absorbing seats and passengers. The ISM gives correct direct paths and early reflections for the two targets (0.3-1 m) and for nearby passenger talkers (1.5-5 m), so the spatial cues the 2-mic array sees are right. The late tail of a cluttered cabin is only approximate because seats and people do not scatter. No published bus RT60 was found, so sweep RT60 (about 0.3-0.6 s).
sources.meeting_relevance: Meeting rooms are close to shoeboxes. The ISM reproduces how DRR falls with distance, which is the main driver of far-talker intelligibility, for 20 seats at 1-6 m. RT60 of 0.5-0.9 s needs a high reflection order or a hybrid ISM plus ray-tracing tail.
sources.two_mic_reality: For 2.5-6 cm spacing the inter-mic delays are at most 0.17 ms (2.8 samples at 16 kHz). Fractional-delay ISM reproduces them exactly, so simulated TDOA and coherence for point sources can be trusted. A symmetric shoebox can make the reverberant field too regular, so use randomized ISM and several room sizes and positions per seed. Not modelled: scattering from the table and device body, mic port acoustics, and head shadow beyond simple source directivity.
sources.implementation: Use pyroomacoustics (C++ ISM core) rather than writing it. A numpy-only ISM is about 150 lines but slow at RT60 0.9 s.

sources.title: Pyroomacoustics: A Python package for audio room simulation and array processing algorithms
sources.authors: Robin Scheibler, Eric Bezzam, Ivan Dokmanic
sources.key_idea: A 2D/3D room builder with a fast compiled image-source engine (plus an experimental ISM/ray-tracing hybrid), source and mic directivities, and reference beamforming, DOA and adaptive-filter code. It is a complete digital twin for testing 2-mic algorithms.
sources.algorithm: room = pra.ShoeBox(dims, fs=16000, materials=pra.Material(e_abs), max_order=mo, air_absorption=True, use_rand_ism=True, max_rand_disp=0.08), with (e_abs, mo) = pra.inverse_sabine(rt60, dims). Use per-wall pra.make_materials for absorptive seats or carpet. room.add_source(pos, signal=x, delay=t0, directivity=CardioidFamily(...)); directivity works in 3D rooms only. room.add_microphone(2 x M positions). premix = room.simulate(return_premix=True) returns an array of shape (n_sources, n_mics, n_samples): each source's reverberant image at each mic, i.e. ground-truth components for exact SIR and per-talker metrics. room.measure_rt60() checks the RT60 actually achieved. Split each RIR at direct path + 50 ms to build early-reflection references. Optional room.set_ray_tracing() for the late tail (documented as experimental). Seed numpy's RNG so randomized-ISM scenes can be regenerated exactly instead of cached.
sources.bus_relevance: Simulates 2 targets, 4-8 nearby passenger talkers and many far babble sources in a cabin-shaped box. Premix keeps target, babble and noise images separate for exact babble-leakage bookkeeping. Cardioid source directivity lets the two targets face each other rather than the device.
sources.meeting_relevance: Place 20 talkers at 1-6 m with random head yaw and sweep RT60 0.5/0.7/0.9 s via inverse_sabine. Premix gives each talker's image at the device for per-talker ESTOI, SI-SDR and level.
sources.two_mic_reality: Geometry is exact for any spacing and orientation, but the mics are ideal. You must add INMP441 self-noise yourself (equivalent input noise about 94-61 = 33 dBA SPL, independent per mic), plus +/-1 dB gain mismatch, about 2 mm position error, and optionally a fixed sub-sample inter-channel offset as a robustness case. A shoebox only approximates a cluttered bus.
sources.implementation: pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 (released 2026-05-01) has macOS universal2 wheels for cp312, cp313 and cp314, about 1.1 MB each. It requires numpy, scipy and Cython. MIT license.

sources.title: Generating sensor signals in isotropic noise fields
sources.authors: Emanuel A. P. Habets, Sharon Gannot
sources.venue: J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 122(6):3464-3470 (plus 'Comments on ...', internal report 2010)
sources.key_idea: Diffuse (spherically or cylindrically isotropic) noise at an arbitrary array can be generated by summing many mutually uncorrelated plane waves spread uniformly over a sphere or cylinder. The common shortcut of using an RIR without its direct path does not reproduce the isotropic field accurately.
sources.algorithm: Target coherence for mics a distance d apart: spherical Gamma(f) = sin(2*pi*f*d/c)/(2*pi*f*d/c); cylindrical Gamma(f) = J0(2*pi*f*d/c). INF-Generator sinf_1D.m (1-D arrays): use N_phi = 64 directions with cos(theta_n) evenly spaced in [-1,1]. For each direction draw an independent complex Gaussian spectrum X_n(k) and add X_n(k)*exp(-j*w_k*d_m*cos(theta_n)/c) to sensor m. Divide by sqrt(N_phi), build a Hermitian spectrum and IFFT. About 25 lines of numpy. Check the result by comparing the Welch coherence estimate with sinc.
sources.bus_relevance: Models the far crowd, engine and road field as diffuse. Computed here: the spherical-diffuse coherence stays above 0.5 up to about 4.1/2.6/1.7 kHz for d = 2.5/4/6 cm (first zeros at 6.9/4.3/2.9 kHz). Bus noise is therefore strongly coherent across the pair at low frequencies, which caps what any 2-mic spatial filter can do. Use it to stress-test diffuse-babble suppression.
sources.meeting_relevance: Use for diffuse HVAC/projector noise at NC 25-35 levels and as a check on the reverberant tail.
sources.two_mic_reality: Produces Gaussian noise only. Real babble and engine noise are nonstationary and partly directional (nearby passengers are point sources), so combine this with ISM point-source babble and the 2008 method for real recordings. For small d the spherical vs cylindrical choice matters; measure the real 5 cm bus coherence (DEMAND TBUS) to decide.
sources.implementation: MATLAB INF-Generator (GPL-3.0) at github.com/ehabets/INF-Generator. A numpy port from scratch is about 25 lines.

sources.title: Generating nonstationary multisensor signals under a spatial coherence constraint
sources.authors: Emanuel A. P. Habets, Israel Cohen, Sharon Gannot (extension: D. Mirabilii, S. J. Schlecht, E. A. P. Habets, JASA 149(3):1425-1433, 2021, DOI 10.1121/10.0003565)
sources.key_idea: Imposes any target spatial coherence on M mutually independent signals, which may be nonstationary real recordings, by mixing them per frequency with a factor of the target coherence matrix. The result is realistic babble or engine noise with the correct inter-mic coherence for the actual mic spacing.
sources.algorithm: Take the STFT N_m(k,t) of M independent inputs. Per frequency, build Gamma(k), e.g. Gamma_12 = sinc(2*pi*f_k*d/c). Factor Gamma(k) = C(k)^H C(k) by Cholesky (smooth but unbalanced) or EVD (balanced but not smooth). Output X(k,t) = C(k)^H N(k,t), then ISTFT. Mirabilii et al. 2021 add unitary-Procrustes post-processing for balanced and smooth mixing, which reduces audible artifacts and coherence error. Python API: params = anf.CoherenceMatrix.Parameters(mic_positions (M x 3), sc_type 'spherical' | 'cylindrical' | 'corcos', sample_frequency=16000, nfft=1024); then out, coh, mix = anf.generate_signals(inputs, params, decomposition='evd', processing='balanced+smooth').
sources.bus_relevance: Turns single-channel babble (a sum of 20-40 LibriSpeech talkers) or one DEMAND TBUS channel into a 2-mic diffuse field for any spacing from 2.5 to 6 cm, while keeping the nonstationarity (babble bursts, engine rpm changes). The inputs must be independent: use non-overlapping segments or different talker sets per channel.
sources.meeting_relevance: Diffuse HVAC and background chatter at the true spacing. The 'corcos' model can add wind-like noise if an HVAC vent blows on the device.
sources.two_mic_reality: For M = 2 the mixing is a 2x2 matrix per frequency bin, simple and exact in coherence. A purely diffuse model ignores the directionality of nearby interferers; a real bus is directional near passengers plus a diffuse crowd, so simulate both.
sources.implementation: anf-generator 0.1.3 (2026-04-12): pure-Python wheel of 13 KB, MIT license, declares numpy, scipy and matplotlib. If disk is tight, try --no-deps after checking its imports. The README example uses 'balance+smooth' while the documented option is 'balanced+smooth'; check the source. MATLAB original: github.com/ehabets/ANF-Generator.

sources.title: DEMAND: a collection of multi-channel recordings of acoustic noise in diverse environments
sources.authors: Joachim Thiemann, Nobutaka Ito, Emmanuel Vincent
sources.venue: Zenodo dataset record 1227121 (v1.0, 9 June 2013) with documentation DEMAND.pdf
sources.key_idea: Real 16-channel noise recordings, 300 s each, in 18 environments, including TBUS (public transit bus), TMETRO, PCAFETER (busy cafeteria), PSTATION, OMEETING (meeting room) and OOFFICE. Neighbouring mics in the planar array are exactly 5 cm apart, so an adjacent pair gives real spatial coherence for a 5 cm pair, inside our 2.5-6 cm range.
sources.algorithm: Array: 16 Sony ECM-C10 omni electret mics in 4 staggered rows, 5 cm to immediate neighbours (largest spacing 21.8 cm), plane parallel to the floor at about 1.4 m. Recipe: (1) take an adjacent channel pair from TBUS, PCAFETER or OMEETING at 16 kHz. (2) Equalize per-channel gain using the long-term low-frequency PSD ratio; channels are not gain-matched, and levels are unnormalized but not SPL-calibrated. (3) Measure magnitude-squared coherence and compare with sinc/J0 to choose the diffuse model. (4) Scale to the target dBA, using dBFS = dB SPL - 120 for the INMP441, so 75 dBA is about -45 dBFS. (5) For other spacings, regenerate with anf-generator from non-overlapping segments. (6) Split the 300 s into disjoint chunks per seed and per dev/test set.
sources.bus_relevance: TBUS is real bus-interior noise (engine, road and passengers; Rennes, 2012-13) with real 5 cm coherence. It is the most realistic background available without your own field recording. PCAFETER and PSTATION add dense crowd babble.
sources.meeting_relevance: OMEETING (people discussing in a meeting room) and OOFFICE (3 people using computers) give realistic room noise and background talk. Rescale them to NC 25-35-equivalent levels.
sources.two_mic_reality: Exact match only for a 5 cm pair; other spacings need regeneration. Recordings contain whatever talkers were present, so label intelligible passenger speech in TBUS as interferer, not noise. The electret mics differ from the INMP441 in self-noise and frequency response, and absolute SPL is unknown.
sources.implementation: Download only the 16 kHz zips you need: TBUS_16k 128.9 MB, PCAFETER_16k 107.4 MB, OMEETING_16k 82.7 MB, TMETRO_16k 126.6 MB. The full set is 7.4 GB; do not download it. Read with soundfile or scipy. License: CC BY-SA 3.0 per DEMAND.pdf (the Zenodo metadata says CC BY 4.0).

sources.title: Estimation of room acoustic parameters: The ACE Challenge (ACE corpus of measured multichannel RIRs and matched noise)
sources.authors: James Eaton, Nikolay D. Gaubitch, Alastair H. Moore, Patrick A. Naylor
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. 24(10):1681-1693; corpus on Zenodo record 6257551
sources.key_idea: Measured RIRs plus noise (ambient, fan, and babble from real seated talkers) recorded in the same 7 rooms: 2 offices, 2 meeting rooms, 2 lecture rooms and a lobby. Several real devices were used, including a 2-channel laptop (Chromebook). This is a cheap sim-to-real check for a 2-mic device in real meeting rooms.
sources.algorithm: Use as a validation set. Convolve LibriSpeech with the measured 2-channel Chromebook RIRs (48 kHz, resample to 16 kHz). Add the matched noise at ACE's SNRs (18/12/-1 dB) or at NC-equivalent levels. Run the same metrics on pyroomacoustics scenes with identical dimensions and T60, and compare the metric changes between simulated and measured. Rooms: Meeting Room 1 6.61 x 5.11 x 2.95 m (T60 about 0.44 s), Meeting Room 2 10.3 x 9.07 x 2.63 m (about 0.37 s), Lecture Room 2 13.6 x 9.29 x 2.94 m (about 1.25 s; T60s from a secondary table). Babble was produced by 4-7 real seated talkers at documented positions.
sources.bus_relevance: Low: no vehicles. Its babble and fan recordings are still useful for multi-talker robustness tests.
sources.meeting_relevance: High: real meeting and lecture rooms, real source-to-device distances (about 1.4-4.1 m for the Chromebook), occupied-room measurements and real fan noise similar to HVAC. It is the closest open substitute for field recordings of test case 2.
sources.two_mic_reality: The Chromebook mic spacing and orientation are documented in ACE_Corpus_Microphone_arrangements_v02.pdf; this was not verified here, so check it against 2.5-6 cm. There is only one source position per mic position per room, so use ACE to validate the simulator, not to replace the 20-seat sweep. Room T60s of 0.37-1.25 s bracket the 0.5-0.9 s target.
sources.implementation: ACE_Corpus_RIRN_Chromebook.tbz2 is 1.1 GB (48 kHz); ACE_Corpus_Speech is 148 MB; the MATLAB tools are 0.6 MB. Zenodo lists CC BY 4.0, while other ACE pages say CC BY-ND 4.0; check. With about 4.8 GB free, extract only the meeting and lecture rooms and downsample.

sources.title: Noise levels associated with New York City's mass transit systems
sources.authors: Richard Neitzel, Robyn R. M. Gershon, Marina Zeltser, Allison Canton, Muhammad Akram
sources.venue: American Journal of Public Health 99(8):1393-1399 (DOI 10.2105/AJPH.2008.138297)
sources.key_idea: Dosimeter measurements of rider exposure: inside buses Leq 75.3 dBA (SD 2.6, n = 14); at bus stops 76.0 dBA; mean bus Lmax 86.8 dBA; highest in-bus Lmax 96.8 dBA; subway cars 79.3 dBA. These numbers calibrate the background level for the bus test.
sources.algorithm: Use as the level prior. Draw bus background Leq from N(75, 2.6) dBA, or sweep 70/75/80 dBA. Inject transients up to 87-97 dB Lmax (doors, brakes, horn) to test AGC and limiter behaviour. With the INMP441 calibration (-26 dBFS at 94 dB SPL, so 0 dBFS = 120 dB SPL), 75 dBA is about -45 dBFS and a 97 dB peak about -23 dBFS, so there is no clipping risk.
sources.bus_relevance: Direct. It sets the crowded-bus noise level; combined with the Lombard data it fixes a realistic SNR range.
sources.meeting_relevance: None (transit only).
sources.two_mic_reality: Gives A-weighted levels only, from ear-level dosimeters in NYC in 2007; no spectra or spatial information. Take spectral shape and coherence from DEMAND TBUS, and check unweighted low-frequency energy for headroom, since A-weighting hides most engine rumble.
sources.implementation: No code; level numbers only.

sources.title: Characteristics of real-world signal to noise ratios and speech listening situations of older adults with mild to moderate hearing loss
sources.authors: Yu-Hsiang Wu, Elizabeth Stangl, Octav Chipara, Syed Shabih Hasan, Anne Welhaven, Jacob Oleson
sources.key_idea: 894 real-world listening situations. As noise rose from 40 to 74 dBA, talkers raised speech from 60 to 74 dBA and SNR fell from about 20 to 0 dB. 62.9% of SNRs were between 2 and 14 dB; only 7.5% were below 0 dB. Median SNR for 'indoors crowd' was 5.3 dB and for 'traffic' 5.6 dB. Restates Pearsons et al. (1977): speech stays at 55 dBA below 45 dBA noise, then rises 0.6 dB per dB of noise, reaching SNR 0 dB at 70 dBA noise. Smeds et al. (2015, hearing-aid industry) found SNRs 3-5 dB higher, with speech-in-babble averaging about 5 dB.
sources.algorithm: Lombard rule for setting talker levels at about 1 m: L_s = 55 + 0.6*(L_n - 45) dBA for L_n > 45; Wu's own fit has slope 0.54 dB/dB above 59.3 dBA. Computed here for 75 dBA bus noise: L_s(1 m) is about 73 dBA, so the direct-path SNR at the device is about -2 dB at 1 m, +2.4 dB at 0.6 m and +8.5 dB at 0.3 m (at 80 dBA: -4, +0.4, +6.5 dB). Hence sweep the input SNR at mic A over {-5, 0, +5, +10} dB, with 0 to +5 dB as the typical cell. For meetings, use normal effort (about 60 dBA at 1 m) with per-talker spread.
sources.bus_relevance: Turns 'loud bus' into defensible SNR numbers and justifies raising the talkers' level (Lombard) rather than testing implausible -10 dB cases.
sources.meeting_relevance: Real-world SNRs are mostly positive; in quiet rooms the hard part is reverberation and level spread, not noise.
sources.two_mic_reality: Levels were measured at ear or chest level by listeners about 1 m from the talker. The device sees the same talkers at 0.3-1 m (bus) or 1-6 m (meeting), so recompute SNR with distance and DRR instead of copying the numbers.
sources.implementation: Numbers only; encode as a level model in the scene generator.

sources.title: SDR - half-baked or well done?
sources.authors: Jonathan Le Roux, Scott Wisdom, Hakan Erdogan, John R. Hershey
sources.key_idea: The BSS-Eval SDR, which tolerates a long distortion filter, is easy to game and ill-defined for single-channel outputs. Scale-invariant SDR (SI-SDR) projects the estimate onto the reference; it is simpler, more robust, and now the standard enhancement and separation score.
sources.algorithm: Remove the mean from output s_hat and reference s. alpha = <s_hat, s>/||s||^2; e_t = alpha*s; e_r = s_hat - alpha*s; SI-SDR = 10*log10(||e_t||^2/||e_r||^2). Report SI-SDRi = SI-SDR(out, s) - SI-SDR(micA, s). Project rules: (i) compensate the algorithm's latency (cross-correlation) before scoring; (ii) use as reference the target image at mic A truncated to the direct path plus 50 ms of early reflections (split the pyroomacoustics RIR); (iii) bus: reference = sum of both targets' early images, plus per-talker SI-SDR on the shadow components; (iv) meeting: per-talker SI-SDR over that talker's active segments.
sources.bus_relevance: Main objective measure of whether babble and engine were removed without distorting the two targets. Compute it on the full output and on the shadow target component alone (the latter measures pure target distortion).
sources.meeting_relevance: Per-talker SI-SDR with an early reference across the 20 seats exposes far-talker degradation. Report the minimum and 10th percentile, not only the mean.
sources.two_mic_reality: SI-SDR penalizes any linear coloration, so a 2-mic beamformer's frequency response on the target lowers the score even when it sounds fine; pair it with ESTOI and DNSMOS. At -5 dB input SNR, values are often negative and noisy, so use 20 or more seeds per cell.
sources.implementation: Implement in numpy (about 10 lines); no package needed.

sources.title: ITU-T P.862.2: Wideband extension to Recommendation P.862 for the assessment of wideband telephone networks and speech codecs (PESQ-WB)
sources.authors: ITU-T Study Group 12 (P.862 family); Python wrapper 'pesq' by ludlows et al.
sources.venue: ITU-T Recommendation P.862.2 (11/2005, 11/2007). ITU deleted the whole P.862 family on 5 Jan 2024 and points to P.863.
sources.key_idea: Intrusive perceptual quality model: compares a time-aligned reference and degraded signal and outputs MOS-LQO. Wideband (16 kHz) PESQ is the quality number most often reported in enhancement papers, so it keeps results comparable with the literature.
sources.algorithm: pesq(fs=16000, ref, deg, mode='wb') returns MOS-LQO (about 1.04-4.64). Internally it aligns level and time (utterance-based delay estimation), applies a Bark-domain loudness model and aggregates asymmetric disturbances. pesq_batch(...) uses multiple processes. Use ref = clean early target image at mic A (bus: sum of both targets) and deg = system output, on segments of 8-10 s or more containing speech. Pass on_error=PesqError.RETURN_VALUES so silent segments do not crash a sweep.
sources.bus_relevance: Rates the quality of the two-target output; sensitive to musical noise and over-suppression artifacts from aggressive babble removal.
sources.meeting_relevance: Weak. P.862 was built for telephony codecs and networks, not reverberant far-field pickup; use it as a secondary metric for near seats only.
sources.two_mic_reality: Assumes a single channel and a single talker, so it is unreliable when the reference holds two overlapping talkers or reverberation, and it tracks intelligibility poorly at negative SNR. ITU withdrew P.862.x in 2024 and the current standard P.863 (POLQA) is licensed, so treat PESQ as a legacy, relative metric.
sources.implementation: PyPI 'pesq' 0.0.4 (2022) is sdist-only (38.7 KB) and needs clang, numpy and Cython. That build fails to import with numpy 2 or later ('numpy.core.multiarray failed to import'). numpy 2 support was merged on GitHub on 18 Mar 2026 (PR #59) without a PyPI release, so install from the GitHub master or build with --no-build-isolation against numpy 2.4. The wrapper is MIT; the underlying ITU code has its own IP terms.

sources.title: An algorithm for intelligibility prediction of time-frequency weighted noisy speech (STOI); An algorithm for predicting the intelligibility of speech masked by modulated noise maskers (ESTOI)
sources.authors: Cees H. Taal, Richard C. Hendriks, Richard Heusdens, Jesper Jensen; Jesper Jensen, Cees H. Taal
sources.venue: IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. 19(7):2125-2136 (2011). ESTOI: IEEE/ACM TASLP 24(11):2009-2022 (2016, DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2016.2585878)
sources.key_idea: Intrusive intelligibility predictors that correlate short-time (384 ms) one-third-octave temporal envelopes of clean and processed speech. STOI was validated on noisy and noise-reduced (time-frequency weighted) speech. ESTOI extends it to fluctuating, modulated maskers such as babble, which is exactly the bus case.
sources.algorithm: Resample to 10 kHz and drop silent frames (more than 40 dB below the maximum). STFT with 256-sample Hann frames, 50% overlap, 512-point FFT; 15 one-third-octave bands from 150 Hz (about 150 Hz-4.3 kHz); segments of 30 frames (384 ms). STOI: per band and segment, normalize and clip the degraded envelope (-15 dB SDR floor), take the Pearson correlation, and average to get d in [0,1]. ESTOI: no clipping; normalize each segment's band envelopes along time (rows), then each frame's spectrum (columns), and average the inner products. pystoi call: stoi(clean, proc, fs, extended=True) with equal-length, time-aligned 1-D arrays. Summarize an SNR sweep as an 'intelligibility-equivalent SNR gain': the horizontal shift between the processed and unprocessed ESTOI-versus-input-SNR curves.
sources.bus_relevance: Primary intelligibility metric for the two targets in babble; use ESTOI. Also score each babble talker's image as the 'reference': a good system should lower their ESTOI, a proxy for 'background talkers are no longer intelligible'.
sources.meeting_relevance: Per-talker ESTOI with a direct + 50 ms early reference across the 20 seats; report the worst talker. Bradley, Sato and Picard (2003, JASA) found that early reflections within about 50 ms help intelligibility about as much as the direct sound.
sources.two_mic_reality: Predicts relative intelligibility, not absolute word scores. The output is mono, so binaural spatial release from masking is ignored. Validity under strong nonlinear processing is partial: Tang, Cooke and Valentini-Botinhao (2016, Computer Speech & Language 35:73-92) found that objective intelligibility metrics lose predictive power on modified and synthetic speech, which is one reason not to use TTS sources. Needs at least a few seconds of speech per score.
sources.implementation: pystoi 0.4.1: pure-Python wheel of 8 KB, needs numpy and scipy, validated against Taal's MATLAB code to 1e-3. Works on Python 3.12-3.14.

sources.title: DNSMOS P.835: A non-intrusive perceptual objective speech quality metric to evaluate noise suppressors
sources.authors: Chandan K. A. Reddy, Vishak Gopal, Ross Cutler
sources.venue: IEEE ICASSP 2022; arXiv:2110.01763
sources.key_idea: Reference-free CNN trained on ITU-T P.835 crowdsourced ratings. It predicts SIG (speech distortion), BAK (background intrusiveness) and OVRL (overall), with reported Pearson correlations of 0.94 (SIG) and 0.98 (BAK, OVRL) against human ratings. It also works on real device recordings, where no clean reference exists.
sources.algorithm: Input is 16 kHz mono. Slide 9.01 s windows with a 1 s hop; shorter clips are tiled. Feed the raw float32 waveform (shape 1 x 144160) to sig_bak_ovr.onnx. Map the raw outputs with these polynomials: OVRL = poly([-0.06766283, 1.11546468, 0.04602535]); SIG = poly([-0.08397278, 1.22083953, 0.0052439]); BAK = poly([-0.13166888, 1.60915514, -0.39604546]). Average over windows. The P.808 model (model_v8.onnx) needs a 120-band mel spectrogram (n_fft 321, hop 160). A roughly 50-line onnxruntime + numpy wrapper avoids librosa and pandas. A 'personalized' P.835 model (pDNSMOS) is also in the repo; it is linked to the personalized-DNS challenge track, whose raters were told to treat interfering talkers as undesirable.
sources.bus_relevance: BAK tracks residual engine and babble annoyance; SIG tracks damage to the two talkers. The standard model may score leaked babble speech as 'speech', so cross-check with component SIR and leakage, and try pDNSMOS as a leakage-aware variant (that it behaves this way is unverified).
sources.meeting_relevance: Scores each talker's turns, and later real recordings, without a reference. Low SIG on far seats flags reverberation or over-processing.
sources.two_mic_reality: A single-channel output metric that does not know which talker is present, so it cannot verify 'only the two targets' or 'all 20 captured'. Needs windows of at least 9 s, so concatenate a talker's turns.
sources.implementation: Models from github.com/microsoft/DNS-Challenge (DNSMOS folder): sig_bak_ovr.onnx is 1,157,965 bytes and model_v8.onnx 224,860 bytes. onnxruntime 1.31.1 (2026-10-26) has macOS arm64 wheels for cp311-cp314, about 20.9 MB. Skip the 'speechmos' wrapper (2023, 9.4 MB; its README requires librosa).

sources.title: A method to measure the effect of noise reduction algorithms using simultaneous speech and noise
sources.authors: Bjorn Hagerman, Ake Olofsson (multi-signal extension: H. Husstedt, A. Mertins, M. Frenz, Trends in Hearing 22, 2018, DOI 10.1177/2331216518803198)
sources.venue: Acta Acustica united with Acustica 90(2):356-361
sources.key_idea: The hearing-aid industry's phase-inversion method. Process speech plus noise twice, inverting the noise polarity the second time. The sum and difference of the two outputs separate the output speech from the output noise, which gives the true output SNR of any black-box processor, including nonlinear and adaptive ones. Hagerman and Olofsson measured up to about 4 dB of hearing-aid noise reduction: more effective at positive SNR, almost useless at negative SNR.
sources.algorithm: y+ = F(s+n) and y- = F(s-n), with identical initial state and seeds. s_out = (y+ + y-)/2; n_out = (y+ - y-)/2; SNR_out = 10*log10(sum s_out^2 / sum n_out^2) over target-active frames; dSNR = SNR_out - SNR_in(micA). With K components (targets, near babble, diffuse babble, engine), apply sign patterns a_k in {+1, -1} to the components and solve a linear system for each output component (Husstedt 2018); a full Hadamard design needs 2^(K-1) runs, e.g. 4 runs for 3 components. Sanity check: y+ - s_out - n_out should be close to 0. Validity drops when the processor depends on signal polarity, e.g. fast compression or unstable adaptive filters.
sources.bus_relevance: Measures babble leakage and target preservation for any candidate, including small ONNX denoisers or nonlinear post-filters whose internal gains cannot be logged.
sources.meeting_relevance: Measures per-talker output SNR and the side effects of AGC or compression when the processing is a black box.
sources.two_mic_reality: Works on 2-channel input: invert the noise component in both channels. For your own linear time-varying algorithms, exact 'shadow filtering' is better: apply the logged beamformer weights and gains to each premix component. Use Hagerman only for black boxes.
sources.implementation: Implement in numpy (about 20 lines) on top of the pyroomacoustics premix components.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams Audio Test Specification V5.0 incl. Addendum A, as implemented in the HEAD acoustics ACQUA 'MS Teams' test suite (Code 60026)
sources.authors: Microsoft (specification); HEAD acoustics GmbH (test-suite data sheet)
sources.venue: Industry certification test specification; vendor data sheet Code 60026 Rev. 10 (05/2026)
sources.key_idea: How the conferencing industry certifies pickup. Devices are tested in an anechoic room, then in a specified reverberant room with simulated background noise. Shared-space speakerphone tests include send 'signal level with normal speech' and 'signal level with quiet speech', idle- and active-channel speech-to-noise ratio (SpNR), SDNR, frequency response, 3QUEST S-/N-MOS under various background-noise types, and 'speech level' and 'speech quality' for alternating near-end talkers. The open-office headset module measures 'distractor attenuation (average and minimum)'. The spec builds on ITU-T P.502 and ETSI TS 103 106.
sources.algorithm: Mirror these as simulation acceptance tests. (1) Alternating-talker level test: turns alternating near (1 m), far (6 m) and quiet-voice (-8 dB) talkers with 0.5 s gaps. Measure each turn's active speech level, including the first 1-2 s to expose AGC convergence, with ITU-T P.56 method B (official ANSI-C sv56 in the ITU-T G.191 STL at github.com/openitu/STL, CMake build) or BS.1770-4 via pyloudnorm. Metrics: max-min level across talkers and per-turn settling time. (2) Idle- and active-channel SpNR: output noise level in pauses relative to speech level, which also detects noise pumping. (3) Distractor attenuation: output-minus-input level of a babble or talker distractor, average and minimum over 1 s windows (bus). (4) Quality in background noise: use DNSMOS P.835 SIG/BAK/OVRL as the open stand-in for 3QUEST S-/N-/G-MOS.
sources.bus_relevance: 'Distractor attenuation (average and minimum)' is exactly the 'only the two talkers audible' requirement, and the quality-in-background-noise tests mirror the bus condition.
sources.meeting_relevance: 'Speech level/quality for alternating near-end talkers' and 'signal level with quiet speech' map directly onto 'capture all 20 people at even loudness'. Conferencing devices are tested at mouth-to-mic distances above 1 m (personal speakerphones at 1 m or less).
sources.two_mic_reality: The data sheet does not publish the numeric pass limits (the spec comes through Microsoft certification), so reuse the test structure and set your own targets, e.g. at most 6 dB max-min across seats. The physical tests need a head-and-torso simulator with artificial mouth; in simulation, use source directivity and calibrated SPL instead.
sources.implementation: No open code; replicate in Python. Level meters: pyloudnorm 0.2.0 (pure-Python, 11 KB, BS.1770-4), or compile the ITU G.191 STL sv56 (ITU-T GPL license).

sources.title: An analysis of environment, microphone and data simulation mismatches in robust speech recognition
sources.authors: Emmanuel Vincent, Shinji Watanabe, Aditya Arie Nugraha, Jon Barker, Ricard Marxer
sources.venue: Computer Speech & Language 46:535-557 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2016.11.005)
sources.key_idea: Uses CHiME-3, which has real and simulated noisy speech for a 6-mic tablet in bus, cafe, pedestrian and street environments. Most enhancement and ASR methods performed consistently on real and simulated data, except MVDR beamforming. The number of microphones had a significant effect, which motivated CHiME-4's 1- and 2-mic tracks.
sources.algorithm: Lessons for the protocol: (1) Simulated scenes are valid for ranking most algorithms, but steering-vector beamformers (MVDR/GEV) can look better in simulation, where relative transfer functions match the model exactly. Add model errors (+/-1 dB gains, +/-2 mm geometry, unknown 2.5-6 cm spacing, talker movement, a possible inter-channel sub-sample offset) and confirm on real data. (2) For the field check, record each source separately with the ESP32 device (loudspeaker-played speech at each seat, then the noise alone) and add them digitally, so the real-acoustics components are known exactly. (3) Report 2-mic results on their own; gains measured with more mics do not transfer.
sources.bus_relevance: CHiME-3 BUS is the closest published benchmark of real bus noise on a mic array. A later beamforming study (arXiv:1903.09341) reports higher WER on real BUS than on simulated BUS, so validate bus results on real noise (DEMAND TBUS).
sources.meeting_relevance: Supports developing in simulated meeting rooms, but MVDR-style far-talker gains need confirmation in a real room (ACE or your own recordings).
sources.two_mic_reality: Warns directly that fewer mics bring much less benefit and that simulation can overstate MVDR. With 2 closely spaced mics, robustness to steering errors matters more than optimal-noise performance.
sources.implementation: Paper only. CHiME-3/4 data is too large for 4.8 GB of disk; use DEMAND and ACE instead.

sweep.takeaways:
BOTTOM LINE: build one deterministic "digital twin" harness and score every algorithm on component-wise ("shadow") outputs. DNSMOS or PESQ alone cannot show whether only the two bus talkers remain, or whether all 20 meeting talkers come through evenly.

RANKED BUILD ORDER (both test cases)

(1) Scene generator.
- pyroomacoustics 0.10.1 ShoeBox with use_rand_ism=True, air_absorption=True, cardioid source directivity, and simulate(return_premix=True) to keep every source's image at each mic.
- Device model: 2 omni mics at d in {2.5, 4, 6} cm with random yaw. Add INMP441 self-noise of about 33 dBA SPL (94 - 61 dB SNR), independent per mic, plus a random per-mic gain of up to +/-1 dB and about 2 mm of position error.
- Calibrate 0 dBFS = 120 dB SPL (from -26 dBFS at 94 dB SPL). Then 75 dBA bus noise is about -45 dBFS, a 60 dBA talker about -60 dBFS, and self-noise about -87 dBFS.
- Always also run each algorithm with a deliberately wrong spacing assumption (assume 4 cm while the truth is 2.5 or 6 cm), because the real spacing is uncertain.
- Hardware check to verify: put a source at broadside and confirm TDOA = 0. This would catch any fixed sub-sample offset between the I2S left and right slots, which would bias the 2.3–4 cm spacing estimate.
- Regenerate scenes from stored seeds instead of caching premix arrays: about 1,000 scenes of premix would exceed 4.8 GB.

(2) Real noise and real speech.
- Noise: DEMAND at 16 kHz — TBUS (bus), PCAFETER (crowd), OMEETING and OOFFICE (meeting). Adjacent mics are 5 cm apart.
- First measure the TBUS 5 cm coherence and compare it with the sinc (spherical) and J0 (cylindrical) models to pick the diffuse model. For other spacings, regenerate with anf-generator (Habets 2008 / Mirabilii 2021) using non-overlapping segments as the independent inputs.
- Speech: LibriSpeech test-clean (346 MB, 40 speakers, 20 F / 20 M, CC BY 4.0), not TTS. TTS lacks Lombard effort, natural variability and turn-taking, and Tang et al. (2016) found objective intelligibility metrics lose predictive power on synthetic or modified speech.
- Vary the number of babble talkers (e.g., 4/8/16/32); Krishnamurthy & Hansen (2009) model babble as depending on talker count.

(3) Metric harness.
- Shadow-filter every component. This is exact for beamformer-plus-gain pipelines; log the weights and gains and apply them to each premix component.
- For black-box (e.g., ONNX) stages, use Hagerman phase inversion, or Husstedt's linear-system extension for more than two components.
- Metrics: SI-SDRi, ESTOI (plus STOI), PESQ-WB, DNSMOS P.835 via your own onnxruntime wrapper, and P.56 or BS.1770 output levels.
- Reference for all intrusive metrics: the direct path plus 50 ms of early reflections at mic A. Time-align before scoring.
- Statistics: at least 20 seeds per cell; paired bootstrap 95% CIs and Wilcoxon tests against unprocessed mic A and against a 2-mic delay-and-sum baseline.
- Summarize each SNR sweep as an "intelligibility-equivalent SNR gain": the horizontal shift between the processed and unprocessed ESTOI-vs-input-SNR curves.

(4) Sim-to-real checks.
- The ACE Chromebook data has real 2-channel RIRs and fan/babble noise: Meeting Rooms T60 about 0.37–0.44 s, Lecture Room 2 about 1.25 s.
- Then one ESP32 session: play each LibriSpeech source alone from each position, record the noise alone, and mix digitally. This gives exact real-acoustics components.
- Vincent et al. (2017) found that most methods transfer from simulated to real data, but MVDR does not. Treat MVDR/GEV gains from simulation as optimistic until confirmed.

CASE 1 — BUS TEST MATRIX

Scene:
- Cabin about 12 x 2.5 x 2.3 m. Sweep RT60 at 0.3 and 0.5 s; I found no published bus RT60.
- Background at 70/75/80 dBA. Neitzel et al. (2009) measured an in-bus Leq of 75.3 +/- 2.6 dBA, with Lmax up to 96.8 dBA.
- Background components: 4–8 nearby point-source talkers at 1.5–5 m, diffuse crowd babble of 20–40 talkers, and DEMAND TBUS engine/road noise. Sweep the babble-to-engine ratio over -5/0/+5 dB.
- Targets at 0.3/0.6/1.0 m, facing each other, with Lombard-raised levels: L_s(1 m) = 55 + 0.6 (L_n - 45) (Pearsons, via Wu et al. 2018).
- At 75 dBA this gives a direct-path SNR from about -2 dB (1 m) to +8.5 dB (0.3 m), so sweep the input SNR at mic A over {-5, 0, +5, +10} dB.

Primary metrics:
- ΔSIR versus babble.
- Babble leakage / "distractor attenuation", average and minimum over 1 s windows (the Microsoft Teams test structure).
- Per-target level change: both talkers within +/-2 dB of each other, so neither is suppressed.
- SI-SDR of the target component (distortion).
- ΔESTOI, plus babble talkers' ESTOI, which should fall.
- A pickup-versus-distance map from a probe talker at 0.3–5 m. Proposed target: at least 10 dB between 0.5 m and 2 m or more.

What to expect with 2 omni mics:
- The MVDR bound I computed with the diffuse-coherence model in endfire geometry is about 5.5–6 dB below 2 kHz when bus noise is about 40 dB above self-noise. A plausible ±1 dB mic mismatch, which acts like noise only about 20 dB down, cuts that to about 2–4 dB at 250–500 Hz.
- Broadside geometry gives only about 0–1 dB below 2 kHz.
- First-order patterns: cardioid and figure-8 4.8 dB, hypercardioid 6.0 dB.
- Orient the mic axis along the talker–talker line: a figure-8 or dual beam keeps both talkers.
- Single-channel post-filters add SNR but little intelligibility at negative SNR (Hagerman & Olofsson: at most about 4 dB, nearly useless below 0 dB).
- Level cues for near-vs-far are weak: about 1.1 dB inter-mic level difference at 0.3 m with 4 cm endfire. So test CDR-based (Schwarz & Kellermann 2015) or DOA-mask post-filters and measure their distortion.
- Realistic goal (my engineering estimate, not sourced): ΔSIR about 5–10 dB and ΔESTOI about +0.05–0.15 at 0 dB input SNR. Babble will not become inaudible at -5 dB.

CASE 2 — 20-PERSON MEETING TEST MATRIX

Scene:
- Rooms 8–12 x 5–8 x 2.7–3.2 m, RT60 0.5/0.7/0.9 s. Device on the table at 0.75 m.
- 20 seats at 1–6 m, mouth height 1.2 m, head yaw within ±45°.
- Per-talker effort drawn from N(60, 3) dBA at 1 m, plus soft talkers at 52–55 dBA.
- Noise: HVAC at NC 25–35 (about 35–45 dBA; secondary sources quote ASHRAE NC 25–30 for conference rooms), a projector fan as a point source, DEMAND OMEETING, and 33 dBA self-noise.

Physics:
- For 210 m³ at T60 0.7 s, the critical distance is about 1.0 m. DRR is about -6 dB at 2 m and -15.7 dB at 6 m.
- Yet total received level falls only about 2.8 dB from 1 m to 6 m.
- So uneven loudness comes mainly from vocal effort and AGC behaviour, and low intelligibility mainly from DRR.

Metrics:
- Per-talker ESTOI and SI-SDR against the early reference.
- Spread of per-talker P.56 output level. Proposed target: at most 6 dB max–min.
- Worst-talker ESTOI (minimum and 10th percentile).
- Alternating near/far/quiet turns to measure AGC settling and noise pumping.
- DNSMOS per talker (windows of 9 s or more).

Expectations:
- In a quiet room the noise is only about 5 dB above INMP441 self-noise. Here the computed MVDR bound gives only about 1–3 dB at 1 kHz and below, so aggressive beamforming buys little.
- Prioritize per-talker AGC/levelling plus 2-mic dereverberation (CDR/WPE), and expect only modest far-seat ESTOI gains.
- Spacing: 6 cm beats 2.5 cm at low frequencies (computed MVDR 1.0/2.1/3.7 dB vs 0.6/0.9/1.7 dB at 250/500/1000 Hz), at the cost of spatial aliasing above about 2.9 kHz. Recommend testing all three spacings and measuring the real one with calipers.

SMALL-DISK TOOLCHAIN (checked on PyPI/GitHub; works on Python 3.12–3.14)

Packages:
